- ⚙️ [Configure](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/) rule selection, contracts, and the Python version.
- 📏 Browse the [35 rules](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/).
- 🔧 Read how [fixes are proven safe](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/).
- 🪜 [Adopt it gradually](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/) with a Ratchet baseline in CI.
- 🖥️ Use it from [your editor](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/lsp/) or 🤖 [a coding agent](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/).

## 📛 Name

*heki* is 壁, "wall", in its Sino-Japanese (*on*) reading, the one used in compounds such as
防火壁 (*bōkaheki*, "firewall"). On its own the character is usually read *kabe*.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/

# Scope and Limitations

This page says what heki checks, what it leaves to other tools, where its knowledge comes from,
and what it does when it cannot tell.

## Where heki fits

| Tool | Looks at | Example |
| ---- | -------- | ------- |
| A linter such as [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) | Syntax and style, one file at a time | `time.sleep()` written directly in an `async def`; a discarded `asyncio.create_task(...)` |
| A type checker such as [ty](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty) | Whether values match their declared types | a `str` passed where an `int` is expected |
| An import-graph checker such as [tach](https://github.com/gauge-sh/tach) or [import-linter](https://github.com/seddonym/import-linter) | Which modules may import which | `app.api` importing `app.db` when the declared layers forbid it |
| heki | What code does, not what types it has: effects and aliases, through any number of calls | an `async def` that reaches `requests.get` three helpers away; a model field written outside the store that owns it; an attribute `__hash__` reads changing after the object went into a `set` |

The difference is the model, not reaching across files: heki models effects and aliases, and
leaves syntax, types, and imports to the tools that model them, also as they grow. Where another
tool covers part of a case, heki keeps the rest: Ruff's `RUF006` reports discarded tasks, so
`EFF107` reports only the tasks bound to a variable.

### Clean for Ruff, ty, and tach; broken all the same

```python
# app/clients.py
import requests


def fetch_json(url: str) -> dict:
    return requests.get(url, timeout=5).json()


# app/users.py
from app.clients import fetch_json


def load_profile(user_id: int) -> dict:
    return fetch_json(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}")


def load_user(user_id: int) -> dict:
    return {"id": user_id, **load_profile(user_id)}


# app/api.py
from app.users import load_user


async def handler(user_id: int) -> dict:
    return load_user(user_id)  # blocks the event loop three calls down
```

```python
# app/models.py: only `Store.*` may write `Model.fields` (a write-owners contract)
class Model:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.fields: list[str] = []


class Store:
    def add_field(self, model: Model, name: str) -> None:
        model.fields.append(name)


def add_default(fields: list[str]) -> None:
    fields.append("id")


def parse(model: Model) -> None:
    fields = model.fields
    add_default(fields)  # changes `Model.fields` behind the store's back
```

```toml
[[tool.heki.write-owners]]
name = "model-store"
targets = ["Model.fields"]
allowed-writers = ["Store.*"]
```

Each of these passes, because each tool sees one step:

| Command | Sees | Does not see |
| ------- | ---- | ------------ |
| `ruff check --select ASYNC,B,RUF,PERF,PL,SIM,FURB,S` | `requests.get` only when it is written in the `async def` itself | the call three helpers down |
| `ty check` | a `list[str]` passed where a `list[str]` is expected | that `add_default` changes `Model.fields` |
| `tach check` (with `app.api` → `app.users` → `app.clients` declared) | `app.api` importing `app.users`, which is allowed | what `load_user` does |

heki follows the call into `load_user` and the alias into `add_default`:

```console
$ heki check --output-format concise
app/api.py:5:12: EFF101 `handler` reaches the blocking call `requests.get` on the event loop
app/models.py:17:5: MUT201 `parse` writes `Model.fields` (indirect_helper) via `app.models.add_default` outside the write owners of `model-store`
Found 2 diagnostic(s) in 4 file(s).
```

## Where heki pays off

| Code | What heki finds |
| ---- | --------------- |
| Async services, and web or database code written in layers of helpers | blocking calls that reach the event loop, clients and queries created inside loops (N+1), I/O while a lock or a transaction is held |
| Large code bases that protect shared state by convention, review, or their own checkers | contract violations, followed through aliases, helpers, and subclasses |
| Loops over growing collections | proven-safe rewrites and suggestions for quadratic patterns |

In small scripts, or code that is mostly synchronous and self-contained, a linter and a type
checker cover most of what matters, and heki reports little.

## What heki does not do

| Check | Use instead |
| ----- | ----------- |
| Style, formatting, and syntax | a linter such as Ruff |
| Type errors | a type checker such as ty |
| Import layering and import cycles | [tach](https://github.com/gauge-sh/tach) or [import-linter](https://github.com/seddonym/import-linter), and Python 3.15's `lazy import` |
| Dead code and duplicated code | Ruff or [vulture](https://github.com/jendrikseipp/vulture) |
| Constant-factor micro-optimizations, such as hoisting `re.compile` | no heki rule |

- heki does not change your code's shape: it adds no decorators, contract types, or runtime
  checks, and it does not compile or rewrite code at build time.
- heki never runs or instruments your program. `--profile` only reads a profile you recorded
  yourself.

## Where heki's knowledge comes from

| Source | What it tells heki | Extend it with |
| ------ | ------------------ | -------------- |
| Its own analysis | an SSA form of every function; aliases (copies, attributes, and the iterators and views derived from an object); what each function mutates and which effects it reaches, propagated over the project's call graph until nothing changes | - |
| A catalog of library behavior | `requests.get` blocks on the network; `asyncio.to_thread(fn)` and `@sync_to_async` run a function on another thread; `logging` calls are never reported; `sqlite3.connect()` returns a `Connection`; `threading.Lock` is a synchronous lock | [`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#ecosystem-knowledge-toolhekiecosystem) |
| Contracts you declare | who may write, read, or call (`write-owners`, `read-owners`, `call-owners`); which returned objects are shared (`readonly-returns`); which changes must be announced (`invalidation`); which functions must not reach I/O or writes (`effect-boundaries`) | [contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) in the configuration |
| Type annotations, as hints only | which class an object has and which method a call reaches: `session: Session` makes `session.execute(...)` a database call | annotations in your code |

- heki does not analyze the source of the standard library or of installed packages: the
  catalog declares their effects.
- Contracts need no decorators, no special types, and nothing at run time.
- The checking rules (`MUT`, `EFF`, `DATA`, `OPT112`, `OPT113`) use annotations. The rewriting
  rules never read them, because a subclass can override any method (see
  [Fixes and Safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/#what-a-fix-must-prove)).

### How a call is resolved

heki looks for the callee in this order:

1. local constructors and imports;
2. annotations;
3. attributes assigned in `__init__`;
4. the class hierarchy, up to eight overriding methods.

It also follows container item types (`list[Model]`), return annotations along the MRO,
`isinstance` narrowing, unions of up to three classes, and project `Protocol`s.

## When heki cannot tell

The two kinds of rules make opposite choices when information is missing:

| | A rewrite (`OPT` fix) | A report (checking rules) |
| - | --------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Needs | a proof | evidence |
| What heki cannot see | counts as shared and blocks the fix | is not followed |
| What you get | the diagnostic names the failed obligation: `[not auto-fixable: ...]` | no report: a missed finding, never a guess |

A report that crosses functions shows its call chain as related locations. A call heki cannot
resolve is not followed:

- a value of type `Any`, or an unannotated parameter;
- a method name computed at run time;
- a call with more than eight possible overrides;
- a function outside the checked files that the catalog does not list.

Two more cases stay quiet by design:

- A branch the caller's arguments switch off is not followed: `load(name, cache=False)` does not
  reach the request under `if cache:`.
- A client or query created only while an attribute is unset counts once per object, not once
  per loop iteration, and so does a `functools.cached_property` getter; one created only while
  a module global or a local variable the loop carries is unset (or a first-iteration flag
  holds), or right before the loop ends (`break`, `return`, `raise`), counts once per loop.
- A blocking wait on a `concurrent.futures.Future` known to be done (`if f.done():`, after
  `await asyncio.wrap_future(f)`) returns at once.

A function whose model would pass its size budget (4 units per byte of its source, at most
50,000; real code stays below one unit per byte) is left unmodeled: heki rewrites nothing in it
and treats its body as one call it cannot resolve. `heki assumptions` lists it with the hazard
`unmodeled`. A function whose proof state (a fact per variable per block) would pass 8 cells per
byte of its source, at most 250,000, gets no `OPT` finding: heki does not try to prove a rewrite
in it. A function whose lazy initializations (the blocks each covers, and the walks that find
them) would take more than 8 cells per byte of its source, at most 250,000, has none of them
recognized: its clients and queries count as made on every iteration.

Missed findings close as heki learns more:

| heki lacks | Add |
| ---------- | --- |
| the class of a value | an annotation |
| your blocking or offloading APIs | an entry in [`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#ecosystem-knowledge-toolhekiecosystem) |
| the rules of your shared state | a [contract](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) |

## Known limitations

### Dynamic names

`setattr(obj, "fields", v)`, `getattr(obj, "fields")`, `getattr(obj, "method")(...)`, and
`obj.__dict__["fields"]`:

- **Followed** when the name is a constant: a literal, a module-level `Final` string
  (`KEY: Final = "_key"`), also when imported, re-exported, or bound to another `Final` name, a
  module-level string bound once in its module, or a class constant declared `ClassVar` or
  `Final` and bound once (`Model.KEY`, `self.KEY`, `cls.KEY`).
- **Not followed** for a module-level name without `Final` that another module rebinds or deletes,
  one bound in a loop or before a star import that may rebind it, a class constant stored on its
  class or an instance outside the class body (`Model.KEY = "x"`; from another module, only one
  without `Final`), a class constant a subclass defines again, is given its own value
  (`Child.KEY = "x"`), or inherits first from another base it lists before the class
  (`class Child(Other, Model)`; read on that subclass, or on an instance or `cls` that may be one),
  a `Final` field of a dataclass or of a class a `dataclass_transform` builds read on an instance
  (`Keys("x").KEY` is `"x"`), or on a class object whose default a class with `slots=True` or built
  by a transform replaces, or a computed name.
- A `write-owners` contract with `unresolved = "report"` reports the writes heki cannot tie to a
  class ([`MUT205`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/)).

### Objects without a known class

- Reads and writes through `Any` or unannotated parameters are not tied to a class, so contracts
  on that class do not see them. A contract with `unresolved = "report"` reports them by name:
  writes under [`MUT205`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/), reads under
  [`MUT206`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-read/), and method calls under
  [`MUT207`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-call/).
- A write in an unannotated helper is still found where a caller passes it an object of a known
  class. A read is not.
- Not typed: values declared `Any`, generics substituted through `TypeVar`s, and calls of
  `type[C]` attributes.

### Names the catalog does not list

Catalog lookups are exact. These contribute no effect until you add them with
[`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#ecosystem-knowledge-toolhekiecosystem):

- a class reached through another public name: `from sqlalchemy import Engine` for
  `sqlalchemy.engine.Engine`, `redis.StrictRedis` for `redis.Redis`;
- a method the catalog does not list;
- objects reached through subscripts or framework attributes, which have no known class:
  `client["app"]["users"]`, Django's `Model.objects`.

### Properties

- **Followed:** reading a `@property` or `functools.cached_property` of a project class runs its
  getter. Its effects, writes, and the attributes it reads count for the reader, also through
  base classes, overriding subclasses, and `super()`. The getter's return annotation types the
  value read.
- **Not followed:** a property that also defines a setter or deleter (`@x.setter`), and
  `x = property(get_x)`.

### Read-only types

- `MUT110` follows `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `ReadOnly` parameters into the helpers they are
  handed to, any number of calls deep. A helper parameter annotated with a mutable type is left
  to the type checker, and a container inside the argument does not count.
- `MUT108` (opt-in) follows frozen dataclasses, `NamedTuple`s, classes that a
  `dataclass_transform(frozen_default=True)` in the checked files builds, `Final` / `ReadOnly`
  attributes, and `ReadOnly` `TypedDict` keys. It does not see the transforms of installed
  packages (attrs, Pydantic), and an instance the function constructs itself counts as under
  construction.

### Generators and coroutines

A generator's body runs where it is iterated:

| Followed | Not followed |
| -------- | ------------ |
| a `for` loop or a comprehension | a generator handed to anything else: `StreamingResponse(rows())`, a container |
| unpacking, `yield from` | a generator only stepped with `next()` |
| a consuming call: `list(...)`, `"".join(...)`, `items.extend(...)` | a generator unpacked into a call: `f(*rows())` |
| a lazy wrapper iterated there: `enumerate(...)` | |
| a project function iterating it | |

- A generator a function returns runs where its caller iterates it.
- A generator expression counts where it is written.
- A coroutine runs where it is awaited; one only scheduled (`asyncio.create_task`) is checked on
  its own.
- Iterating an object runs its class's `__iter__` only for classes the catalog lists (a
  SQLAlchemy `Query`). The `__iter__` methods of project classes are not followed.

### Guards

- **Followed:** a test of the function's own input: truthiness, `is None`, `isinstance` with
  builtin classes, the `io` classes, or `os.PathLike`, or `hasattr` with a string literal, also
  after the function rebinds the input on some paths (`if buf is None: buf = StringIO()`).
- **Decided by:** constants, displays and comprehensions, `io.StringIO` / `io.BytesIO` objects
  the caller constructs, and the literal defaults of omitted parameters (`hasattr` only for the
  methods of the file protocol: `read`, `write`, `close`, ...); not by an f-string, the result of
  another call, or an instance of a subclass.
- **Not followed:** `a or b` (no guard on either value), and `isinstance` with project classes or
  annotated types.
- A lazy initialization needs a direct test and the store in the function itself: a test in a
  caller of the method that stores, a test combined with `or` / `and`, and memos keyed by an
  argument (`@lru_cache`, a dict) are not followed.
- A future is known to be done only through `f.done()` and `await asyncio.wrap_future(f)`, not
  through an event or another future its done callback sets.
- `EFF201` does not use guards.
- An object a factory function returns counts as obtained once, like a pooled connection.

### Separate scopes

- Generator expressions and lambdas are analyzed as functions of their own:
  `next(b for b in bs if b.id == a.id)` inside a loop is not reported as a nested-loop join.
- Two lambdas in one function share the qualified name `f.<locals>.<lambda>`, so heki may
  attribute one lambda's effects to a call of the other:

```python
import requests


async def handler(url: str) -> int:
    fetch = lambda: requests.get(url, timeout=5)
    size = lambda: len(url)
    return size()  # reported as reaching `requests.get` (EFF101)
```

### Metaprogramming and frameworks

`__getattr__` proxies, metaclasses, classes created at run time, and framework machinery
(validators, ORM lazy loading, dependency injection) are not modeled. heki has no
framework-specific rules.

### The target Python version

Results follow [`target-version`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#top-level-settings), which defaults to the
oldest version `requires-python` admits.

- From Python 3.12, list, set, and dict comprehensions run in the enclosing function (PEP 709): a
  comprehension inside a loop can be reported for `py312` and not for `py311`.
- From Python 3.14, annotations are evaluated lazily in `__annotate__` scopes (PEP 649).
- The parser reads Python 3.15 syntax for every target version: `lazy import` (PEP 810) is a lazy
  import also in code for an older version.
- Syntax newer than the target version is analyzed, not reported: that is Ruff's check.

### Source encodings

heki reads the encoding a PEP 263 declaration names: UTF-8 (with or without a BOM), Latin-1, and
ASCII. A file declaring any other encoding is reported as an error and not checked.

### Sizes known only at run time

Whether a collection is small is decided from the code: a list whose size depends on the
input counts as large, even when it always holds three items. The rules this affects are marked size-dependent;
[Fixes and Safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/#when-the-size-is-fixed) lists what counts as a fixed size.

### Callers outside the checked files

Contracts reason about the callers heki sees: a private helper hands its reports to its callers,
and a function called only from allowed writers is not reported. Code outside the run, such as
tests left out of it, is not known.

## How a rule gets into heki

heki only takes checks that need what it can prove. A proposed rule goes through four questions,
in order:

1. **Can the syntax of one file decide it?** Then it belongs in a linter such as Ruff.
2. **Is it a type error, or can an annotation express it?** Then it belongs in a type checker
   such as ty.
3. **Is it about which modules may import which?** Then it belongs in tach or import-linter.
4. **Does it need at least one of the proofs below?** Only then is it a heki rule.

A heki rule is measured on a corpus and reviewed by hand before it is enabled by default. Where
another tool covers part of it, heki keeps only the rest (`EFF107` and Ruff's `RUF006`).

The proofs heki can make, on five axes:

| Axis | What heki establishes | Used by |
| ---- | --------------------- | ------- |
| Control flow | which statements can run after which: CFG paths, loops and their bounds, exception edges | `MUT106`, `MUT109`, `MUT113`, `EFF102`, `EFF103`, `EFF106`, `DATA101`, `OPT` |
| Calls | which functions a call reaches across modules, and what they do (summaries propagated over the call graph) | `EFF101`, `EFF201`, `MUT103`, `MUT108`, `MUT109`, `MUT110`, `MUT112`, `MUT113`, `MUT201`–`MUT204` |
| Aliases | which names, iterators, and views refer to one object; whether it is unique to its frame and of an exact builtin type | `MUT202`, `MUT201`, `MUT204`, `MUT108`, `MUT110`, `MUT112`, `EFF107`, `OPT101`–`OPT130` |
| Effects | which blocking, network, file, or database work runs, from the catalog of library behavior | `EFF101`–`EFF106`, `EFF201`, `DATA101` |
| State | which attributes and containers a function reads, writes, or mutates, and who may do so | `MUT101`, `MUT107`, `MUT108`, `MUT109`, `MUT110`, `MUT111`, `MUT112`, `MUT113`, `MUT201`–`MUT204` |


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/installation/

# Installation

heki is a single executable: its Python package ships only that executable and installs no
Python dependencies into your environment.

## With uv, pipx, or pip

=== "uv"

    ```console
    $ uv tool install heki
    $ uvx heki check            # or run it without installing
    ```

=== "pipx"

    ```console
    $ pipx install heki
    ```

=== "pip"

    ```console
    $ pip install heki
    ```

As a development dependency of a project:

```console
$ uv add --dev heki
```

Wheels are published for these platforms:

| OS | Architectures |
| -- | ------------- |
| Linux | x86-64, AArch64, x86-64 musl |
| macOS | Apple silicon, Intel |
| Windows | x86-64 |

## From source

heki needs Rust 1.99 or newer:

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki
$ cd heki
$ cargo install --path crates/heki
```

## Check the installation

```console
$ heki --version
$ heki rule --all
```

## Supported Python versions

- heki analyzes code written for Python 3.11 to 3.15.
- It does not need a Python interpreter to run.
- The version of the checked code comes from
  [`target-version`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#top-level-settings), or from `requires-python`; see
  [Scope](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#the-target-python-version) for what it changes.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/getting-started/

# Getting Started

This page runs heki on a project, reads a diagnostic, applies a fix, and picks the rules.

## Run it

From the root of a project (the directory with `pyproject.toml`):

```console
$ heki check
```

heki checks every Python file under the current directory, except the
[excluded and ignored ones](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#which-files-are-checked). Pass files or directories
to narrow it:

```console
$ heki check src/ tests/test_api.py
```

## Read a diagnostic

```console
app/api.py:5:12: EFF101 (async-blocking-call) [error] `handler` reaches the blocking call `requests.get` on the event loop
  |
5 |     user = load_user(user_id)
  |            ^
  = related: app/api.py:5:12: `handler` calls `app.users.load_user`
  = related: app/users.py:5:12: `load_user` calls `requests.get`
  = help: offload it with `asyncio.to_thread`, or use an async client
```

| Part | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- |
| `app/api.py:5:12` | where to look |
| `EFF101 (async-blocking-call)` | the rule's code and name |
| `[error]` | its severity: `error`, or `warning` for the `OPT` rules (slower code, not wrong code); both make `heki check` fail |
| the message | what heki proved, in one sentence: here, an `async def` reaches a blocking network call |
| `related` lines | the hops of the chain of calls behind it, to follow it across files; editors show them as related information you can jump to |
| `help` line | what to do about it |

`heki rule EFF101` explains the rule, its exclusions, and what to do instead. The
[rules reference](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/) has the same text for every rule.

## Fix what heki can prove

`--fix` applies the rewrites heki proves safe and always faster (`OPT101`, `OPT102`), and
`--diff` shows them first:

```console
$ heki check --diff
--- a/app/report.py
+++ b/app/report.py
@@ -1,5 +1,5 @@
 def rows_of(items):
     rows = []
     for item in items:
-        rows = rows + [item]
+        rows.append(item)
     return rows
Would fix 1 issue(s) in 1 file(s).
$ heki check --fix
Fixed 1 issue(s) in 1 file(s).
```

`--fix` then reports what is left, such as the `EFF101` above, which has no automatic fix.

When heki cannot prove a fix safe, the help says why and nothing is rewritten. Here the list is
also handed to other code inside the loop:

```console
$ heki check app/shared.py
app/shared.py:4:9: OPT101 (list-quadratic-concat) [warning] `rows = rows + [...]` copies the whole list on every iteration (quadratic)
  |
4 |         rows = rows + [item]
  |         ^
  = help: append in place with `rows.append(...)` / `rows.extend(...)` [not auto-fixable: Unique(rows): it may be shared: passed to code heki cannot see (line 5)]

Found 1 diagnostic(s) in 1 file(s).
```

[Fixes and Safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/) lists which rules are fixed, and what a fix must prove.

## Silence a diagnostic

Append a suppression comment to the reported line:

```python
user = load_user(user_id)  # heki: ignore[EFF101]
```

The other forms (`# heki: ignore`, `# noqa: EFF101`) and `per-file-ignores` are in
[Inline suppressions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#inline-suppressions).

## Choose the rules

```console
$ heki check --select EFF,MUT        # only these families
$ heki check --extend-select EFF105  # add an opt-in rule
$ heki check --ignore OPT110         # everything except one rule
```

Codes, code prefixes, and rule names (`async-blocking-call`) are accepted. A prefix does not
enable the opt-in rules: see [Rule selection](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint).

## Output formats

```console
$ heki check --output-format json
```

| Format | Prints |
| ------ | ------ |
| `full` (default) | each diagnostic with its source line, call chain, and help |
| `concise` | one line per diagnostic: the message, without the help |
| `json` | every field: also the help, the evidence, the blocker that stops a fix, and the fix edits ([fields](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#use-the-cli-in-the-agents-loop)) |
| `github` | GitHub Actions annotations with the message ([CI](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#continuous-integration)) |
| `sarif` | the message, the location, the call chain, and the help (`properties.help`), for code-scanning dashboards (no evidence or blocker) |

Every format, `--diff`, and the errors of files that cannot be read or parsed print a file's
path relative to the working directory when the file is inside it (otherwise as given), as Ruff
does, and with `/` separators on every platform, Windows included.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- |
| `0` | no diagnostics |
| `1` | diagnostics found (or Ratchet regressions, or `--diff` would change files) |
| `2` | configuration error, unreadable file, unknown rule, or syntax error |


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/

# Configuration

heki reads `[tool.heki]` from `pyproject.toml`, or a `heki.toml` / `.heki.toml` file with the same
keys without the `tool.heki` prefix. Keys are kebab-case, as in Ruff.

```toml
[tool.heki]
target-version = "py312"            # default: inferred from project.requires-python
extend-exclude = ["generated"]      # added to the default excludes
baseline = "heki-baseline.toml"     # Ratchet baseline (heki check, --watch, the server)

[tool.heki.lint]
select = ["MUT", "EFF", "DATA", "OPT"]
extend-select = ["EFF105"]
ignore = ["OPT110"]
per-file-ignores = { "tests/**" = ["EFF"], "scripts/*.py" = ["OPT"] }
relax-async-in-tests = true

[tool.heki.lint.severity]
OPT103 = "warning"
```

## Where heki finds the configuration

1. The project root is the nearest directory at or above the first path given (the current
   directory when no path is given) that holds `heki.toml`, `.heki.toml`, `pyproject.toml`, or
   `.git`. When none does, it is the first path's own directory (the directory given, or the
   given file's directory).
2. heki reads the first of `heki.toml`, `.heki.toml`, and `pyproject.toml` in that directory. A
   `pyproject.toml` without `[tool.heki]` still marks the root: its project gets the defaults.
3. `--config <path>` names the file instead. The project root stays where step 1 finds it.

One run checks one project: its configuration applies to every file of the run, also to files
given from another project. `heki check a/one.py b/two.py` uses `a/`'s configuration for both, so
check projects with their own configurations in separate runs: `heki check a/`, then
`heki check b/`.

### Which tables hold the settings

The file's name decides, as Ruff reads `pyproject.toml` and `ruff.toml`:

- A file named `pyproject.toml` holds the settings in `[tool.heki]` (`[tool.heki.lint]`,
  `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`, ...). Its other tables belong to the packaging standards and other
  tools, and heki does not read them.
- Any other file (`heki.toml`, `.heki.toml`, or the file `--config` names, whatever its name)
  holds the same keys at its top level, without the `tool.heki` prefix (`[lint]`,
  `[[ecosystem]]`).

heki never ignores a setting. These are configuration errors (exit code 2):

- an unknown key in any of heki's tables (the message names it: ``unknown field `bogus` ``);
- a `[tool.heki]` table in a file that is not named `pyproject.toml`;
- a heki setting at the top level of a `pyproject.toml` (`[[ecosystem]]` instead of
  `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`).

### Module names follow the project root

Module names are the paths below the project root (`app/api.py` is `app.api`; a `src/` layout
drops `src`). heki resolves the imports between the project's modules by these names, and they
appear in messages that name a function by its full name and in the `target`s of
[baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines) entries, whose `path`s are relative to the root too.
Without a `heki.toml`, `.heki.toml`, or `pyproject.toml` in the project's directory or above it,
the root is the top of the enclosing Git working tree (the directory holding `.git`), so the
names depend on where the project sits in the checkout: in a repository, `services/api/app.py`
is `services.api.app`, and its `from helpers import slow` does not find
`services/api/helpers.py`; the same files checked out on their own are `app` and `helpers`.
Without any of them and outside a Git working tree, `heki check pkg` is rooted inside the
package: its modules are `a` and `b`, not `pkg.a` and `pkg.b`, and `from pkg.b import slow` is
not resolved. Put a `pyproject.toml` or a `heki.toml` in the project's directory to fix the root.

## Top-level settings

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `target-version` | the oldest version `project.requires-python` admits, else `py312` | Python version of the code: `py311` … `py315` (or `3.11` … `3.15`). `--target-version` overrides it. See [below](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#the-default-target-version) for the inference and [Scope](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#the-target-python-version) for what the version changes. |
| `exclude` | the Ruff defaults (`.git`, `.venv`, `build`, `dist`, `node_modules`, …) | Replaces the excluded paths: globs, matched against the project-relative path and each of its components, and covering everything below a matched directory. |
| `extend-exclude` | `[]` | Adds excluded paths. |
| `baseline` | none | Ratchet baseline file, relative to the project root, used when `--baseline` is not given: by `heki check`, `--watch`, and the language server. See [Ratchet baselines](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines). |

### The default target version

Without `target-version`, heki reads `requires-python` from the `pyproject.toml` that holds the
configuration, or from the one next to `heki.toml` or the `--config` file. It takes the oldest
supported version that every clause admits:

| `requires-python` | Target |
| ----------------- | ------ |
| `>=3.11` | `py311` |
| `>=3.11, !=3.11.*` | `py312` |
| `>=3.9, <3.11` (only older versions) | `py311` |
| `>=3.16` (only newer versions) | `py315` |
| `<4` (no lower bound, admits 3.12) | `py312` |
| missing, or not a version specifier | `py312` |

### Which files are checked

- Without paths, `heki check` checks every `.py` and `.pyi` file under the current directory.
- Discovery skips hidden files and directories, the paths `exclude` and `extend-exclude` match,
  and the entries of `.gitignore` (inside a Git repository), `.ignore`, and `.hekiignore` files.
- Files named on the command line are always checked.

## Rule selection: `[tool.heki.lint]`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `select` | every rule except the opt-in ones | Rules to enable instead of the defaults. An empty list enables no rule before `extend-select`, as in Ruff. |
| `extend-select` | `[]` | Rules to add. |
| `ignore` | `[]` | Rules to disable. |
| `per-file-ignores` | `{}` | Glob → rules disabled in matching files (project-relative POSIX paths). As in Ruff, `*` also matches `/`: `scripts/*.py` covers `scripts/tools/worker.py` too. |
| `severity` | `"warning"` for the `OPT` rules, `"error"` for the others | Rule → `"error"` or `"warning"`. It changes the output and the SARIF level; both make `heki check` fail. |
| `relax-async-in-tests` | `true` | Skip `EFF101`, `EFF105`, and `EFF106` in `test_*` functions and in files under `tests/`. |

- A rule is named by its code (`EFF101`), its name (`async-blocking-call`), a code prefix
  (`EFF`, `MUT2`), or `ALL`. An unknown rule is a configuration error.
- A prefix or `ALL` enables only the default rules. The opt-in rules (`EFF105`, `EFF106`,
  `EFF107`, `MUT101`, `MUT103`, `MUT106`, `MUT108`, `MUT111`, `MUT112`, `MUT113`) need their
  exact code or name. In `ignore`, a prefix covers every rule it matches.
- The command line wins: `--select` replaces `select`, and `--extend-select` and `--ignore` add
  to the configured lists.

## Contracts

Contracts declare what no type can say. Each kind is an array of tables with its own rule:

| Contract | Declares | Rule |
| -------- | -------- | ---- |
| [`write-owners`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#write-owners) | who may write an attribute | `MUT201`; `MUT205` with `unresolved = "report"` |
| [`read-owners`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#read-owners) | who may read an attribute | `MUT203`; `MUT206` with `unresolved = "report"` |
| [`call-owners`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#call-owners) | who may call a function or construct a class | `MUT204`; `MUT207` with `unresolved = "report"` |
| [`effect-boundaries`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#effect-boundaries) | what a scope must not reach: I/O, writes, reads, or calls | `EFF201` |
| [`readonly-returns`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#readonly-returns) | results every caller shares | `MUT202` |
| [`invalidation`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#invalidation) | writes that must be announced | `MUT109` |

- These rules report nothing until a contract exists, except `MUT202`, which also protects the
  results of `@lru_cache` / `@cache` functions.
- Every name in a contract is a dotted pattern. It matches the full name or any dotted suffix
  (`DataModel.fields` matches `pkg.model.DataModel.fields`, not `pkg.BigModel.fields`), and it
  may be a glob (`*`, `?`, `[...]`, `{a,b}`).
- A `Class.attr` target covers the subclasses of the class too.
- A contract heki cannot use is a configuration error: a target that is not `Class.attr`, an
  invalid glob, or an unknown value of `forbid`, `fresh-objects`, or `unresolved`.
- With `unresolved = "report"`, a contract also reports the accesses it cannot tie to a class,
  each under its own rule (`MUT205` writes, `MUT206` reads, `MUT207` calls): an attribute or
  method named like a target, accessed on an object of unknown class (an unannotated parameter,
  a loop variable, an untyped call result, `Any`, a protocol whose implementations heki cannot
  list). A baseline counts them apart from the violations the typed rules prove.
- An attribute named through a string (`setattr`, `getattr`, `__dict__`) is followed when the
  string is a constant: see [Dynamic names](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#dynamic-names).

### `write-owners`

```toml
[[tool.heki.write-owners]]
name = "generation-store"
targets = ["pkg.model.DataModel.fields", "DataType.data_types", 'DataModelFieldBase.extras["init"]']
allowed-writers = ["pkg.parser.generation.*", "Store.*"]
exempt-methods = ["__deepcopy__", "copy_deep"]
forbid-cached-property-on = ["DataModel"]
message = "use GenerationStore.set_fields() instead"
fresh-objects = "allow"
unresolved = "report"
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The contract's name in reports. |
| `targets` | `[]` | `Class.attr` attributes, or `Class.attr["key"]` for one entry of the container an attribute holds. |
| `allowed-writers` | `[]` | Functions allowed to write the targets. |
| `forbidden-writers` | `[]` | When set, only writes by these functions are reported: see [Allowed and forbidden functions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#allowed-and-forbidden-functions). |
| `exempt-methods` | `[]` | Construction and copy methods allowed to write the targets. A plain name (`__deepcopy__`) matches any method of that name; a name with a dot or a glob (`DataModel.copy_deep`, `create_*`) is a pattern, as in `allowed-writers`. |
| `forbid-cached-property-on` | `[]` | Classes on which defining a `@cached_property` is itself reported. |
| `message` | none | The help of every report of the contract: where to write instead. |
| `fresh-objects` | `"allow"` | `"allow"` or `"report"`: whether a write that constructs the object it writes is reported. |
| `unresolved` | `"ignore"` | `"ignore"` or `"report"`: whether the writes the contract cannot tie to a class are reported under [`MUT205`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/). |

A container entry (`Class.attr["key"]`):

- matches the writes of that constant key (a literal or a string constant), not a write of the
  whole container or with a computed key;
- is reported once, under the entry, when its container is a target too.

A write into the entries of a target's container (`model.meta["kw"][name] = v`) is a write of
the target.

With `fresh-objects = "allow"`, a write is no violation when it constructs the object it writes:

- the object was allocated in the same call chain: by calling its class, by a copy, or by a
  project function returning a new object;
- nothing can hold it yet: no store, `yield`, closure, or call that may keep it ran before the
  write.

A shallow copy's containers are the original's: only rebinding its attributes constructs it.

With `unresolved = "report"`, `MUT205` reports:

- an attribute named like a target, written on an object of unknown class;
- a computed attribute name (`setattr(obj, name, v)`, `obj.__dict__[name] = v`) written on a
  target class.

### `read-owners`

```toml
[[tool.heki.read-owners]]
name = "reference-children"
targets = ["pkg.reference.Reference.children"]
allowed-readers = ["*GenerationIndex*", "*GenerationStore*"]
exempt-methods = ["__deepcopy__"]
message = "read children through GenerationIndex instead"
unresolved = "report"
```

The read side of `write-owners`. A read is `ref.children`, a read through a local alias,
`getattr(ref, "children")`, or `ref.__dict__["children"]`.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The contract's name in reports. |
| `targets` | `[]` | `Class.attr` attributes. A container entry (`Class.attr["key"]`) is a write target only, and a configuration error here. |
| `allowed-readers` | `[]` | Functions allowed to read the targets. |
| `forbidden-readers` | `[]` | When set, only reads by these functions are reported. |
| `exempt-methods` | `[]` | Methods allowed to read the targets, matched as in `write-owners`. |
| `message` | none | The help of every report of the contract. |
| `unresolved` | `"ignore"` | `"ignore"` or `"report"`: whether the reads of a target's attribute name on an object of unknown class are reported under [`MUT206`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-read/). |

`MUT203` does not see a read through a parameter without a project-class annotation; with
`unresolved = "report"`, `MUT206` reports it unless every caller binds the parameter to an
instance of a project class outside the targets' classes.

### `call-owners`

```toml
[[tool.heki.call-owners]]
name = "reference-mutators"
targets = ["DataType.replace_reference", "pkg.util.reset_cache", "FinalFacts"]
allowed-callers = ["pkg.parser.generation.*"]
exempt-methods = ["__deepcopy__"]
message = "use a GenerationStore operation instead"
unresolved = "report"
```

The call side of `write-owners`.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The contract's name in reports. |
| `targets` | `[]` | Functions, methods, or classes. A `Class.method` target covers the method's overrides in subclasses; a class target means constructing the class or a subclass. |
| `allowed-callers` | `[]` | Functions allowed to call the targets. |
| `forbidden-callers` | `[]` | When set, only calls by these functions are reported. |
| `exempt-methods` | `[]` | Methods allowed to call the targets, matched as in `write-owners`. |
| `message` | none | The help of every report of the contract. |
| `unresolved` | `"ignore"` | `"ignore"` or `"report"`: whether the calls of a method named like a target (its last name) on an object of unknown class are reported under [`MUT207`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-call/). |

- A call is reported only when every function it may call (each candidate in the class
  hierarchy) is a target: `text.replace(...)` on a `str` is never a call of
  `DataType.replace_reference`.
- Bound-method aliases (`replace = dt.replace_reference`) and `getattr(dt, "replace_reference")`
  with a constant name are followed.
- The targets of a contract may call each other: a call of the guarded operation is checked where
  it is made, so what the operation does inside is part of it.

### Allowed and forbidden functions

`allowed-writers`, `allowed-readers`, and `allowed-callers` name the functions a contract
allows. `forbidden-writers`, `forbidden-readers`, and `forbidden-callers` name where it applies
instead, so a layer rule ("the parser must not read `Reference.children`") needs no list of every
other layer:

```toml
[[tool.heki.read-owners]]
name = "parser-reads"
targets = ["Reference.children"]
forbidden-readers = ["pkg.parser.*"]
allowed-readers = ["pkg.parser.index.*"]
```

| `allowed-*` | `forbidden-*` | Reported |
| ----------- | ------------- | -------- |
| unset | unset | every access |
| set | unset | accesses outside the allowed functions |
| unset | set | accesses by the forbidden functions |
| set | set | accesses by the forbidden functions, except the allowed ones |

- An access counts as one by a forbidden function when the function that is reported, a private
  helper it hands the access through, or the function making the access is forbidden.
- `allowed-*` and `exempt-methods` win wherever they apply on that path, as does the rule for
  functions that [only run inside allowed functions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#how-contracts-report).

### `effect-boundaries`

```toml
[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]
name = "pure-render"
scopes = ["*.render", "*.render_module_code", "pkg.domain.*"]
forbid = ["writes-targets", "blocking"]
write-targets = ["DataModel.*", "DataType.*"]
allowed-callees = ["pkg.logging.*"]
message = "render entry points must not mutate model state"

[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]
name = "decisions-read-final-facts"
scopes = ["pkg.model._decisions.*"]
forbid = ["reads-targets", "calls"]
read-targets = ["DataType.is_optional", "DataModel._additional_imports"]
call-targets = ["GenerationStore.*"]

[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]
name = "pass-sort-base-classes"
scopes = ["pkg.parser.passes.sort_base_classes"]
allow-writes = ["DataModel.base_classes"]
write-universe = ["DataModel.*", "DataModelFieldBase.*", "DataType.*"]
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The boundary's name in reports. |
| `scopes` | `[]` | Modules, classes, or functions whose functions must stay inside the boundary; nested functions are included. |
| `forbid` | `[]` | What the scope functions must not reach (tokens below). |
| `write-targets` | `[]` | `Class.attr` targets of `writes-targets`, required with it. `Class.attr["key"]` names one entry, as in `write-owners`. |
| `read-targets` | `[]` | `Class.attr` targets of `reads-targets`, required with it: reads as `read-owners` sees them, also inside property getters. A container entry is a configuration error. |
| `call-targets` | `[]` | Functions, methods, or classes of `calls`, required with it, matched as the `targets` of `call-owners`. |
| `write-universe` | `[]` | `Class.attr` entries: a reached write of one that `allow-writes` does not name is reported, once per written `Class.attr`. |
| `allow-writes` | `[]` | `Class.attr` writes the boundary allows, exempt from `write-targets` too. Needs `write-universe`. |
| `allowed-callees` | `[]` | Functions, classes, modules, or ecosystem symbols whose effects are allowed: paths through them are not followed, and calls of them are no `calls` violation. |
| `fresh-objects` | `"allow"` | `"allow"` or `"report"`: whether a write that constructs the object it writes (as in `write-owners`) counts as a write of the boundary. |
| `message` | none | The help of every report of the boundary. |

| `forbid` token | Forbids |
| -------------- | ------- |
| `blocking-net`, `blocking-db`, `blocking-fs`, `blocking-subprocess`, `blocking-sync`, `sleep` | that blocking effect |
| `blocking` | all six blocking effects |
| `mutates-params` | changing a parameter in place (for a method, `self` is a parameter) |
| `writes-targets` | writing a `write-targets` attribute |
| `reads-targets` | reading a `read-targets` attribute |
| `calls` | calling a `call-targets` function or class |

- Each scope function is checked through any number of calls.
- A violation inside another scope function is reported there only, once.
- One report per scope function and forbidden kind (or target) stands for every distinct site of
  it that the function reaches.

### `readonly-returns`

```toml
[[tool.heki.readonly-returns]]
name = "schema-graph"
producers = ["pkg.parser.SchemaGraphBuilder.schema"]
deep = true
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The contract's name. |
| `producers` | `[]` | Functions, methods, external symbols, or attributes (`Class.attr`) whose result every caller shares. |
| `deep` | `false` | Protect the values below the result too: its attributes, items, and elements. |

- Functions decorated with `@lru_cache` / `@cache` are protected without configuration, also
  through an import alias, but not a `cache` decorator the module defines itself.
- Every function that returns a protected value, or a part of it, on some path is protected too:
  wrappers and property getters need no entry of their own.

### `invalidation`

```toml
[[tool.heki.invalidation]]
name = "graph-index"
targets = ["DataType.data_types", "DataModel.fields"]
invalidators = ["GenerationStore.note_changed_models", "GenerationStore.refresh_now"]
exempt-writers = ["pkg.parser.generation.*"]
message = "tell the store which models changed"
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The contract's name in reports. |
| `targets` | `[]` | `Class.attr` attributes whose writes must be announced. |
| `invalidators` | `[]` | Functions or methods whose call announces the change. |
| `exempt-writers` | `[]` | Functions whose writes need no announcement of their own: the owner's operations, which announce or batch the change themselves, and construction methods. |
| `message` | none | The help of every report of the contract. |

An invalidator call counts when it runs on every path from the write to the function's normal
return:

- directly, or in each branch;
- behind a boolean flag the path sets after the write;
- through a helper that calls one on every path of its own.

What needs no announcement:

- a path that ends by raising: only normal returns count;
- writes to objects that did not exist before the call: an initializer's own `self` (not the
  objects reached through its attributes), and objects the function constructs or copies;
- writes to objects the function gets from a call;
- a function whose every caller announces the change after calling it.

A write is followed through local aliases, container methods, `setattr` / `__dict__`, and
helpers. A helper changing an argument it does not type writes the field or instance its caller
binds to it. At most 64 `invalidation` contracts can be declared.

### How contracts report

These hold for `write-owners`, `read-owners`, and `call-owners`, and the reporting at callers
holds for `invalidation` too:

- **A class's own initialization is allowed.** An initializer (`__init__`, `__post_init__`,
  `__new__`, `model_post_init`, `__setstate__`) of a target class or a subclass may access its own
  `self`: directly, through `super().__init__()`, or through helpers it passes `self` to.
- **A function that only runs inside allowed functions is allowed.** Every path of project
  callers above it starts in an allowed function, an exempt method, or such an initialization.
- **A private helper reports at its callers.** An access in a private helper (`_name`) with
  project callers is reported at the call sites of its first non-private callers. A private
  function called only by its own recursion reports its accesses itself.
- **One report stands for every site behind it.** A report at a call stands for every access
  behind the call, and an effect boundary's report for every site its scope function reaches.
  JSON output gives their number as `sites`, and a
  [Ratchet baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines) counts each of them.

## Ecosystem knowledge: `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`

heki ships a catalog of blocking, async-safe, and offloading APIs of the standard library and
common packages (`requests`, `httpx`, `aiohttp`, `sqlalchemy`, `django`, `redis`, `pandas`, …).
Add your own or override an entry:

```toml
[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]
symbol = "mypkg.db.run_query"
effects = ["blocking_db", "db_query"]

[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]
symbol = "mypkg.workers.in_thread"
offloads-blocking-arg = 0     # calls its first argument on a thread
async-safe = true

[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]
symbol = "mypkg.logging.emit"
excluded = true               # never reported
```

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | ------- |
| `symbol` | Fully qualified function or method name (`package.module.Class.method`). |
| `effects` | Any of `blocking_net`, `blocking_db`, `blocking_subprocess`, `blocking_sync`, `sleep`, `blocking_fs`, `unpooled_client_alloc`, `db_query`, `quadratic_realloc`. |
| `async-safe` | Safe to call from `async def`: it never blocks the event loop, so the blocking effects in `effects` are ignored (`db_query` and `unpooled_client_alloc` still count in loops). |
| `offloads-blocking-arg` | Index of the callable argument this function runs on another thread (the receiver is not counted). |
| `excluded` | Never reported (logging and similar). |
| `copy-sanitizer` | Returns a copy of its first argument (or receiver), ending `MUT202` protection: `"deep"` copies everything below it too; `"shallow"` (or `true`) copies only the object itself, so the values below it stay protected. |
| `return-type` | The class of the objects the call returns (a factory: `mypkg.db.open` returning `sqlite3.Connection`), whose methods are then looked up in the catalog. |
| `sync-lock-or-tx` | A `with` over an instance of this class, or over the result of this call, holds a synchronous lock or a database transaction (`EFF106`). |

- An override sets the keys it lists on the built-in entry for the same symbol. The keys it leaves
  out keep their built-in values; `effects = []` removes every effect.
- An entry may name a function or method of the project, by the module that defines it (the
  built-in catalog never describes the project's own functions).

For a project function:

| Key | Effect |
| --- | ------ |
| `effects` | added to what heki finds in its body |
| `excluded` | keeps every effect of the body from its callers |
| `async-safe` | keeps the blocking effects of the body from its callers |
| `return-type` | types its result, over its annotation |
| `offloads-blocking-arg` | the parameter the body offloads, counted as for a library method |
| `copy-sanitizer`, `sync-lock-or-tx` | not read: library symbols only |

## Inline suppressions

```python
x = load()            # heki: ignore[EFF101]
y = load()            # heki: ignore[EFF101, async-blocking-call]
z = load()            # heki: ignore
w = load()            # noqa: EFF101
```

- A suppression applies to the line of the diagnostic.
- Codes and rule names are accepted.
- A comment without codes (`# heki: ignore`, `# noqa`) silences every rule on that line.
- A bracketed list that is not closed or names no rule (`# heki: ignore[`, `# heki: ignore[]`)
  silences nothing.
- To keep a rule away from whole files, use [`per-file-ignores`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint).


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/

# Fixes and Safety

`heki check --fix` rewrites an `OPT` finding only when heki proves that the rewrite keeps what
the program does. This page shows the fix commands, what each finding offers, and what a fix
must prove.

## Fix commands

```console
$ heki check --diff                              # preview (exit code 1 when something would change)
$ heki check --fix                               # apply safe, unconditional fixes
$ heki check --fix --include-size-dependent      # also the proven-safe size-dependent rewrites
$ heki check --fix --profile profile.txt         # size-dependent rewrites in hot functions only
```

- `--diff` takes the same flags as `--fix` and writes nothing.
- `--include-size-dependent` applies the size-dependent rewrites in every function, with or
  without `--profile`.
- `--profile` alone applies them only in the functions a [profile](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/#profiles) shows hot.

## What each finding offers

Every `OPT` rule finds a quadratic or linear-per-iteration pattern that has a faster equivalent.
Two independent questions decide whether heki offers the rewrite:

| Question | Possible answers |
| -------- | ---------------- |
| **Safety:** does the rewrite keep the program's behavior? | every proof obligation is `Established`, `Blocked` (cannot be proven here), or `Disproved` (a concrete counterexample shape exists) |
| **Profitability:** is the rewrite faster for every input? | unconditional, or size-dependent (it can be slower for tiny inputs or for loops that run zero times) |

### Safety

| Obligations | What you get |
| ----------- | ------------ |
| All established | A diagnostic with a fix. A statement whose shape heki does not rewrite (a parenthesized `x = (x + [i])`, an annotated `x: list = x + [i]`) gets a diagnostic saying the rewrite is proven safe, to be made by hand. |
| One blocked | A diagnostic naming the first blocking obligation, and no fix. |
| One disproved | Nothing: the pattern only looks quadratic, and rewriting it would be a bug. |

### Profitability

| Profitability | Rules | Applied by |
| ------------- | ----- | ---------- |
| Unconditional (faster from the first iteration) | `OPT101`, `OPT102` | `heki check --fix` |
| Size-dependent | `OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130` | `heki check --fix --include-size-dependent`, or `--fix --profile <dump>` in hot functions |
| Size-dependent, no rewrite | `OPT103`, `OPT112`, `OPT113` | none: suggestion only |

### When the size is fixed

A size-dependent rule reports nothing when the code fixes the size:

- the container holds at most 16 items and nothing grows it past that or lets it escape. It
  is a display without `*` / `**` unpacking, a string constant, a builtin constructor of an
  iterable the code fixes (`list(range(7))`, `tuple(".;:")`, `sorted(NAMES)`, `list()`), a
  slice with constant bounds (`cases[:3]`, `paths[-2:]`), or a comprehension over fixed
  iterables (`[c for c in LABELS if c in wanted]`). Shrinking it (`expected.pop(0)` on
  `expected = [b"a", b""]`) and read-only builtins are fine, and so is filling a new list a
  fixed number of times (`ids.append(card["id"])` in a loop over at most 6 cards). A tuple or
  a string stays fixed whatever other code does with it, unless other code rebinds its name
  (`cfg.STATEMENTS = tuple(rows)`). This holds also through local names,
  module constants, and other modules' module-level displays and class attributes, read in a
  function or in a module body;
- the loop runs a fixed number of times: over such a container, a `range` of constants with at
  most 16 steps, or an iterable a test on every path to the loop caps (`if not 1 <= len(cards)
  <= 6: raise ValueError(...)`, `assert len(xs) <= 3`, also after a loop that shrinks it, when
  nothing on the way to the loop grows it or hands it to other code);
- the list is rebuilt in every iteration;
- the loop's own test caps the accumulator: `while len(buf) < 10`.

These facts decide profitability only, never safety. A size known only at run time does not
count: a list whose size depends on the input is reported even when it always holds three items.

## What a fix must prove

The analysis behind the `OPT` rules is separate from the one behind the other rules, and
deliberately conservative:

| Obligation | Why | Example |
| ---------- | --- | ------- |
| No type annotation is trusted | a subclass can override `__contains__` or `__add__` | `x: list[int] = WeirdList(...)` is not a list for heki |
| The object is created in the function and never escapes | heki counts anything it cannot see as shared: parameters, globals, attributes, values passed to unknown functions, names captured by closures | `sink(rows)` inside the loop blocks `rows.append(...)` |
| Access is exclusive: no other variable, iterator, or view still refers to the old object after the statement | an in-place update would change what they see | `for v in x: x = x + [v]` ends, but `x.append(v)` would loop forever, so heki reports nothing |
| Evaluation order and exceptions are kept | a rewrite must not call anything earlier or later | `{**d, f(): g()}` becomes `d.update({f(): g()})`, not `d[f()] = g()`, which would call `g` first |
| Builtin names are the builtins | the module can rebind them | trusted only while nothing rebinds them: an assignment, a `global` store, `from m import *`, `globals()`, or a module that patches `builtins` (a `.pyi` stub never runs, so its `import builtins` does not count) |
| Locals change only through the code | `eval`, `exec`, `locals()`, `sys._getframe`, and frame attributes can change them behind any analysis | candidates in such functions are always blocked; `heki assumptions` lists these places in a project |

The scope analysis is checked against CPython's `symtable`, and adversarial programs that break a
naive rewrite are run on CPython: see [Development](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/development/#checks-against-cpython).

## How `--fix` applies fixes

1. It applies the fixes that do not overlap.
2. It analyzes the result again and repeats until nothing changes, at most ten passes: a fix that
   becomes provable after another one is applied too.
3. It reports what is left.

| Case | What happens |
| ---- | ------------ |
| A suppressed diagnostic (`# heki: ignore[...]`) | It is never fixed. |
| A file that changed on disk meanwhile (an editor saved it) | It is not written: the run keeps that save, reports an error, and exits with code 2. Run `--fix` again. |
| Fixes of a pass that would leave a file that does not parse | None of them is applied to that file, and the run exits with code 2 (a heki bug to report). |
| `\n`, `\r\n`, or lone `\r` line breaks | Fixes work the same, and the lines they insert use the file's own line break. |

`--diff` prints the paths every other output format prints (relative to the working directory),
so `patch -p1` applies it where heki ran.

## Fixes keep type checkers and isort satisfied

A `collections.deque` rewrite (`OPT120`, `OPT121`) also rewrites the variable's annotation and
adds the import:

```console
$ heki check --diff --include-size-dependent jobs.py
--- a/jobs.py
+++ b/jobs.py
@@ -1,11 +1,12 @@
 """Job queue."""
 
+import collections
 import os
 
 
 def drain(jobs: list[int]) -> int:
-    queue: list[int] = list(jobs)
+    queue: collections.deque[int] = collections.deque(list(jobs))
     total = 0
     while queue:
-        total += queue.pop(0)
+        total += queue.popleft()
     return total
Would fix 1 issue(s) in 1 file(s).
```

- An annotation the fix cannot rewrite (`Sequence[int]`, a union), or another annotated
  declaration of the variable, blocks the fix.
- `import collections` goes into the module's block of standard-library imports, in the order
  that block follows: straight imports first, or sorted by module as with
  `force-sort-within-sections`.
- Without such a block, it starts one before the other imports. In a module without imports, it
  follows the docstring and `__future__` imports, with the blank lines isort expects.
- It never goes above a shebang, an encoding declaration, or a `from __future__` import, and only
  imports run before it, so the rewritten function cannot run before `collections` is bound.
- An existing `from collections import deque` or `import collections` is reused only when it runs
  unconditionally (not under `if TYPE_CHECKING:`) and names the standard library's module (not
  `from .collections import deque`).

## Profiles

`--profile` reads a sampling profile you recorded offline. It is experimental; see [experimental.md](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

| Profiler | Command |
| -------- | ------- |
| CPython 3.15's sampling profiler | `python -m profiling.sampling run --collapsed -o stacks.txt app.py`, or `--gecko -o profile.json` |
| py-spy | `py-spy record --format raw -o stacks.txt -- python app.py` |

- A function is hot when it is on the stack in at least 1 % of the samples.
- The profile promotes size-dependent fixes in hot functions and adds the sample share to the
  diagnostics' evidence. It never makes an unsafe rewrite safe.

A frame counts for a function when all of these hold:

- its name names the function on a dotted boundary: `run` or `A.run` for `A.run`, never `BA.run`;
- its file is the function's file, as a basename, a relative path, or an absolute path;
- its line, when the profiler recorded one, lies inside the function.

A frame that fits several functions counts for none: a plain `run` without a line in a file with
two `run` methods, or a `models.py` that two packages have. `--watch` matches frames by their
names only.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/

# Adopting heki in a Code Base

An existing code base usually has findings you cannot fix at once. This page shows how to adopt
heki step by step:

1. Record today's findings in a [Ratchet baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines), so heki fails only on
   new ones.
2. Run it in [pre-commit](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#pre-commit) and [continuous integration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#continuous-integration).
3. [Roll out more rules](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#rolling-out-rules): contracts for your shared state, and the opt-in
   rules where they matter.
4. For a library, save [effect snapshots](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#effect-snapshots-mut103) of its public functions.

## Ratchet baselines

A Ratchet baseline records the findings you have today and fails only on new ones:

```console
$ heki check --baseline heki-baseline.toml --update-baseline   # record today's findings
$ heki check --baseline heki-baseline.toml                     # fail on regressions only
```

Set `baseline = "heki-baseline.toml"` in the [configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#top-level-settings)
to use it without the flag, also in `--watch` and the language server.

Entries are keyed by file, function, rule, and target, not by line number, so unrelated edits and
reformatting do not break the baseline:

```toml
# heki Ratchet baseline: counts may only shrink (`heki check --update-baseline`).
version = 2

[[entries]]
path = "app/api.py"
qualname = "get_user"
rule_code = "EFF101"
target = "requests.get"
count = 1
```

The recorded set can only shrink:

| Situation | `heki check` | `heki check --update-baseline` |
| --------- | ------------ | ------------------------------ |
| No baseline file yet | an error (exit code 2) | records today's findings |
| A finding was fixed | a note that the entry can shrink | records the smaller entry |
| An entry grew, or a new finding appeared | reports it, with a note on the allowed and found counts (exit code 1) | reports it the same way and leaves the file as it is (exit code 1) |
| A file could not be analyzed (a syntax error, an unreadable file) | reports the error (exit code 2) | writes nothing, so the entries of that file are not lost (exit code 2) |

To record new findings on purpose, delete the baseline and record it again.

### What an entry counts

Each entry counts violation sites, not reports (`sites` in JSON output):

- a contract report at the caller of a private helper stands for every write, read, or call
  inside the helper;
- an effect boundary report stands for every forbidden call or write its scope function reaches.

So a second violation behind a recorded report is a regression too.

A baseline without `version = 2` was written before heki counted sites, and counts reports:

- `heki check` says so in a note, and a second site behind a recorded report is no regression;
- `--update-baseline` compares in the old unit first, so nothing that grew is taken in, then
  rewrites the file with `version = 2`.

A version this heki does not know is an error, and so is a file listing one entry twice (a hand
merge of two baselines).

## pre-commit

heki ships as one binary on PyPI, so a hook needs no Rust toolchain. Its checks follow calls
across files, so the hook checks the whole project instead of the staged files only.

=== "uv"

    ```yaml
    # .pre-commit-config.yaml
    repos:
      - repo: local
        hooks:
          - id: heki
            name: heki
            entry: uvx heki check
            language: system   # needs uv on PATH
            types: [python]
            pass_filenames: false
    ```

=== "Without uv"

    ```yaml
    # .pre-commit-config.yaml
    repos:
      - repo: local
        hooks:
          - id: heki
            name: heki
            entry: heki check
            language: python
            additional_dependencies: [heki]
            types: [python]
            pass_filenames: false
    ```

With a baseline configured, the hook fails only on new findings.

## Continuous integration

=== "GitHub Actions annotations"

    ```yaml
    - run: uvx heki check --output-format github
    ```

=== "Code scanning (SARIF)"

    ```yaml
    # The job needs `permissions: security-events: write`.
    - run: uvx heki check --output-format sarif > heki.sarif || test "$?" -eq 1
    - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
      with:
        sarif_file: heki.sarif
    ```

With SARIF:

- findings (exit code `1`) become code-scanning alerts and keep the step green;
- a configuration, read, or syntax error (exit code `2`) still fails the step: heki then writes
  SARIF only for the files it could analyze, which would hide the others;
- results carry the message, the location, the call chain (`relatedLocations`), and the help
  (`properties.help`; SARIF's `rules[].help` is one text per rule, and a report's help can name
  the object it is about).

For custom tooling, `--output-format json` gives every field: see
[Coding Agents](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#use-the-cli-in-the-agents-loop).

## Rolling out rules

1. Start with the default rules and a baseline, or `--select` one family at a time.
2. Declare [contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) for the shared state and the operations you
   care about, and effect boundaries for the code that must stay pure. `MUT201`, `MUT203`,
   `MUT204`, `MUT109`, and `EFF201` report nothing until a contract exists.
3. Enable the opt-in rules where they matter:

    | Rule | Turn it on for |
    | ---- | -------------- |
    | [`EFF105`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-fs/), [`EFF107`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unretained-async-task/) | async services |
    | [`EFF106`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-or-tx-held-across-io/) | threaded code, and code that holds database transactions |
    | [`MUT103`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/summary-effect-regression/) | library APIs (with [effect snapshots](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#effect-snapshots-mut103)) |
    | [`MUT106`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterator-double-consumption/) | code that passes iterators and generators around |
    | [`MUT108`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-type-mutation/) | code that relies on frozen dataclasses and `ReadOnly` fields |

4. Use `per-file-ignores` rather than broad `ignore` lists, so new code stays covered.

## Effect snapshots (`MUT103`)

For a library, a change in what a public function *does* is worth reviewing even when no rule
fires: it starts mutating an argument, or doing network I/O. Save the effect summaries of the
public functions and check against them:

```console
$ heki snapshot --write                        # writes .heki-summary-snapshot.json
$ heki check --extend-select MUT103            # reports functions that gained effects
```

1. Commit `.heki-summary-snapshot.json`.
2. When a new effect is intended, refresh the snapshot in the same pull request: the diff of the
   JSON file shows reviewers what changed.

A run that cannot analyze every file (a syntax error, an unreadable file) does not write the
snapshot: it reports the errors and exits with code 2, so the entries of those files are not
lost.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/cli-reference/

# CLI Reference

Exit codes: `0` no diagnostics, `1` diagnostics (or Ratchet regressions, or pending `--diff` changes), `2` configuration / I/O / syntax errors.

## `heki`

```text
Experimental static checker for Python that tracks side effects and mutations across function calls

Usage: heki <COMMAND>

Commands:
  check        Run semantic checks across Python files or directories (Ruff-aligned)
  server       Start the incremental Language Server Protocol (LSP) server [alias: lsp]
  rule         Explain a rule, its Proof Obligations, and counterexamples (`ruff rule` style) [alias: explain]
  snapshot     Manage interprocedural effect summary snapshots (`MUT103`)
  assumptions  List Assumption A1 hazards (`eval`, `exec`, `locals()`, frame introspection, functions too large to model) in a project
  help         Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help     Print help
  -V, --version  Print version
```

## `heki check`

```text
Run semantic checks across Python files or directories (Ruff-aligned)

Usage: heki check [OPTIONS] [PATHS]...

Arguments:
  [PATHS]...  Files or directories to check [default: .]

Options:
      --fix
          Apply `safe` + `unconditional` fixes (`OPT101`/`OPT102`)
      --include-size-dependent
          Also apply the proven-safe `size-dependent` fixes, in every function
      --diff
          Preview fixes as a unified diff without writing files
      --select <SELECT>
          Comma-separated rule codes, prefixes, or slugs to enable
      --extend-select <EXTEND_SELECT>
          Additional rules to enable on top of defaults/config
      --ignore <IGNORE>
          Comma-separated rule codes or slugs to ignore
      --output-format <OUTPUT_FORMAT>
          Output format [default: full] [possible values: full, concise, json, github, sarif]
      --config <CONFIG>
          Explicit configuration file: a `pyproject.toml` (its `[tool.heki]` table) or a file with the keys at its top level, like `heki.toml`
      --target-version <TARGET_VERSION>
          Target Python version (`py311`, `py312`, `py313`, `py314`, `py315`)
      --baseline <BASELINE>
          Ratchet baseline TOML file (line-number-independent)
      --update-baseline
          Generate or shrink-update the Ratchet baseline file
      --profile <PROFILE>
          Experimental: offline profile dump (collapsed stacks of CPython 3.15's profiler or py-spy, or `--gecko` JSON): apply the `size-dependent` fixes in its hot functions (in every function with `--include-size-dependent`)
      --watch
          Watch for file changes and re-run incrementally
  -h, --help
          Print help
```

## `heki server`

```text
Start the incremental Language Server Protocol (LSP) server

Usage: heki server [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --stdio  Use stdio transport (default LSP mode)
  -h, --help   Print help
```

## `heki rule`

```text
Explain a rule, its Proof Obligations, and counterexamples (`ruff rule` style)

Usage: heki rule [OPTIONS] [RULE]

Arguments:
  [RULE]  Rule code (`EFF101`) or slug (`async-blocking-call`), or `--all` to list all rules

Options:
      --all                            
      --output-format <OUTPUT_FORMAT>  `text`, or `json` with each rule's metadata and documentation [default: text] [possible values: text, json]
  -h, --help                           Print help
```

## `heki snapshot`

```text
Manage interprocedural effect summary snapshots (`MUT103`)

Usage: heki snapshot [OPTIONS] [PATHS]...

Arguments:
  [PATHS]...  Files or directories to summarize [default: .]

Options:
      --write
          Write `.heki-summary-snapshot.json` at the project root (default: print it)
      --config <CONFIG>
          Explicit configuration file: a `pyproject.toml` (its `[tool.heki]` table) or a file with the keys at its top level, like `heki.toml`
      --target-version <TARGET_VERSION>
          Target Python version (`py311`..`py315`)
  -h, --help
          Print help
```

## `heki assumptions`

```text
List Assumption A1 hazards (`eval`, `exec`, `locals()`, frame introspection, functions too large to model) in a project

Usage: heki assumptions [OPTIONS] [PATHS]...

Arguments:
  [PATHS]...  [default: .]

Options:
      --target-version <TARGET_VERSION>
          Target Python version (`py311`, `py312`, `py313`, `py314`, `py315`)
      --json
          Output machine-readable JSON
  -h, --help
          Print help
```

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/

# Rules

heki has 35 rules in four families. Every rule is enabled by default except the opt-in rules marked 🔌, which need their exact code or name in `select` / `extend-select` (a prefix such as `EFF` does not enable them).

## Legend

- 🛠️ The fix is applied by `heki check --fix` when heki proves it safe.
- 🔧 A proven-safe rewrite applied only with `--fix --include-size-dependent` or in functions a `--profile` dump shows hot (it can be slower for tiny inputs).
- 🔌 Opt-in rule.
- 🧪 Experimental rule. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## Mutation & State (MUT)

Shared state written behind its owner's back: stale caches, write-ownership contracts, shared return values, and effect regressions against a saved snapshot.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| MUT101 | [cached-property-stale-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-mutation/) | Mutating an attribute read by `@cached_property` without invalidating the cache. | 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT103 | [summary-effect-regression](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/summary-effect-regression/) | Interprocedural mutation/escape/effect regression against saved summary snapshot. | 🔌 |
| MUT106 | [iterator-double-consumption](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterator-double-consumption/) | Opt-in: consuming a single-pass iterator or generator a second time (the second pass sees no items). | 🔌 |
| MUT107 | [hash-attr-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/hash-attr-mutation/) | Mutating an attribute read by `__hash__` after initialization (stored `set` / `dict` entries become unreachable). |  |
| MUT108 | [readonly-type-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-type-mutation/) | Opt-in: changing in place a field that a standard type declares read-only (frozen dataclass / `NamedTuple` / `dataclass_transform` fields, `Final` / `ReadOnly` attributes, `ReadOnly` `TypedDict` keys), directly, through an alias, or in a helper. | 🔌 |
| MUT109 | [write-without-invalidation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/write-without-invalidation/) | Writing a declared `invalidation` target (directly, via alias, or via helper) without reaching one of its invalidators on every path to the function's return. |  |
| MUT110 | [readonly-param-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-param-mutation/) | Handing a `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `ReadOnly` parameter to a function that changes it in place (directly, through an alias, or through helpers). |  |
| MUT111 | [cached-property-stale-read](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-read/) | Opt-in: reading a `@cached_property` that a method of its class family can leave stale (a write `MUT101` reports). | 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT112 | [conditional-ownership-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/conditional-ownership-mutation/) | Opt-in: changing in place a value that is a new object on one path and borrowed state (a parameter, an attribute, a global, or what a function returns of such state) on another. | 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT113 | [iterated-container-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterated-container-mutation/) | Opt-in: a dict, set, or deque of the instance changed while a method iterates it, by another method while a generator is suspended in the loop or by a function the loop's body calls (the next step raises `RuntimeError`). | 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT201 | [write-owner-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/write-owner-violation/) | Writing a guarded attribute/container (directly, via alias, or via helper) outside declared `write-owners`. |  |
| MUT202 | [readonly-return-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-return-mutation/) | Mutating a shared object returned by a declared `readonly-returns` producer or `@lru_cache`, directly or through the functions that return it. |  |
| MUT203 | [read-owner-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/read-owner-violation/) | Reading a guarded attribute (directly, via alias, `getattr`, or `__dict__`) outside declared `read-owners`. |  |
| MUT204 | [call-owner-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/call-owner-violation/) | Calling a guarded function or method, or constructing a guarded class (directly, via a bound method, `getattr`, or a helper), outside declared `call-owners`. |  |
| MUT205 | [unresolved-guarded-write](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/) | Strict mode of a `write-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): writing an attribute named like a target on an object of unknown class, or a computed attribute name on a guarded class. |  |
