| MUT206 | [unresolved-guarded-read](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-read/) | Strict mode of a `read-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): reading an attribute named like a target on an object of unknown class. |  |
| MUT207 | [unresolved-guarded-call](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-call/) | Strict mode of a `call-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): calling a method named like a target on an object of unknown class. |  |

## Execution Effects (EFF)

Work that runs where it should not: blocking calls on the event loop, clients and queries inside loops.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| EFF101 | [async-blocking-call](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-call/) | Direct or indirect blocking network/DB/subprocess/sleep call reachable from `async def`. |  |
| EFF102 | [loop-unpooled-client](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-unpooled-client/) | Allocating an unpooled HTTP/DB/RPC client or sessionless request inside a loop. |  |
| EFF103 | [loop-db-query](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-db-query/) | Explicit DB query / external RPC executed inside a loop (N+1). |  |
| EFF105 | [async-blocking-fs](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-fs/) | Opt-in: blocking local filesystem I/O reachable from `async def`. | 🔌 |
| EFF106 | [lock-or-tx-held-across-io](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-or-tx-held-across-io/) | Opt-in: `await` or blocking network I/O while holding a `threading` lock or a DB transaction. | 🔌 |
| EFF107 | [unretained-async-task](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unretained-async-task/) | Opt-in: an `asyncio.create_task` result bound to a local variable but never awaited, returned, or stored. | 🔌 |
| EFF201 | [effect-boundary-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/effect-boundary-violation/) | Reaching a forbidden effect (directly or through calls) from a declared `effect-boundaries` scope. |  |

## Data Pipelines (DATA)

Quadratic re-allocation of DataFrames and arrays across loop iterations.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| DATA101 | [loop-carried-concat](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-carried-concat/) | Loop-carried quadratic `pandas.concat` / `numpy.vstack` / `numpy.append` accumulation. |  |

## Complexity Rewrites (OPT)

Quadratic patterns heki can rewrite, each proven safe by the alias analysis before a fix is offered.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| OPT101 | [list-quadratic-concat](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-quadratic-concat/) | Unconditionally profitable `list` quadratic concatenation (`x = x + [e]` -> `x.append(e)`). | 🛠️ |
| OPT102 | [set-dict-quadratic-merge](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/set-dict-quadratic-merge/) | Unconditionally profitable `set`/`dict` quadratic merge (`{**d, ...}` with `d` first). | 🛠️ |
| OPT103 | [immutable-quadratic-concat](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/immutable-quadratic-concat/) | Size-dependent immutable quadratic accumulation (`bytes`/`tuple`/attr `str`). |  |
| OPT110 | [loop-linear-membership](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-membership/) | Size-dependent `e in lst` inside a loop -> hoist `set` outside loop. | 🔧 |
| OPT111 | [loop-linear-dedup](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-dedup/) | Size-dependent `if v not in seen: seen.append(v)` -> auxiliary `set`. | 🔧 |
| OPT112 | [loop-linear-list-lookup](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-list-lookup/) | Size-dependent `list.index` / `list.remove` / `list.count` inside a loop (repeated linear scans). |  |
| OPT113 | [nested-loop-equijoin](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/nested-loop-equijoin/) | Size-dependent nested-loop equi-join (`for a in A: for b in B: if a.k == b.k`) -> `dict` index. |  |
| OPT120 | [list-front-pop](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-pop/) | Size-dependent `q.pop(0)` / `del q[0]` / `q = q[1:]` -> `collections.deque`. | 🔧 |
| OPT121 | [list-front-insert](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-insert/) | Size-dependent `q.insert(0, v)` -> `collections.deque`. | 🔧 |
| OPT130 | [loop-invariant-container-rebuild](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-invariant-container-rebuild/) | Size-dependent loop-invariant container reconstruction (`e in set(keys)`). | 🔧 |


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/

# Experimental Features

Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. A feature leaves this page when it becomes stable.

An experimental rule is never enabled by default: it runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name, and `heki check` then reports it like any other rule. `heki rule <CODE>` and the rule's page say that it is experimental.

| ID | Kind | Target | Since | Tracking |
| -- | ---- | ------ | ----- | -------- |
| `cli-option.profile` | cli-option | `heki check --profile` | 0.1.1 | - |
| `rule.MUT101` | rule | [`MUT101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-mutation/) | 0.1.0 | - |
| `rule.MUT111` | rule | [`MUT111`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-read/) | 0.1.1 | - |
| `rule.MUT112` | rule | [`MUT112`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/conditional-ownership-mutation/) | 0.2.0 | - |
| `rule.MUT113` | rule | [`MUT113`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterated-container-mutation/) | 0.2.0 | - |

## `cli-option.profile`

- **Kind:** cli-option
- **Target:** `heki check --profile`
- **Since:** 0.1.1

It reads the output of CPython 3.15's sampling profiler, and that format can still change.

## `rule.MUT101`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`MUT101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-mutation/)
- **Since:** 0.1.0

Its precision outside a few code bases is still low.

## `rule.MUT111`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`MUT111`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-read/)
- **Since:** 0.1.1

It reports the readers of the stale writes `MUT101` finds, so it shares `MUT101`'s precision.

## `rule.MUT112`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`MUT112`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/conditional-ownership-mutation/)
- **Since:** 0.2.0

Its precision on real code bases is still low: much of what it reports is code that changes a borrowed container on purpose.

## `rule.MUT113`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`MUT113`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterated-container-mutation/)
- **Since:** 0.2.0

It has few reports, and most of them are still false.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/lsp/

# Editors (LSP)

`heki server` (alias `heki lsp`) is a Language Server Protocol server on stdin / stdout: it shows
heki's diagnostics and fixes while you edit, with the results `heki check` reports.

## Set up your editor

=== "VS Code"

    heki does not ship its own extension yet. Any generic LSP client extension that starts a
    command for a language works; configure it to run `heki server` for `python` documents, for
    example:

    ```json
    {
      "command": "heki",
      "args": ["server"],
      "languages": ["python"]
    }
    ```

=== "Neovim"

    ```lua
    vim.lsp.config("heki", {
      cmd = { "heki", "server" },
      filetypes = { "python" },
      root_markers = { "pyproject.toml", "heki.toml", ".git" },
    })
    vim.lsp.enable("heki")
    ```

=== "Helix"

    ```toml
    # languages.toml
    [language-server.heki]
    command = "heki"
    args = ["server"]

    [[language]]
    name = "python"
    language-servers = ["pyright", "heki"]
    ```

=== "Zed"

    ```json
    {
      "lsp": {
        "heki": {
          "binary": { "path": "heki", "arguments": ["server"] }
        }
      },
      "languages": {
        "Python": { "language_servers": ["...", "heki"] }
      }
    }
    ```

## What the server provides

- Diagnostics for open files, with every hop of a call chain (for example the path from an
  `async def` to `time.sleep`) as related information you can jump to. The message is the
  report's one sentence; its help, what to do about it, is the last related-information entry
  (`help: ...`) at the diagnostic's own range, the way rust-analyzer shows a `help:` note.
- Quick fixes for the safe `OPT101` / `OPT102` rewrites.
- `refactor.rewrite.heki` code actions for the proven-safe size-dependent rewrites. A fix whose
  result would not parse is never offered, as `heki check --fix` refuses it.
- A quick fix that appends `# heki: ignore[CODE]` to the line of any diagnostic, unless a comment
  cannot go there (the line ends inside a string or with a `\` continuation).

Code actions edit the version of the document their diagnostics were computed on:

- while an edit waits for its analysis, none are offered;
- a client that applies versioned workspace edits (`workspaceEdit.documentChanges`) gets them
  with that version, so it rejects them if the document changed meanwhile.

## The same results as `heki check`

- The server reads the same [configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/), including the Ratchet baseline:
  with `baseline` configured, a file shows what `heki check` reports against it (every finding of
  an entry that grew).
- A file belongs to the project when `heki check` would find it. A file that an ignore file, a
  hidden directory, or `exclude` leaves out is not analyzed, also when it is created or opened.
- A file that does not parse is left out of the project until it parses again.
- A configuration `heki check` rejects (an unknown rule, a contract target that is not
  `Class.attr`, an invalid pattern) is logged as a warning, and the server analyzes nothing until
  it is fixed.

One difference is deliberate. When more than ten `async def` boundaries reach the same blocking
call, `heki check` reports them once, with a count; the server groups them per file, so the file
you edit always shows its own boundary.

## When the server re-analyzes

The server indexes the workspace in the background, then keeps only the per-function effect
summaries in memory.

| Event | Re-analyzed |
| ----- | ----------- |
| An edit, 250 ms after the last keystroke | the edited file alone |
| A save | the saved file, and the files whose results depend on the edit (below) |
| A file created, changed, or deleted outside the editor (`git checkout`, code generators) | as for a save; needs a client that supports watching files |
| A change to the configuration or to an ignore file | the whole workspace, indexed again |
| A change to the baseline file | every file |
| Closing a document with unsaved changes | the file as it is on the disk (or it leaves the project when it was never saved), and everything that affects |

On a save, the edit reaches other files only through what it changes:

| The edit changes | Also re-analyzed |
| ---------------- | ---------------- |
| a function's effects, or what the object it returns may be (a new one, its argument, or state it keeps) | its callers, and the functions of a call cycle through it (their effects change with it) |
| a declaration that names resolve through: a re-exported class, a new method or base class, a property getter, a subclass, an offloading decorator | every file that resolved names through it |
| a method of a class family | the classes of that family; with `MUT112` selected, every changed method counts: a value stored in `self.<attr>` is reported when a method of the family changes that attribute in place |
| what a function changes of its own containers, or what it does with the generators it calls (`MUT113`, when selected) | the classes of its family with generators suspending inside an iteration of their containers, and those of the generators it calls |
| the writes that leave a `@cached_property` stale (`MUT111`, when selected) | the files reading such a property: whether a read is reported depends on every writer of the class family, wherever it is |
| a function generators are handed to | those generators: whether it iterates them decides where their writes and reads are reported |
| a function's own in-place changes or its calls, while its effects stay the same | the files with `MUT108` / `MUT110` reports above it: a report's call chain ends at the first function whose body makes the change |
| the position of a call site, also when its bytes stay where they were | the files whose call chains show that call site |
| the position of a method's own change of a container | the files whose `MUT113` reports show it |

Contracts reach further when a function changes its calls:

| Configured | Also re-analyzed | Because |
| ---------- | ---------------- | ------- |
| an ownership or `invalidation` contract | every function below it | whether a function only runs inside allowed callers, or whether its callers announce its writes, depends on all callers above it |
| a contract on calls (`call-owners`, an effect boundary forbidding `calls`) | every function above it | a call of a target is reported at the callers of the private helper making it, and at the scope functions reaching it |
| an effect boundary, when the function changes its calls of library APIs | every function above it | a boundary may allow one API and forbid another of the same effect, and counts every call it reaches |

Edits that change none of these, such as most comments, stop at the edited file.

### Files outside the editor

When the client supports watching files, the server registers for
`workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles` on:

- Python files (`**/*.{py,pyi}`);
- the configuration: `pyproject.toml`, `heki.toml`, `.heki.toml`, and the summary snapshot of
  `MUT103`;
- the ignore files: `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, `.hekiignore`;
- TOML files, for the Ratchet baseline.

An open document stays the file's text until it is closed:

- indexing the workspace again keeps documents that were never saved;
- a file deleted on the disk while its document is open stays in the project until the document
  closes.

## Without an editor: `--watch`

```console
$ heki check --watch
```

- It re-checks the changed files and the files affected by them, with the same incremental
  engine, and prints the full list of diagnostics after every change, compared with the Ratchet
  baseline as `heki check` compares them.
- It only reports: `--fix`, `--diff`, and `--update-baseline` are ignored, with a warning.
- It reloads everything when the configuration (`pyproject.toml`, `heki.toml`, `.heki.toml`, or
  the `--config` file), the summary snapshot, or the baseline changes. So does `src/__init__.py`
  or a root `__init__.py` appearing or disappearing: module names under `src/`, or relative
  imports that climb to the root, change with the module layout. The server does the same.
- What fails once the watch runs (a configuration that no longer parses, a watched path that
  disappears) is reported, and the watch goes on until it is fixed.
- A file counts as changed when its size, its modification time, or (on Unix) its inode or
  status-change time changes, so a replacement that keeps the modification time is seen too. A
  file stamped within the last two seconds is also compared by content, for file systems whose
  timestamps are coarse.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/

# Coding Agents

heki gives coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and similar) the checks it gives people:
every diagnostic says what was proven, where the evidence is, and what blocks a fix.

## Use the CLI in the agent's loop

A typical instruction for the agent:

> After changing Python files, run `heki check --output-format json`. For each diagnostic,
> read its `help` and `heki rule <rule_code>`, follow `related` to the root cause, and fix it
> there. Apply
> `heki check --fix` for the safe rewrites. Never silence a diagnostic with `# heki: ignore`
> unless the rule's documentation describes the case as intended.

```console
$ heki check --output-format json
```

Each diagnostic has:

| Field | Content |
| ----- | ------- |
| `path`, `line`, `column`, `span` | location (byte span in the file) |
| `rule_code`, `rule_slug`, `severity`, `message` | the finding: `message` is one sentence saying what happens |
| `help` | what to do about it (`null` when the rule has no advice for the report) |
| `qualname`, `target` | the function and the object involved |
| `related` | every hop of the call chain behind the finding |
| `evidence` | what was established (for `OPT` rules: the proof obligations) |
| `blocker` | the obligation that blocks an automatic fix, if any |
| `fix` | byte-span edits for proven-safe rewrites |
| `sites` | the violation sites a contract report stands for, when more than one |

`heki rule <CODE>` prints a rule's documentation: what it does, why it matters, and what to do
instead, which makes a good prompt for the fix. `heki rule --all --output-format json` gives
every rule's metadata and documentation.

## Use the LSP server

Agents that talk LSP (for example through an editor or an MCP bridge) can start `heki server`
and use its diagnostics, related information, and code actions directly, as editors do. See
[Editors (LSP)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/lsp/).

## Documentation for models

| File | Content |
| ---- | ------- |
| [llms.txt](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/llms.txt) | an index of every page, with a one-line description |
| [llms-full.txt](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/llms-full.txt) | the full text of every page, including all rules |


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/development/

# Development

This page covers building and testing heki, its checks against CPython, the memory budget, the
documentation, releases, and the crates. [`AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/AGENTS.md)
lists the invariants every change must keep and the checks to run.

## Build and test

```console
$ cargo build
$ cargo test --workspace
$ cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
```

- The tests are end to end first: they run the real `heki` binary and the real LSP server
  (`heki server --stdio`) on small projects.
- The `--fix` tests run the original and the rewritten programs on CPython and require identical
  output. They use `python3.15`, or the interpreter in `HEKI_TEST_PYTHON`.

### Coverage

```console
$ cargo llvm-cov --workspace --show-missing-lines --fail-uncovered-lines 3
```

- Every line is covered except three that cannot run: the `_ => {}` arms for assignment,
  augmented-assignment, and `del` targets in `crates/heki_ir/src/builder.rs`, which the parser
  rejects. CI fails on any other uncovered line.
- The summary counts the unit-test build and the normal build of a function separately and keeps
  the better one, and it counts a closure that never runs as missed. Cover each function
  completely from one side: end to end for analysis code, unit tests only for small guard
  functions.

## Checks against CPython

```console
$ cargo build
$ python3 tests/symtable_verify/verify_symtable.py --heki target/debug/heki tests/symtable_verify/fixtures/ tests/corpus/
$ python3 tests/sentinel/verify_soundness_kb.py
$ python3 tests/difftest/counterexamples.py
$ python3 tests/difftest/soundness_e2e_counterexamples.py
$ python3.15 tests/difftest/ir_counterexamples.py
```

CI runs them on CPython 3.11 to 3.15 (`ir_counterexamples.py` on 3.15 only).

| Script | Checks |
| ------ | ------ |
| `verify_symtable.py` | heki's scope analysis against CPython's `symtable`: the scope tree (kind, name, definition line, parent), bindings, parameters, `global` / `nonlocal` declarations, and every read. Every target must exist and every file must parse on the running CPython, except fixtures marked for a newer one in their name (`312_315`, `313_315`, `_314`, `pep810`); a run that compares no file fails. |
| `verify_soundness_kb.py` | every claim of the Layer 1 knowledge base (`kb/soundness/builtins.toml`), on the running interpreter |
| `counterexamples.py` | that the naive rewrites heki refuses really change behavior |
| `soundness_e2e_counterexamples.py` | that the rewrites earlier versions of heki made of these shapes change behavior; the end-to-end tests check that heki now blocks or disproves each |
| `ir_counterexamples.py` | that the rewrites heki made before the IR modeled a shape (a binding, an alias, a path) change behavior; needs CPython 3.15 |

## Memory

```console
$ cargo build --release
$ python3 scripts/check_memory.py --heki target/release/heki
```

- CI fails when the peak memory of `heki check` (with and without an ownership contract) or of
  the `--watch` engine on a generated project exceeds its budget in the script.
- The peak is the lowest of three runs: the resident set size on Linux, the physical footprint
  on macOS, each platform with its own budgets.
- The generated project is shaped after what dominates heki's memory on real code bases: typed
  field writes reached through long chains of private helpers (with an ownership contract, every
  caller keeps the write sites they hand over, with their chains), effect chains below
  `async def` entry points, and many modules and classes (every file's check reads the project's
  declarations).

When a budget is exceeded, find what grew before raising it:

- `/usr/bin/time -l` (macOS) or `-v` (Linux) gives the peak of a run;
- a counting global allocator in a scratch build gives the live bytes per phase.

## Analysis cost

heki's time and peak memory grow about linearly with the size of the source. The shapes that
break this are rare in small samples and common in large generated files: a module of tens of
thousands of lines, a function of several hundred. A new walk, fixpoint, or per-function state
follows these rules:

- A walk through the inputs of a phi, or through both operands of an expression, keeps its
  answer per value and question. A depth limit does not bound it: with k inputs per step, depth
  8 is k^8 paths. A loop header's phi is its own input once per `continue`, and chains of
  `isinstance` tests and `match` statements multiply the inputs.
- A fixpoint joins its facts and never replaces them, so each pass can only grow them, and it
  also has a pass limit. Past the limit the facts are unknown, and no rule reports from them.
- Facts are kept per SSA value, not per variable per block. State that grows with a function has
  a budget proportional to the function's source bytes, as the IR and proof-state budgets in
  [scope](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/) do. Past the budget the function gets no finding, never a guess.
- A `finally` body is built once per way out of the `try`. Anything made per copy, such as a
  class body, is made once.
- Dead code is modeled too. A loop after a `return` has only its back edge, and copies around it
  (`y = x; x = y`) can close a cycle. A walk along copies ends on such a cycle.
- A rule that follows exception edges, one from each call that can raise, runs a dataflow over
  blocks with one fact per tracked value. It never enumerates paths.

Each bound comes with a shape in `crates/heki/tests/e2e_analysis_bounds.rs` that is slow without it,
checked against a time limit: comparisons sharing an operand thirty deep, many `match` statements of
slicing or pass-through cases, `t1 = t0[t0]` chains in a loop, a loop with many `continue`s and
`isinstance` tests, a long chain of assignments a loop carries, many loops one after another, each
with a lazy initialization (the blocks each covers count toward a budget proportional to the
source), many waits on one future before many `await`s of it, task factories at the end of a long
chain of copies, a long chain of aliases of a class with an attribute store through the last one per
alias, a class with thousands of subclasses whose class constant as many functions read on an
instance, a strict `read-owners` target on such a class that as many functions read on an object of
unknown class, as many calls of a method of such a class that a call target naming no class names, a
module binding thousands of names each to an attribute of the one before, a function making twenty
thousand calls of eight operands each, a helper that types nothing making thousands of strict
accesses of one name that one caller calls as many times, a helper that types nothing reading,
calling, or writing one strict target name thousands of times, which a caller calls as many times,
many `is` tests each followed by a conditional expression on the tested parameter, many branches on
a long chain of copies of one `is` test, a long chain of returned calls each handed the previous
call's result as two of its arguments, a long chain of returned aliases each appended to one list or
to a new list of its own, a long chain of conditional expressions each choosing between a call of
the previous value and the value, one returned call handed the last of a long chain of item reads as
each of its arguments, a loop carrying a long chain of assignments in reverse, a loop rotating
aliases of many `self` containers, a chain of merges of many `self` containers, a loop over a
generator whose body makes many calls, loops whose bodies hold many conditional blocks one after
another, a function consuming a generator's result many times in a row, a loop over a `zip` of many
generator results whose body makes as many calls, a loop over a `zip` of thousands of `self`
containers whose body makes as many calls, one `zip` of thousands of `self` containers stepped by as
many `yield from`s, a generator handed on through thousands of private wrappers, each returning the
one before's result, an edit through the language server changing every method of a class of
thousands of methods, methods changing a typed dict of `self` thousands of times, a method storing
under a key after each of hundreds of tests that such a dict holds the key, and a function reading
attributes down a chain ten thousand deep (`x = x.child`).

A change to the IR builder, a walk, a fixpoint, or a rule's state is also run over a large
corpus of real projects before it is merged, every run under a memory cap and a timeout. No
project may take tens of times more per byte than the rest.

## Documentation

```console
$ cargo build --release
$ python scripts/build_docs.py --heki target/release/heki   # rules and CLI reference pages
$ python scripts/build_llms_txt.py                          # llms.txt / llms-full.txt
$ uvx --from "zensical==0.1.2" zensical serve
```

- Rule documentation lives in `crates/heki_rules/rule-docs/<CODE>.md`: `heki rule <CODE>` prints
  it, and the generator copies it into `docs/rules/`. CI fails when the generated pages are
  stale.
- Experimental features are listed, each with why it is experimental, in
  `crates/heki_rules/src/experimental.rs`. `heki rule <CODE>` and the generated pages (the rule
  pages and [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/)) read the list, and the generator fails
  when a hand-written page marks a rule differently. An experimental feature can change or go
  away in any release, and the release notes list each change; once it is stable, its entry is
  removed.
- The Docs workflow deploys the site to Cloudflare Pages (heki.koxudaxi.dev) once a published
  release is on PyPI (the newest release only), or when it is run by hand on `main`, so the site
  documents the released version. That job runs in the `docs-production` environment, which
  admits only `main` and release tags.
- A pull request from this repository gets a preview deployment of the same Pages project, on the
  branch `pr-<number>`. Both use the repository secrets `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and
  `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`.

## Releases

The Release Draft workflow (`.github/workflows/release-draft.yml`) keeps a draft GitHub release
of the next version. Publishing the draft runs `release.yml`, which builds and publishes heki, and
the Release Sync workflow (`.github/workflows/release-sync.yml`), which brings `main` to the
release. A draft is published by hand, and only while no Release Draft run is queued or running.

The release tag is the version (`v` + the version), so nothing is bumped before a release. Right
after checking out the tag, every `release.yml` job that builds writes the version into
`pyproject.toml`, `Cargo.toml` (`workspace.package.version` and the internal crates under
`workspace.dependencies`), and the workspace entries of `Cargo.lock`
(`scripts/set_release_versions.py`, which fails when a value it rewrites is not found exactly
once), and the release fails unless every wheel, the source distribution, and the executable
declare it. Nothing is committed: `main` declares the newest release once the sync pull request
is merged.

### How a draft accumulates

After each push to `main`, the workflow takes the pull requests merged at the commits the push
added (several when a stack merges at once). For each one, Claude reads the merged diff and
decides whether it breaks something the newest published release has. A change is breaking
when:

- existing code gets new reports from the rules enabled by default: a new rule enabled by
  default, a rule turned on by default, or wider detection in a rule enabled by default;
- a rule enabled by default becomes opt-in or is removed;
- a rule's default severity changes;
- a rule code or name changes;
- configuration keys or their meaning, command-line options, or exit codes change, including how
  `requires-python` selects the target Python version;
- fields of the JSON or SARIF output are removed or change meaning;
- the language server behavior that editors rely on changes;
- the format of `--fix` rewrites changes;
- the supported Python versions or platforms change.

These are not breaking: a change that only removes false reports, in a default or an opt-in rule
(a fixed false positive), even though it narrows what the rule detects; new opt-in rules; new
optional keys and new output fields; and any change to a feature that `docs/experimental.md`
lists. The analysis context that Claude reads holds that page as the trusted checkout of `main`
has it (while the page does not exist, no feature is experimental), and Claude describes each
change to an experimental feature separately. The workflow then:

- adds the breaking changes to the draft's `## Breaking Changes` section, under one heading per
  kind, the changes to experimental features to `## Experimental`, and a line
  `* <title> (#<number>)` to `## Changes`, except for pull requests labeled `maintenance` or
  `dependencies`; every item ends with `(#<number>)`;
- labels a breaking pull request `breaking-change`, comments the result on every pull request,
  and labels each `breaking-change-analyzed`, so that a re-run skips it. A pull request analyzed
  again keeps one comment, which is updated, and loses `breaking-change` when it is no longer
  found breaking.

The draft's tag is the version after the newest published release: a breaking change bumps the
minor version (0.1.x to 0.2.0), anything else the patch, and manifests that already name a
later version win (a pull request that sets a later version in them picks a larger bump). Text
added to the draft by hand is kept. Pull requests that change only tests, documentation,
development scripts, or the CI workflows skip Claude and count as not breaking. While no release is published, the workflow does nothing: the notes of the first
release come from `CHANGELOG.md`.

### Publishing a release

1. Check that the first unreleased section of `CHANGELOG.md` is headed
   `## [<version>] - Unreleased`, with the version of the draft's tag: the sync dates that
   section.
2. Wait until no Release Draft run is queued or in progress
   (`gh run list --workflow release-draft.yml`), then reload the draft and publish it on GitHub.
   GitHub cannot make a draft update conditional on the release still being a draft, so a run
   that updates the draft while it is published rewrites the published tag, title, and notes
   (the run then warns), and a draft page loaded before the run's update publishes without it.
3. The Release Sync workflow opens the pull request `chore: sync release metadata for <version>`
   from the branch `release/sync-<version>`, labeled `maintenance` to keep it out of the next
   draft's changes. It writes the version into the manifests and `Cargo.lock`, renames the
   section heading to `## [<version>] - <publish date>` (the UTC date), and makes the
   `[<version>]` compare link end at the release tag instead of `HEAD` (a missing link compares
   the previous release with the tag). When a section is headed `[Unreleased]`, its link compares
   the tag with `HEAD`. The entries stay as they were written.
4. GitHub creates the CI runs of a pull request that a workflow opens with `GITHUB_TOKEN` in an
   approval-required state, and the checks of a run started with `workflow_dispatch` do not
   count for the required checks of `main`. Close and reopen the pull request to start CI
   (`gh pr close <number> && gh pr reopen <number>`), or select **Approve workflows to run** in
   its merge box, and merge it once CI passes.

When the sync fails, for example because `CHANGELOG.md` has no section for the version, fix
`main` in a pull request and run it again with
`gh workflow run release-sync.yml --ref main -f tag=v<version>`. A run whose changes `main`
already has opens nothing, and a run for an open sync pull request updates it. A pre-release,
and a release older than the version `main` declares (a backport published late), leave `main`
as it is.

The builds can be tried without publishing:
`gh workflow run release.yml --ref <branch> -f version=<version>` builds and checks the
distributions with that version (it cannot be combined with `publish`), and without `version` they
keep the version of the committed manifests.

One-time setup, done for this repository: **Settings > Actions > General > Workflow permissions >
Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests**, which lets the sync open its pull
request with `GITHUB_TOKEN`. The sync needs no secret, and the ruleset of `main` is unchanged.

### Replays and dry runs

```console
$ gh workflow run release-draft.yml --ref main -f pr_number=123
$ gh workflow run release-draft.yml --ref <branch> -f pr_number=123 -f dry_run=true
```

- A replay on `main` analyzes one merged pull request again, for example after a failed run. A
  pull request labeled `breaking-change-analyzed` is skipped: remove the label first. One that a
  published release already holds is skipped too, so that its changes are not listed again in
  the next draft; a dry run still analyzes it.
- Up to 100 runs wait for the one in progress, in order. GitHub cancels a run that arrives while
  100 are waiting, and a later run does not take over its pull requests. A canceled run shows in
  `gh run list --workflow release-draft.yml --status cancelled`. Its pull requests are among those
  merged after the first published release that still lack `breaking-change-analyzed`. List them
  with `gh pr list --state merged --limit 1000 --search "-label:breaking-change-analyzed
  merged:>=<first-release-date>"` (`gh pr list` shows 30 without `--limit`, and a search returns
  at most 1,000, so split the date range when it lists 1,000), and replay each of them, in merge
  order.
- A dry run works from any branch, so a change to the workflow can be tried before it is on
  `main`. It prints the analysis, the planned draft, and the comments in the run's log, and
  changes no label, comment, or release. The pull request must be merged into `main`, and a
  release must be published.

The Claude step authenticates with the repository secret `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, an OAuth
token of a Claude subscription (`claude setup-token` creates one). No other step receives it.

The scripts of the workflow have tests, which CI runs on every pull request:

```console
$ uvx --python 3.12 --from "pytest==8.4.2" --with "pyyaml==6.0.3" --with "jsonschema==4.25.1" pytest scripts/tests
```

## Architecture

The workspace is split by responsibility (`crates/`):

| Crate | Role |
| ----- | ---- |
| `heki_ast` | the only crate that depends on the parser (`ruff_python_parser`, pinned) |
| `heki_semantic` | scopes and bindings, checked against CPython's `symtable` |
| `heki_ir` | SSA control-flow-graph IR with explicit exception edges and loop information |
| `heki_kb` | the knowledge bases: Layer 1 (builtins semantics for the soundness lane) and Layer 2 (ecosystem effects) |
| `heki_env` | configuration loading and the runtime profile of the target Python version |
| `heki_effect` | call graph, per-function effect summaries, incremental project index |
| `heki_soundness` | the alias analysis and proof obligations behind `OPT` rewrites (never depends on `heki_effect`, never reads annotations) |
| `heki_rules` | the rules, rule selection, project discovery |
| `heki_diagnostics` | output formats, inline suppressions, Ratchet baselines, fix application |
| `heki_profile` | offline profile dumps |
| `heki_lsp` | the incremental LSP server and the `--watch` engine |
| `heki` | the command-line interface |

The internal design docs are in the repository:

| Document | Content |
| -------- | ------- |
| [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md) | the design |
| [`docs/ANALYSIS_AND_KB_SPEC.md`](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/docs/ANALYSIS_AND_KB_SPEC.md) | the analyses and knowledge bases |
| [`docs/DESIGN_HISTORY_AND_ADR.md`](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/docs/DESIGN_HISTORY_AND_ADR.md) | the decisions |


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-call/

# async-blocking-call (EFF101)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Direct or indirect blocking network/DB/subprocess/sleep call reachable from `async def`.

## What it does
Checks `async def` functions that reach a blocking call on the event loop, directly or through
synchronous helpers: network I/O (`requests`, `httpx.Client`, `urllib`), host name lookups
(`socket.getaddrinfo` / `gethostbyname` / `getfqdn`; the event loop has `loop.getaddrinfo()`;
`getaddrinfo` with the `AI_NUMERICHOST` flag only parses an address and is not reported),
database drivers
(`sqlite3`, `psycopg`, `pymongo`, ...; the fetches of a named, server-side psycopg cursor
`conn.cursor("name")` too), subprocesses waiting for completion, `time.sleep`, and
waits on other threads (acquiring a `threading` lock, `Event.wait()`, `Thread.join()`,
`queue.Queue.get()` / `put()`, `Future.result()`, `concurrent.futures.wait()`; a zero timeout or
`blocking=False` / `block=False` returns at once and is not reported, also when a helper passes
on its own flag parameter and its caller passes `False`: `close(wait=False)` over
`shutdown(wait=wait)`; so does `result()` / `exception()` of a `concurrent.futures.Future` known
to be done: under `if f.done():` (also after `if not f.done(): return`, a `while not f.done():`
poll, or with `and`), or once `await asyncio.wrap_future(f)` has returned, on every path to the
call). A function SQLAlchemy's
`AsyncSession.run_sync(fn)` / `AsyncConnection.run_sync(fn)` runs is called on the event loop:
its database I/O through the session or connection it receives is awaited for it, its other
blocking calls are reported. Where an argument decides what a library call does, a literal
one is followed: `pd.read_csv("https://...")` downloads the file.

Reading a `@property` or `functools.cached_property` attribute of a project class runs its
getter, so the read counts as a call of the getter (`self.client` whose getter opens a
connection). A property that also defines a setter or deleter is not followed.

Calling a generator function only creates the generator; its body runs where the generator is
iterated: a `for` loop or comprehension over it, unpacking it, `yield from` it, a call that
consumes it (`list(...)`, `sorted(...)`, `"".join(...)`, `items.extend(...)`, ...), a lazy wrapper
iterated there (`enumerate(...)`, `zip(...)`, `itertools.islice(...)`, ...), or a project
function iterating the parameter it is handed. A generator returned by a plain function runs
where its caller iterates it. `next(gen)` runs the body only up to its first `yield`, which heki
does not separate from the rest, so it is not followed.

A call whose arguments switch off the callee's branch with the blocking call is not followed
into it: `load(name, cache=False)` does not reach the request under `if cache:`. The branches
are the callee's tests of its parameters: truthiness, `is None`, `isinstance` with builtin,
`io`, or `os.PathLike` classes, and `hasattr` (which a value's class decides for the methods of
the file protocol: `read`, `write`, `close`, ...), also of a parameter the callee rebinds on
some paths (`if buf is None: buf = io.StringIO()`, then `if isinstance(buf, str): open(buf)`
opens a file only for a path argument). The arguments that decide them are constants and the
literal defaults of omitted ones (`False`, `None`, `0`, `""`, empty displays), values whose
exact class the caller knows (a display or comprehension, or an `io.StringIO` / `io.BytesIO` it
constructs, also held in a variable: `fetch(io.BytesIO(data))` does not reach the download
under `if not hasattr(src, "read"):`; an instance of a subclass does not count), and tests the
caller has already made on the same value: a call made only when `isinstance(self._input,
PathLike)` is false does not reach the callee's branch for `isinstance(self._input, PathLike)`.
A generator's branches are decided at the call that creates it. Lazy initialization does not
relax this rule: a connection opened once still blocks the event loop that once.

The rule reports the boundary: the call (or property read, or iteration) inside the `async def`
that leads to the blocking operation, with the call chain as related information. Several
boundaries reaching the same blocking call are shown as one report with a count once more than
ten of them are shown (in the editor, per file). Inline suppressions and Ratchet baselines see
every boundary: suppressing the first one leaves the others reported, and a baseline counts each.

It does not report:

- calls offloaded to a thread (`asyncio.to_thread`, `loop.run_in_executor`,
  `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`, `run_in_threadpool`, `asgiref`'s `sync_to_async`,
  `asyncer.asyncify`, and project wrappers that forward their callable to them; what the
  offloaded function does besides blocking still counts where it is called, such as its
  queries in a loop for `EFF103`);
- functions decorated to run on a thread: `@sync_to_async` (also as a factory,
  `@sync_to_async(thread_sensitive=False)`), `channels`' `@database_sync_to_async`, `@asyncify`,
  and any decorator declared with `offloads-blocking-arg = 0`. `@d def f` is `f = d(f)`, so
  calling `f` calls `d(f)`; other decorators (`functools.wraps` wrappers) are followed;
- generators that leave the `async def` without being iterated there: returned, stored, or
  handed to a call that is not a consuming one, such as `StreamingResponse(rows())` or
  `iterate_in_threadpool(rows())` (whatever iterates them later, often a thread pool, is not
  analyzed);
- `async` APIs, also where they are not awaited directly (`async with`, `asyncio.gather`,
  `asyncio.wait_for`): `httpx.AsyncClient`, `aiohttp`, `redis.asyncio`, SQLAlchemy's
  `AsyncSession`, psycopg's `AsyncConnection`, pymongo's `AsyncMongoClient`, ...;
- clients that connect on first use (`redis.Redis(...)`, `pymongo.MongoClient(...)`, except
  that a `mongodb+srv://` URI literal is resolved in the constructor unless `connect=False`,
  `pymysql.connect(..., defer_connect=True)`, `sqlalchemy.create_engine(...)`) and calls that
  only build an object (`Redis.pipeline()`, a
  lazy Django `QuerySet.filter(...)`): the call that does the I/O is the one reported;
- spawning a process without waiting (`subprocess.Popen(...)`);
- private coroutine functions that only run through a synchronous driver without an event loop
  (`.send(None)`, a `run_sync` function); `asyncio.run(...)` runs its coroutine on an event loop,
  where blocking stops the tasks it starts;
- CLI commands (`@click.command`, `@app.command`), ASGI lifespan handlers, and tests
  (`test_*` functions and files under `tests/`, see the option below).

## Why is this bad?
A blocking call inside a coroutine stops the whole event loop: every other request, timer, and
task waits until it returns.

## Example
```python
import time


def load() -> bytes:
    time.sleep(1)
    return b""


async def handler() -> bytes:
    return load()  # EFF101: reaches `time.sleep`
```

Use instead:
```python
import asyncio


async def handler() -> bytes:
    return await asyncio.to_thread(load)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.relax-async-in-tests` (default `true`): skip test code.
- `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]` declares project functions as blocking (`effects`), as offload
  wrappers (`offloads-blocking-arg`; with `0`, also an offloading decorator), or as async-safe
  (`async-safe`).


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-fs/

# async-blocking-fs (EFF105)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Opt-in · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Opt-in: blocking local filesystem I/O reachable from `async def`.

## What it does
Checks `async def` functions that reach blocking local filesystem I/O: `open(...)`,
`pathlib.Path.read_text` / `write_text` / `read_bytes` / `write_bytes` / `open`, `os.listdir`,
`os.scandir`, iterating `os.walk(...)`, `shutil` copies and removals, file metadata (`os.stat`,
`os.path.exists` / `isfile` / `isdir` / `realpath`, `pathlib.Path.exists` / `stat` / `is_file` /
`is_dir` / `resolve`, Starlette's `StaticFiles.lookup_path`), and the pandas file readers
(`pd.read_csv(path)`; one given a URL literal downloads it and is `EFF101`, one given an
`io.StringIO` / `io.BytesIO` buffer does no I/O). It follows the same boundary,
offload, and guard rules as `EFF101`, generators and offloading decorators included: `await
in_thread(self.open) if isinstance(self._input, PathLike) else self.open()` is not reported
when `open` only opens a file under `isinstance(self._input, PathLike)`, and neither is
`save(text, io.StringIO())` when `save` opens its argument only where `hasattr(buf, "write")`
is false, or `save(text)` when it opens it only where `isinstance(buf, str)` holds after
`if buf is None: buf = io.StringIO()`.

This rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select EFF105` or `extend-select = ["EFF105"]`.
Selecting the `EFF` prefix does not enable it.

## Why is this bad?
Local file I/O is usually fast, which is why it is opt-in, but on network file systems, large
files, or busy disks it blocks the event loop like any other blocking call.

## Example
```python
async def read_config(path: str) -> str:
    with open(path) as f:  # EFF105
        return f.read()
```

Use instead:
```python
import asyncio
from pathlib import Path


async def read_config(path: str) -> str:
    return await asyncio.to_thread(Path(path).read_text)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["EFF105"]` enables the rule.
- `lint.relax-async-in-tests` applies as for `EFF101`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-mutation/

# cached-property-stale-mutation (MUT101)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Mutating an attribute read by `@cached_property` without invalidating the cache.

!!! warning "Experimental"

    Its precision outside a few code bases is still low. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Opt-in: enable it with `extend-select = ["MUT101"]`.

Checks for methods that rebind or mutate an attribute that a `@functools.cached_property`
of the same class (or of a subclass) reads, without invalidating the cached value. A method the
class inherits from a project base class and does not override runs on its instances too, so it
is checked against the class's cached properties (reported in the base class).
A decorator is known by what its name is bound to in the module: an import alias counts
(`from functools import cached_property as cached`), a decorator the module defines itself does
not (a `def cache(fn)` of its own), and a name bound by neither counts by its spelling.

## Why is this bad?
A `cached_property` computes its value once and stores it in the instance `__dict__`. Once the
attribute it was computed from changes, the property keeps returning the old value until the
cache entry is deleted. The stale value is usually noticed far away from the write.

The rule follows `self.helper()` calls in both directions (a property that reads through a
helper, a method that writes through a helper) and the getters of the properties the cached
property reads (`self.key` where the `@property` `key` reads `self.name`), and reports the write
itself, once per property. A property that also defines a setter or deleter is not followed.
It does not report:

- two-phase initialization: `__init__`, `__post_init__`, `model_post_init`, `__setstate__`,
  `__enter__`, `setup`, `setup_*` / `_setup_*` / `_init_*` / `_configure_*` methods, and private helpers called from
  `__init__`;
- classes with a metaclass other than `type` / `abc.ABCMeta` along their MRO (also one heki
  cannot resolve): the metaclass may turn attribute writes into descriptor calls (a generated
  property whose setter invalidates the cached value), which heki does not see;
- memo / cache dictionaries (`self._cache[key] = value`, `setdefault`, the
  `if key not in self._memo:` pattern): in-place changes of an attribute with a `cache` or
  `memo` word in its name; rebinding it (`self.cache_size = n`) and names such as
  `memory_limit` are no memo operation;
- constant dictionary keys the property never reads (`self.params["proxy"]` while the property
  reads `self.params["outtmpl"]`);
- writes after which every path invalidates the property (`del self.prop`,
  `self.__dict__.pop("prop", None)`, also with the key in a string constant as `MUT201` follows
  it, a `self` method that does), or before which every path already did and nothing read it
  since; an invalidation under a condition, such as
  `if clear:`, leaves the other path stale and is reported;
- private helpers whose every caller invalidates the property;
- lazy initialization: a write where a `None` / falsy test of the attribute found it unset
  (`if self._conn is None: self._conn = connect()`, also in a `@property` getter), when the
  cached property reads the attribute only through such initializations
  (`return self._connect().db`): computing the cached value set the attribute, so the test
  cannot find it unset again. A cached property that reads it directly
  (`return self._conn is not None`) may have cached its unset value and is reported;
- changes made in place (`clear()`, `append()`, item assignment) to an attribute whose object
  the cached value holds itself, when the getter reads it for nothing else: it returns
  `self.items`, or puts it as itself into a display or a container it returns
  (`{"items": self.items}`, `ctx["k"] = (x, self.items)`). The cached value sees those changes;
  rebinding the attribute (`self.items = []`) is still reported. A getter that also computes
  from it (`len(self.items)`), copies it (`list(self.items)`, `(*self.items,)`), reads it through
  a `self` method or property, or hands `self` to other code is reported as before. A `self`
  call whose result the getter discards (`self.finalize()` before `return self.items`) counts
  only when it writes an attribute the getter reads, itself or through a call whose result it
  uses.

## Example
```python
from functools import cached_property


class Settings:
    def __init__(self, raw: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        self.raw = raw

    @cached_property
    def keys(self) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        return tuple(self.raw)

    def replace(self, raw: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        self.raw = raw  # `self.keys` still returns the old keys
```

Use instead:
```python
    def replace(self, raw: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        self.raw = raw
        self.__dict__.pop("keys", None)  # or `del self.keys` when it was computed
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix: whether to invalidate, recompute, or make the attribute read-only is a design
decision.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-read/

# cached-property-stale-read (MUT111)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Opt-in: reading a `@cached_property` that a method of its class family can leave stale (a write `MUT101` reports).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    It reports the readers of the stale writes `MUT101` finds, so it shares `MUT101`'s precision. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Checks for functions that read a `@functools.cached_property` that a method can leave stale: a
method that changes an attribute the property reads without invalidating the cached value, as
`MUT101` reports it. The rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select MUT111` or
`extend-select = ["MUT111"]`.

A read is one in the function's own body, on any object of the class: `self.prop`, `obj.prop`
on a parameter, attribute, or value whose class heki knows (as for `MUT203`),
`getattr(obj, "prop")`, and `obj.__dict__["prop"]` / `obj.__dict__.get("prop")`. The object may
be an instance of the read's class or of any project subclass of it. The read is reported when
an instance of one of those classes runs both the cached property and the method that leaves it
stale: the first definition of each along its MRO, or one that the definitions before it call
through `super()` without invalidating the property themselves. A method of a sibling class, or
one that a subclass replaces without calling it, does not count for that subclass's instances.

A `@property` getter or a helper that reads the cached property is the function reported; the
functions calling it are not. One new reader of a stale value is one new diagnostic under a
Ratchet baseline. The rule reports one diagnostic per function and property name, at the first
read, and lists every method that can leave the value stale as related locations.

The writes count whatever is selected: `MUT101` need not be enabled, and a `MUT101` diagnostic
suppressed at the write still counts. It does not report what `MUT101` does not: a property
whose writers invalidate it on every path, whose inputs are set only during two-phase
initialization, or that no method changes.

## Why is this bad?
A `cached_property` computes its value once and keeps it in the instance `__dict__`. After a
method changes what the value was computed from, every later read returns the old value. A
function that reads the property depends on whether it runs before or after that method, which
nothing at the read shows.

## Example
```python
from functools import cached_property


class Parser:
    def __init__(self, raw: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        self.raw = raw

    @cached_property
    def dialect(self) -> str:
        return self.raw.get("$schema", "")

    def parse_all(self, docs: list[dict[str, str]]) -> None:
        for doc in docs:
            self.raw = doc  # MUT101: `dialect` keeps the first document's value
            self.parse_one()

    def parse_one(self) -> bool:
        return self.dialect == "draft-07"  # MUT111
```

Use instead:
```python
    def parse_all(self, docs: list[dict[str, str]]) -> None:
        for doc in docs:
            self.raw = doc
            self.__dict__.pop("dialect", None)
            self.parse_one()
```

## How to fix
Invalidate the cached value where it goes stale (`self.__dict__.pop("dialect", None)`, or
`del self.dialect` once it was computed), compute the value without caching it where its inputs
change, or make sure the reading function only runs before the method that changes them.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix: whether to invalidate, recompute, or reorder is a design decision.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/call-owner-violation/

# call-owner-violation (MUT204)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Calling a guarded function or method, or constructing a guarded class (directly, via a bound method, `getattr`, or a helper), outside declared `call-owners`.

## What it does
Checks calls of functions and methods, and constructions of classes, that a
`[[tool.heki.call-owners]]` contract reserves for a set of allowed callers: the call side of
`MUT201` (who may write) and `MUT203` (who may read). A call is reported when it happens outside
the allowed callers and resolves to a target:

- a method called on an instance of the target's class or of a subclass, including an override of
  the method in a subclass (`data_type.replace_reference(ref)`);
- the same method through a bound-method alias (`replace = data_type.replace_reference`, then
  `replace(ref)`) or `getattr(data_type, "replace_reference")(...)` with a constant name;
- a module-level function (`pkg.util.reset_cache()`);
- a class: constructing it or a subclass (`FinalFacts(...)`, `pkg.facts.FinalFacts(...)`,
  `cls(...)` in a class method), also for a dataclass or another class without an `__init__` of
  its own.

A call is reported only when every function it may call is a target: when the receiver's class
hierarchy also offers a method that is no target (a receiver typed with a base class whose own
`replace_reference` is not guarded), the call is not reported. The functions it may call can be
targets of different entries of one contract: with `A.reset` and `B.reset` both listed, `obj.reset()`
on `obj: Base`, whose subclasses `A` and `B` implement `reset`, is one report for
`A.reset|B.reset`. A call on a receiver whose class heki does not know (an unannotated
parameter, `Any`) is not seen; with `unresolved = "report"`,
`MUT207` reports it.

A private helper (`_name`, or a comprehension, generator expression, or lambda scope) with project
callers hands its calls to its callers: the call is reported at the call sites of the first
non-private callers, with the chain of calls down to the call as related information. A call runs
where the body holding it runs, as for `MUT201`: a generator's calls where it is iterated (a
generator an allowed caller creates and returns calls outside it when its caller iterates it), a
coroutine's where it is awaited. Not reported either:

- a function that only runs inside allowed callers: it has project callers, and every path of
  callers above it starts in an allowed caller, an exempt method, or a class's own
  initialization (as for `MUT201`);
- a class's own initialization: an initializer (`__init__`, `__post_init__`, ...) of a class of
  the target's family calling a guarded method on its own `self` (for a target naming no class,
  `reset`, the family is the classes defining the methods it names and their subclasses);
- a target calling a target of the same contract (`remove_reference` calling
  `self.replace_reference(None)`, an override calling `super().replace_reference(...)`): the
  guarded operation is checked where it is called, so what it does inside is part of it.

## Why is this bad?
Some operations keep invariants only when one component runs them: a store that updates its
indexes after redirecting a reference, a factory that builds a sealed object exactly once. A
direct call from elsewhere skips the bookkeeping, and nothing fails until an input exercises the
stale state. A linter cannot tell `data_type.replace_reference(ref)` from `text.replace("a", "b")`
without the receiver's class, and an import rule cannot forbid a method of an object the caller
legitimately imports. The contract states the ownership once in configuration.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.call-owners]]
name = "reference-mutators"
targets = ["DataType.replace_reference", "FinalFacts"]
allowed-callers = ["pkg.store.GenerationStore.*"]
message = "use a GenerationStore operation instead"
```

```python
# pkg/store.py
class GenerationStore:
    def replace_data_type_ref(self, data_type: DataType, ref: Reference) -> None:
        data_type.replace_reference(ref)  # allowed caller


def swap(data_type: DataType, ref: Reference) -> None:
    data_type.replace_reference(ref)  # MUT204: outside `pkg.store.GenerationStore.*`


def rename(text: str) -> str:
    return text.replace("a", "b")  # not reported: a `str`, not a `DataType`
```

Use instead:
```python
def swap(store: GenerationStore, data_type: DataType, ref: Reference) -> None:
    store.replace_data_type_ref(data_type, ref)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.call-owners]]`:
  - `name`: the contract name, shown in messages.
  - `targets`: functions, methods, or classes, as dotted names or globs matched against the fully
    qualified name and any dotted suffix (`DataType.replace_reference`, `pkg.util.reset_cache`,
    `FinalFacts`, `Parser._*`). A `Class.method` target covers the method's overrides in
    subclasses; a class target covers constructing the class and its subclasses; a target
    naming no class (`reset`) covers every project function and method of that name.
  - `allowed-callers`: functions allowed to call the targets, as dotted names or globs matched
    against the function's qualified name and its `Class.method` qualname (`pkg.store.*`).
  - `forbidden-callers`: when set, only calls by these functions are reported (matched like
    `allowed-callers`); `allowed-callers` and `exempt-methods` stay exceptions inside them. A
    call is in scope when the reporting function or one of the private helpers it hands the call
    through is forbidden (`forbidden-callers = ["pkg.parser.*"]`: the parser layer must not call
    the targets).
  - `exempt-methods`: methods allowed to call the targets (`__deepcopy__`); a plain name matches
    any function or method of that name, an entry with a dot or a glob is matched like
    `allowed-callers`.
  - `message`: the help of every report of the contract.
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`: also report the calls the contract cannot
    tie to a class, under `MUT207`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/conditional-ownership-mutation/

# conditional-ownership-mutation (MUT112)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Opt-in: changing in place a value that is a new object on one path and borrowed state (a parameter, an attribute, a global, or what a function returns of such state) on another.

!!! warning "Experimental"

    Its precision on real code bases is still low: much of what it reports is code that changes a borrowed container on purpose. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Checks for a container that is a new object on one path and borrowed state on another, and that
is then changed in place. The rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select MUT112` or
`extend-select = ["MUT112"]`.

A value is a new object where the function makes it: a display (`[]`, `{}`), a comprehension, a
copy (`list(x)`, `dict(x)`, `x.copy()`, `copy.copy`), a constructor call, an operator's result
(`a + b`), or a call of a project function that returns a new object. It is borrowed where it
comes from state that outlives the call: a parameter, an attribute, a global, a variable of an
enclosing function, an element of one of these, or a call of a project function that returns
such state. An attribute of an object the function makes itself (`visitor = Visitor()`, then
`visitor.errors`) is part of that object, not borrowed state. The paths meet in a conditional
expression or an `if`:

- `items = given or []`, `items = given if given else []`;
- `options = dict(defaults, **extra) if extra else defaults`;
- `seen = registry.get(key, {})`, `tags = getattr(obj, "tags", [])`;
- `x = shared`, then `if c: x = []`.

What a project function returns is part of its summary, through any number of wrappers: a
function that returns its argument on one path and a new object on another makes its call's
result both when the caller passes borrowed state, also when that state is what another call
returns (`identity(identity(shared))`), and one returning an attribute it caches makes its
call's result borrowed. Only the returns a run can reach count: a `return` after a
`while True:` loop that no `break` leaves, or under `if False:`, returns nothing.

A change is an item assignment or deletion, a container method (`append`, `extend`, `update`,
`setdefault`, `pop`, ...), an in-place operator on a `list`, `dict`, `set`, or `bytearray`, or a
call of a project function that changes the container it is handed. The rule reports the first
change of the value in the function. It also reports:

- a change made by a closure to a variable of the enclosing function that holds such a value;
- a store of such a value in `self.<attr>` when a method of the class, of a subclass, or of a
  base class changes that attribute in place (`self.items.append(x)`, through an alias, or
  through a helper), at the store.

It does not report:

- a value that is a new object on every path, or borrowed on every path;
- a value rebound to a copy before the change (`x = list(x)`), also when the copy is made only
  where the value is still the borrowed object (`if x is shared: x = shared.copy()`);
- a value that a flag of the caller's copies, a test of parameters alone
  (`if not in_place: x = x.copy()`, `list(x) if copy else x`): where it does not copy, the
  function changes the borrowed object on purpose. A copy that another test picks
  (`x if isinstance(x, set) else set(x)`, `if config.get("strict"): x = set(x)`) still counts;
- the accumulator idiom, where a parameter is replaced by a new object only when it is `None`
  or a sentinel (`if out is None: out = []`, `out = [] if out is None else out`): the function
  fills what its caller hands it. Such a value counts when it may also be a new object the test
  does not select (`x = [] if fresh else out` after it), and when it is also stored on `self`,
  where the instance keeps the caller's object. A test that replaces nothing (`if out is None:
  raise ...`) leaves the parameter borrowed;
- a new object the function stores in other state before the paths meet
  (`rows = table[key] = []`, `table.setdefault(key, rows)`): it is that state's on every path;
- a value stored back where it borrows from, the same attribute of the same object or an item
  of the same container (`self.items = self.items or []`, `d[k] = d.get(k) or []`, but not
  `self.items = other.items or []`);
- attributes named as memos or caches (`_cache`, `memo`), which are meant to be filled;
- removing from a value whose new objects all start empty (`d.get(k, {}).pop(x, None)`): the
  removal does nothing to them;
- a conditional expression changed in place without a name (`(a if c else b).append(x)`): the
  code picks the container on purpose;
- attribute assignments, and changes of a value below the borrowed one (`x[0].append(1)`): a
  copy of `x` shares those too;
- `self` in its own methods, and paths a branch on a constant never takes (`while True:`).

## Why is this bad?
The function treats the value as its own on one path and changes a shared object on the other.
The caller's list, a cached dictionary, or a class attribute changes only when the borrowed path
runs, for example only when the caller passes a non-empty list, so the bug shows up far away and
on some inputs only.

## Example
```python
def collect(name: str, scopes: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:
    use_scopes = scopes or []
    use_scopes.extend(lookup(name))  # MUT112: changes the caller's list when it is not empty
    return use_scopes
```

Use instead:
```python
def collect(name: str, scopes: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:
    use_scopes = list(scopes or [])
    use_scopes.extend(lookup(name))
    return use_scopes
```

## Known limitations
- The paths are not told apart by the tests on them: a value that an `if v is SENTINEL: return`
  excludes, or a callee that returns its argument only when it is not a container, still counts,
  and so does a callee's borrowed return that a constant argument rules out
  (`convert(data, ensure_copy=True)` where `convert` returns `data` itself only without it).
- A new object that a function gets from a project call and stores on its argument before
  returning it (`state = runtime.state = make_state()`) still counts as new for its callers,
  which change the argument's state.
- Calls of `async def` functions and generators are not followed: their results are not what
  their bodies return.
- A store in an attribute is followed for `self` only.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["MUT112"]` enables the rule.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/effect-boundary-violation/

# effect-boundary-violation (EFF201)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Reaching a forbidden effect (directly or through calls) from a declared `effect-boundaries` scope.

## What it does
Checks the functions of a declared effect boundary (`[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]`): they
must not reach a forbidden effect, directly or through the functions they call. Reading a
`@property` or `functools.cached_property` attribute of a project class calls its getter; a
property that also defines a setter or deleter is not followed, so its setter's writes never
count for a read.

- `scopes` select the checked functions. A pattern names a module (`pkg.domain`,
  `pkg.domain.*`), a class (`pkg.Renderer`), or a function (`*.render`); every function defined
  inside a matched name is in scope, nested functions included. Patterns are matched against
  the function's qualified name, its qualname, and every dotted prefix of them, so `render` also
  selects a module named `render`.
- `forbid` lists the forbidden effects:
  - `blocking-net`, `blocking-db`, `blocking-fs`, `blocking-subprocess`, `blocking-sync`,
    `sleep`, or `blocking` for all six: blocking calls of the ecosystem knowledge base
    (`requests.get`, `sqlite3`, `open`, `subprocess.run`, `time.sleep`, ...);
  - `writes-targets`: writes to the `Class.attr` entries of `write-targets` (and their
    subclasses), or to one entry of the container an attribute holds (`Class.attr["key"]`), in
    every form `MUT201` follows, through the receivers whose class `MUT201` sees (the items of
    annotated containers included); a class's own initialization is no write (constructing a
    fresh object runs its `__init__`), and neither is a write that constructs the object it
    writes (`fresh-objects = "allow"`, the default; a write the reached function makes to an
    object it allocated), as for `MUT201`;
  - `reads-targets`: reads of the `Class.attr` entries of `read-targets` (and their
    subclasses), in every form `MUT203` follows (`obj.attr`, `getattr(obj, "attr")`,
    `obj.__dict__["attr"]`, a property getter that reads it); an initializer reading its own
    instance is no read;
  - `calls`: calls of the `call-targets` entries, matched as the targets of `MUT204`: a function,
    a method (with its overrides in subclasses, through bound-method aliases and `getattr` with a
    constant name), or a class (constructing it); a call is one only when every function it may
    call is a target;
  - `mutates-params`: mutating a parameter, its attributes, or its contents. For a method,
    parameter 0 is `self`, so a method writing `self.x` mutates a parameter.
- `write-universe` with `allow-writes` states the writes a scope may make positively: a reached
  write of a `write-universe` entry that no `allow-writes` entry names is reported, in every form
  `writes-targets` follows. `allow-writes` also exempts writes from `write-targets` in the same
  boundary. Without `allow-writes`, the boundary allows no write of the universe.

Each scope function is searched breadth first over the project call graph, so the reported
chain is a shortest one. The search does not enter:

- `allowed-callees` (project functions or ecosystem symbols, matched like `scopes`): their
  effects are allowed, also when a helper hands them a field it was given
  (`helper(model.fields)` writes nothing when `helper` only passes `fields` to an allowed
  callee that changes it);
- other functions of the scopes: each reports its own violations, so a violation is reported
  once, at the boundary, not again by every scope function above it;
- `async def` functions called without `await` (calling one only creates a coroutine), and
  generators that are not iterated (calling a generator function only creates the generator;
  its body is searched where it is iterated, as for `EFF101`, and a generator a function
  returns where the object it returns is iterated);
- functions an offloading decorator or API runs on another thread (`@sync_to_async`,
  `asyncio.to_thread(f)`, ...).

Unlike `EFF101`, the search does not read the callees' guards: a reached function's effects
count whatever its arguments are, so `__repr__` calling `save(text, io.StringIO())` reaches the
`open` that `save` runs only for a path.

A violation is reported once per scope function and forbidden effect (or write, read, or call
target; a `write-universe` write once per written `Class.attr`), at the call in the scope
function that starts the shortest chain (or at the blocking call, write, read, or call itself),
with the chain as related information; `mutates-params` is reported at the function's
definition. The report counts every distinct site of that kind the scope function reaches
(`sites` in JSON; for `mutates-params`, every change of a parameter, in the body making it), so
a Ratchet baseline sees a second blocking call, write, or parameter change below a recorded
report.

`allow-writes` is only as precise as heki's view of which object each write changes. A write
heki cannot tell apart from a write of the pass's input is reported: state that a property
getter writes while rendering, or a store operation whose writes depend on its arguments. A
write that constructs the object it writes is not (`fresh-objects = "allow"`). Treat its
reports as candidates to review, or narrow the universe, rather than gating on it.

## Why is this bad?
Some parts of a code base promise to be pure: rendering a model must not mutate it, domain code
must not do network I/O, a hot path must not sleep. The promise usually breaks several calls
away from the function that makes it, where a reviewer does not look. The boundary states it
once in configuration and checks every path.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]
name = "pure-render"
scopes = ["*.render"]
forbid = ["blocking", "writes-targets"]
write-targets = ["DataModel.fields"]
allowed-callees = ["pkg.cache.*"]
message = "render entry points must not mutate model state"
```

```python
import requests


def get_json(url: str) -> dict:
    return requests.get(url).json()


class Model:
    def render(self) -> str:
        data = get_json("https://example.com")  # EFF201: reaches `requests.get`
        return str(data)
```

Use instead:
```python
class Model:
    def render(self, data: dict) -> str:
        return str(data)  # the caller fetches `data` before rendering
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]`:
  - `name`: the boundary name, used in messages and in the diagnostic target
    (`pure-render:blocking_net`, `pure-render:DataModel.fields` for a write,
    `pure-render:reads:DataModel.fields`, `pure-render:calls:GenerationStore.*`,
    `pure-render:mutates-params`), so a read and a write of one field are two reports.
  - `scopes`: modules, classes, or functions (dotted names or globs).
  - `forbid`: `blocking-net`, `blocking-db`, `blocking-fs`, `blocking-subprocess`,
    `blocking-sync`, `sleep`, `blocking`, `mutates-params`, `writes-targets`, `reads-targets`,
    `calls`.
  - `write-targets`: `Class.attr` entries for `writes-targets` (required with it).
  - `read-targets`: `Class.attr` entries for `reads-targets` (required with it).
  - `call-targets`: functions, methods, or classes for `calls` (required with it), as for the
    `targets` of `[[tool.heki.call-owners]]`.
  - `write-universe`: `Class.attr` entries whose reached writes are reported unless
    `allow-writes` names them; the diagnostic target is the entry, with a glob attribute replaced
    by the written one (`pass:DataModel.fields` for `DataModel.*`).
  - `allow-writes`: `Class.attr` writes the boundary allows (needs `write-universe`).
  - `fresh-objects`: `"allow"` (default) or `"report"`: whether writes that construct the object
    they write count, as for `[[tool.heki.write-owners]]`.
  - `allowed-callees`: functions, classes, modules, or ecosystem symbols whose effects are
    allowed.
  - `message`: the help of every report of the boundary.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/hash-attr-mutation/

# hash-attr-mutation (MUT107)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Mutating an attribute read by `__hash__` after initialization (stored `set` / `dict` entries become unreachable).

## What it does
Checks methods that rebind or mutate an attribute that the class's `__hash__` reads (directly,
through a `self.helper()` call, or through the getter of a property it reads, such as
`hash(self.key)` where the `@property` `key` reads `self.name`), when the class, one of its
subclasses, or a base-class method it inherits without overriding changes the attribute after
initialization. A property that also defines a setter
or deleter is not followed.

The rule reports the write itself, once per method and attribute. It does not report:

- initialization: `__new__`, `__init__`, `__post_init__`, `model_post_init`, `__setstate__`,
  `__enter__`, `setup`, `setup_*` / `_setup_*` / `_init_*` / `_configure_*` methods, and the private helpers they call
  (`self.__setstate(state)` on the instance `__new__` allocates included), and the private
  helpers that only `__init__` and such helpers call on `self` (`__init__` -> `self._load()`
  -> `self._decode()`); class attributes that `__init_subclass__` sets;
- writers whose instances use another hash: a class between the writer's class and the hash's
  defines its own `__hash__`, or `__eq__` without `__hash__` (Python then makes its instances
  unhashable);
- in-place changes (an item store, a mutator method such as `append`) of an attribute
  `__hash__` hands whole to `hash()` (`hash(self.items)`, `hash((self.kind, self.items))`) and
  reads for nothing else: the hash is the value's own, so a list, dict, set, or `bytearray`
  there cannot be hashed at all, and a value of a project class answers for its own hash
  (`MUT107` checks its class). Rebinding the attribute is reported;
