- classes with a metaclass other than `type` / `abc.ABCMeta` along their MRO (also one heki
  cannot resolve): the metaclass may turn attribute writes into descriptor calls (a generated
  property whose setter invalidates the cached value), which heki does not see;
- lazy initialization: a write under a `None` / falsy check of the same attribute
  (`if self._key is None: self._key = ...`, `if not self._parts: ...`);
- memo / cache dictionaries (`self._cache[key] = value`, `setdefault`, the
  `if key not in self._memo:` pattern): in-place changes of an attribute with a `cache` or
  `memo` word in its name; rebinding it (`self.cache_size = n`) and names such as
  `memory_limit` are no memo operation;
- constant dictionary keys `__hash__` never reads (`self.meta["note"]` while `__hash__` reads
  `self.meta["id"]`);
- the hash's own cache: an attribute the hash computation writes itself (`self._hash = ...`
  in `__hash__` or a `self.helper()` it calls), which other methods reset, and a stored hash
  value (`self._hash`, `self._hashcode`) that a deserialization hook recomputes.

## Why is this bad?
A `set` or a `dict` files an object under the hash it had when it was added. Once an attribute
the hash is computed from changes, lookups compute a different hash and look in the wrong
place: `obj in seen` is `False` for an object that is in `seen`, a `dict` holds a key no
lookup finds, and the object can be added a second time.

## Example
```python
class Tag:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name

    def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool:
        return isinstance(other, Tag) and other.name == self.name

    def __hash__(self) -> int:
        return hash(self.name)

    def rename(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name  # a `Tag` in a set can no longer be found
```

Use instead:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Tag:
    name: str


def rename(tag: Tag, name: str) -> Tag:
    return replace(tag, name=name)  # a new object, hashed when it is stored
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix: whether to make the object immutable, hash only fields that never change,
or remove the object from its containers before changing it is a design decision.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/immutable-quadratic-concat/

# immutable-quadratic-concat (OPT103)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` · No automatic fix

Size-dependent immutable quadratic accumulation (`bytes`/`tuple`/attr `str`).

## What it does
Checks quadratic accumulation of immutable values in a loop:

- `acc = acc + chunk` / `acc += chunk` where `acc` is a `bytes` or `tuple`;
- `self.text += piece` on an attribute that the class's methods in the module (or, for another
  receiver, the function) only ever assign a string, bytes, or tuple literal of the pieces'
  kind (`self.text = ""`): `self.values += (i,)` extends a list in place.

Local `str` accumulation is not reported: CPython already appends in place when the string has
no other reference. Neither are:

- an accumulator the loop's own test caps at a small constant (`while len(buf) < 10`, also
  as one `and` operand or with a module constant: at most 4096), whatever the input;
- `obj.attr += x` where `obj` is a different object in every iteration (the loop element, or
  an object created in the iteration): each attribute gets one piece.

## Why is this bad?
Each concatenation copies everything accumulated so far.

## Example
```python
def encode(parts: list[bytes]) -> bytes:
    out = b""
    for p in parts:
        out = out + p
    return out
```

Use instead:
```python
def encode(parts: list[bytes]) -> bytes:
    return b"".join(parts)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix (the rewrite needs a buffer before the loop and a join after it). The
diagnostic still lists the proof obligations: the accumulator must not be read inside the loop
or by an exception handler, and its intermediate values must not escape.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterated-container-mutation/

# iterated-container-mutation (MUT113)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Opt-in: a dict, set, or deque of the instance changed while a method iterates it, by another method while a generator is suspended in the loop or by a function the loop's body calls (the next step raises `RuntimeError`).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    It has few reports, and most of them are still false. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Checks for a `dict`, `set`, or `collections.deque` held in an attribute of `self` that is
changed in place while a method of the class iterates it, by code outside the loop:

- a method of the class that runs while a generator method is suspended inside the iteration (at
  a `yield` from which the loop goes on, or inside a `yield from`);
- a function or method that the loop's body calls.

The rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select MUT113` or `extend-select = ["MUT113"]`.

An iteration is a `for` loop or a `yield from` over the container, over its `keys()`,
`values()`, or `items()` view, or over a lazy wrapper of either (`iter`, `enumerate`, `zip`,
`map`, `filter`, `reversed`, `itertools.chain`, a generator expression, ...). A snapshot
(`list(...)`, `tuple(...)`, `sorted(...)`, `.copy()`) is a container of its own. The
container's class comes from its annotation or its assignment in `__init__` (`OrderedDict`,
`defaultdict`, and `Counter` are mappings).

A change is an in-place change of the attribute's container, made by the method itself, by the
methods and properties it calls on `self`, or by a helper it hands the container to (the
helper's change counts as the same change made in the method):

- inserting, removing, or moving items: `append`, `add`, `update`, `setdefault`, `pop`,
  `popleft`, `discard`, `clear`, `del self.items[k]`, `rotate`, `move_to_end`, `|=`, ...;
- storing an item (`self.items[k] = v`), which counts for a mapping (the key may be new) but not
  for a deque, whose iterators allow it;
- reading a missing key of a `defaultdict` (`self.groups[k].append(v)`).

A store or a `defaultdict` read under a key the container holds adds no key, and does not count:
inside `if k in self.items:`, past `if k not in self.items: return` or
`if self.items.get(k) is None: raise KeyError(k)`, or after a read of `self.items[k]` in the same
block (not for a `Counter`, whose read of a missing key inserts nothing).

Rebinding the attribute (`self.items = {}`) changes no container, and the changes a function makes
after it binds a new container to the attribute on every path (`self.items = {}`, then
`self.items[k] = v`) are that new container's, not the one an iteration steps. Changes that a
method it calls after the rebinding makes (`self.items = {}`, then `self.add(k)`) still count.

What runs while a generator is suspended depends on where its generator object goes:

- A private generator (`_name`) runs only where the project iterates it. Between its steps, the
  body of the loop iterating it runs: the methods of the class that this body calls on the
  generator's instance count, on the same `self`, variable, or attribute (`self.registry`) the
  generator was called on, also through the functions that hand the generator on. A call that
  consumes it (`list(...)`, `sorted(...)`) runs nothing in between, and a generator that
  suspends inside such a loop is followed in turn.
- When the generator object outlives one use of it, any public method of the class, its project
  subclasses, and the bases it inherits from can run in between: it is stored (on the instance,
  in a list), yielded, or handed to code heki does not follow, or a step that leaves it suspended
  (`next()`, `send()`, a loop that leaves early or over a wrapper that stops first, `any()`,
  `islice()`) is followed by another use of it. Initialization does not count: `__init__`,
  `__post_init__`, `__new__`, `__setstate__`, `__enter__`, `setup`, and the other two-phase
  initialization methods `MUT101` names run before any iteration. A private method counts
  through the methods calling it.
- A public generator, `__iter__` included, is an iteration the class offers its callers, as
  `dict.items()` is: its public methods that change the container are the rest of that
  interface, and changing a container while iterating it is the caller's mistake, as for a
  builtin container. Only the changes made by reads count: property getters and the read dunder
  methods (`__getitem__`, `__len__`, `__contains__`, ...). The project's own loops over it count
  as for a private generator.

A change written in the loop's body itself is the linters' check (Ruff's `B909` and
`PLE4703`), and not reported. The rule reports one diagnostic per iteration of a suspended
generator, at the iteration, naming one changing method and listing each one as a related
location, and one per call in a loop's body that changes the container, at the call.

## Why is this bad?
A dict or set iterator raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` (or
`Set changed size during iteration`) at its next step after its container gained or lost an
item, and a deque iterator raises `RuntimeError: deque mutated during iteration` after any
change but an item store. A generator suspended inside such an iteration fails when it resumes
after another method ran, which may be far from both and only for some orders of calls.

## Example
```python
class Subscriptions:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.by_node: dict[str, object] = {}
        self._cursor = self._cycle()

    def _cycle(self):
        while True:
            yield from self.by_node.values()  # MUT113

    def next_subscriber(self) -> object:
        return next(self._cursor)

    def drop(self, node: str) -> None:
        self.by_node.pop(node, None)
```

Use instead:
```python
    def _cycle(self):
        while True:
            yield from list(self.by_node.values())
```

## How to fix
Iterate over a snapshot taken before the loop (`list(self.by_node.values())`), or collect the
changes and apply them after the loop has finished.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix: a snapshot no longer sees the items added during the iteration, which can be
what the code wants.

## Known limitations
- A `list` does not count: a list iterator sees the items appended during the iteration and
  skips or repeats items when others move, without an error.
- A container of an abstract class (`MutableMapping`, `MutableSet`) or of a class heki does not
  know does not count. A `deque()` or `defaultdict(...)` assigned without an annotation has no
  class for heki: annotate the attribute (`self.queue: deque[int] = deque()`).
- An `await` inside a loop, and threads, are not suspensions the rule follows.
- A loop's call on another object than the generator's instance does not count, even on another
  parameter that may be the same object at run time (`for k in source._walk():
  destination.remove(k)` called as `copy_over(r, r)`).
- A method returning an iterator or a view instead of being a generator
  (`return iter(self.items)`) is not followed, and neither is a generator passed to a project
  function that iterates it.
- A generator handed to code heki does not follow counts as outliving the call, also when that
  code consumes it at once (`self.assertCountEqual(gen(), [...])`).
- The tests on the paths to a change are not followed across calls: a change only a lazy
  initialization makes (`if not self.loaded: self._load()`) counts although the iterating method
  ran it first, and so does a change that a constant argument of the call turns off
  (`add(item, check=False)` where `add` changes the container only `if check:`).


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterator-double-consumption/

# iterator-double-consumption (MUT106)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Opt-in · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Opt-in: consuming a single-pass iterator or generator a second time (the second pass sees no items).

## What it does
Checks for a single-pass iterator or generator that is consumed a second time. Once an
iterator is exhausted, every further pass over it sees no items, silently.

Single-pass values are:

- generator expressions (`(x for x in xs)`);
- `iter`, `zip`, `map`, `filter`, `enumerate`, `reversed`, `heapq.merge`, and the single-pass
  `itertools` functions (`chain`, `islice`, `starmap`, `takewhile`, `dropwhile`, `filterfalse`,
  `compress`, `accumulate`, `groupby`, `pairwise`, `batched`, `zip_longest`, `product`,
  `permutations`, `combinations`, `combinations_with_replacement`), resolved through imports
  so a shadowed name is never matched;
- calls of project generator functions (from any module);
- parameters and locals annotated `Iterator`, `Generator`, `AsyncIterator`, or
  `AsyncGenerator` (`typing` or `collections.abc`; `Iterable`, `Sequence`, and `Collection`
  may be re-iterable and are not tracked).

A value is consumed by a `for` loop or comprehension over it, unpacking (`a, *rest = it`),
`yield from`, a call that materializes it (`list`, `tuple`, `set`, `frozenset`, `dict`, `bytes`,
`bytearray`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, `sorted`, `str.join`, `bytes.join`,
`dict.fromkeys`, `list.extend`, `set.update` / `union` / `intersection` / `difference`,
`dict.update`, `collections.deque` / `Counter` / `OrderedDict` / `defaultdict`,
`heapq.nlargest` / `nsmallest`, `functools.reduce`, `math.prod` / `fsum`), a wrapper that is
itself consumed (`enumerate(it)`, `map(f, it)`, `chain(it, other)`, `heapq.merge(it, other)`,
`zip(it, it)`, a generator expression over it, ...), or a project function that iterates the
parameter it is passed to exhaustion (for a method, every implementation the call may run must;
an `@abstractmethod` never runs). `next(it)` and `len` are not consumptions, and neither are
`zip` / `map` over several iterables, `islice`, or `takewhile`: they stop at the shortest one or
early (`zip(range(n), it)` takes `n` items). The same table decides where a generator's body
runs for the effect and contract rules.

The rule reports the second pass when the first one runs to exhaustion and the second is
reachable from it, without rebinding the variable in between. It also reports a value created
outside a loop and consumed to exhaustion inside it: the next iteration sees nothing.

It does not report:

- a first pass that may stop early: a `for` loop with `break`, `return`, or `raise` inside
  (`it = iter(lines)`, then `for line in it: ... break`, then `for line in it:` is the
  idiomatic way to resume), and `any(it)` / `all(it)`, which stop at the first item that decides
  the result (they still run a generator's body where they are called);
- passes on exclusive branches (`if c: list(it) else: sorted(it)`);
- a variable rebound to a fresh iterator in between;
- `itertools.tee` results, `repeat`, `cycle`, and `count`;
- loops that run at most once (`for _ in range(1)`), and a consumption followed by leaving the
  loop (`data = list(it)` then `break`);
- consuming the rest of an iterator inside a loop over that iterator itself.

## Why is this bad?
The second pass silently gets an empty iterator: totals become zero, a second report is empty,
and a retry processes nothing. Nothing fails, so the bug is noticed far away from its cause.

## Example
```python
def summarize(lines: list[str]) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    rows = (line.strip() for line in lines)
    count = sum(1 for _ in rows)
    kept = [r for r in rows if r]  # MUT106: `rows` was consumed by `sum`
    return count, kept
```

Use instead:
```python
def summarize(lines: list[str]) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    rows = [line.strip() for line in lines]  # a list can be iterated any number of times
    count = len(rows)
    kept = [r for r in rows if r]
    return count, kept
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["MUT106"]` (or `--extend-select MUT106`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `MUT` prefix does not enable it.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-insert/

# list-front-insert (OPT121)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Size-dependent `q.insert(0, v)` -> `collections.deque`.

## What it does
Checks loops that insert at the front of a list, `q.insert(0, v)`, and suggests a
`collections.deque` with `appendleft(v)`.

Size-dependent: applied only with `--fix --include-size-dependent` or in profiled hot
functions. A list rebuilt in every iteration of the loop is not reported: its front insert
costs no more than building it.

## Why is this bad?
Inserting at the front shifts every element, so building a list this way is quadratic.

## Example
```python
def reverse(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out = []
    for i in items:
        out.insert(0, i)
    return list(out)
```

Use instead:
```python
import collections


def reverse(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out = collections.deque()
    for i in items:
        out.appendleft(i)
    return list(out)
```

## Fix safety
The same obligations as `OPT120`, and the same rewrite of annotations and imports.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-pop/

# list-front-pop (OPT120)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Size-dependent `q.pop(0)` / `del q[0]` / `q = q[1:]` -> `collections.deque`.

## What it does
Checks loops that remove the first element of a list: `q.pop(0)`, `del q[0]`, and
`q = q[1:]`, and suggests a `collections.deque` with `popleft()`.

Size-dependent: applied only with `--fix --include-size-dependent` or in profiled hot
functions. The rewrite changes the list's creation to `collections.deque(...)`, rewrites the
variable's `list[...]` annotation to `collections.deque[...]`, and adds `import collections`
when needed: in sorted position among the module's standard-library imports, or after the
docstring and `__future__` imports of a module without other imports.

Not reported: a small display that the loop only drains (`expected = [b"a", b""]` and
`expected.pop(0)` in the loop: it never holds more than its items), and a list rebuilt in every
iteration of the loop.

## Why is this bad?
Removing the first element shifts every remaining element, so a queue drained this way is
quadratic. `deque.popleft()` is constant time.

## Example
```python
def bfs(graph: dict[int, list[int]], start: int) -> list[int]:
    queue = [start]
    seen = {start}
    order = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.pop(0)
        order.append(node)
        for child in graph[node]:
            if child not in seen:
                seen.add(child)
                queue.append(child)
    return order
```

Use instead:
```python
import collections


def bfs(graph: dict[int, list[int]], start: int) -> list[int]:
    queue = collections.deque([start])
    seen = {start}
    order = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for child in graph[node]:
            if child not in seen:
                seen.add(child)
                queue.append(child)
    return order
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when the list is created in the function, never leaves it (not returned,
stored, or passed to other code except read-only builtins such as `len`), and every use has a
`deque` equivalent: no sorting, no slicing, no indexes other than `0` and `-1`, no `==`
against lists. An annotation the rewrite cannot turn into a `deque` one (`Sequence[str]`, a
union) or another annotated declaration of the variable blocks the fix, so that a type checker
accepts the fixed file.

A `deque` iterator raises `RuntimeError` when the deque changes under it and is another type
than a list iterator: no iterator of the list may be live at a change, consumed by the changing
call (`q.extend(reversed(q))`), or used for more than its elements (`type(iter(q))`). `list(xs)`
of a value that is not a builtin container becomes `deque(list(xs))`, which keeps the length
query `list` makes; `list(**kw)` and `list(*args)` block the fix (`deque` reads a second
argument as `maxlen`), and so does a list a starred target or pattern makes (`first, *q =
items`), which has no display to rewrite. Only `q = q[1:]` is a front pop: `q[1:n]` and
`q[1::2]` are not.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-quadratic-concat/

# list-quadratic-concat (OPT101)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` · Safe fix (`--fix`)

Unconditionally profitable `list` quadratic concatenation (`x = x + [e]` -> `x.append(e)`).

## What it does
Checks loops that grow a list by building a new one every iteration, `x = x + [e]`, and
rewrites it to `x.append(e)` (`x.extend([...])` for several elements).

## Why is this bad?
`x + [e]` copies the whole list, so the loop is quadratic. `append` is amortized constant time
and is never slower, even for one iteration.

## Example
```python
def squares(n: int) -> list[int]:
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        out = out + [i * i]
    return out
```

Use instead:
```python
def squares(n: int) -> list[int]:
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        out.append(i * i)
    return out
```

## Fix safety
The fix is applied by `heki check --fix` only when heki proves it safe:

- the list is an exact builtin `list` created in the function, not shared (not a parameter,
  not stored in another object, not captured by a closure, not passed to unknown code);
- no other reference to the old list is live after the statement: no alias, no `for` loop
  iterating it, no `iter(x)` or view;
- evaluating the right-hand side does not rebind or mutate the list;
- no exception handler can observe an older binding of another name aliasing it.

Otherwise the diagnostic explains which proof obligation blocks the fix, and nothing is
rewritten. A disproved candidate is not reported at all: `for v in x: x = x + [v]` terminates,
but `x.append(v)` would loop forever, so heki says nothing there and never touches it. Type
annotations are never trusted.

The fix rewrites a plain `x = x + [...]` statement. For other shapes of the same update (a
parenthesized `x = (x + [i])` or `x = (x) + [i]`, an annotated `x: list = x + [i]`), the
diagnostic says that the rewrite is proven safe and leaves it to be made by hand.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-or-tx-held-across-io/

# lock-or-tx-held-across-io (EFF106)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Opt-in · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Opt-in: `await` or blocking network I/O while holding a `threading` lock or a DB transaction.

## What it does
Checks for an `await` (also the implicit ones of `async for` and `async with`), or a call
reaching blocking network I/O (directly or through project helpers, including the getter of a
property read), while a `with` block holds a synchronous lock or a database transaction.

The held resource must be type-certain:

- an instance of `threading.Lock`, `RLock`, `Semaphore`, `BoundedSemaphore`, or `Condition`,
  created in `__init__` (`self._lock = threading.Lock()`), at module level, locally, or given
  by an annotated parameter;
- a transaction started by `sqlalchemy.orm.Session.begin()` / `begin_nested()`,
  `Connection.begin()` / `begin_nested()`, `Engine.begin()`, `sqlmodel.Session.begin()`,
  `django.db.transaction.atomic()`, or `psycopg.Connection.transaction()`.

The rule reports the `await` or the call while the resource is certainly held (on every path),
with the call chain to the network I/O as related information. Leaving the `with` block
releases what that block acquired: a re-entrant lock entered again by a nested `with` stays held
until the outer block exits.

It does not report:

- `async with` and async locks (`asyncio.Lock`, `anyio.Lock`, ...);
- objects whose type is not known, or not a registered lock or transaction;
- work after the `with` block, and handlers reached only after the block exited;
- calls offloaded to a thread (`asyncio.to_thread`, `loop.run_in_executor`, ...);
- database queries inside a transaction, local file I/O, or `time.sleep`;
- CLI commands, ASGI lifespan handlers, and tests, as for `EFF101`.

## Why is this bad?
A synchronous lock held across an `await` blocks every thread that wants it until the coroutine
resumes, and a second coroutine acquiring it on the event loop thread deadlocks the loop. Held
across a network request, the lock serializes every waiting thread behind that request. A
transaction held across a request or an `await` keeps its pooled connection checked out and its
row locks taken, which exhausts the pool under load.

## Example
```python
import asyncio
import threading


class Cache:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._data: dict[str, bytes] = {}

    async def refresh(self, key: str) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self._data[key] = await fetch(key)  # EFF106
```

Use instead:
```python
    async def refresh(self, key: str) -> None:
        value = await fetch(key)
        with self._lock:  # hold the lock only for the update
            self._data[key] = value
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["EFF106"]` (or `--extend-select EFF106`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `EFF` prefix does not enable it.
- `lint.relax-async-in-tests` applies as for `EFF101`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-carried-concat/

# loop-carried-concat (DATA101)

Family: Data Pipelines (DATA) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Loop-carried quadratic `pandas.concat` / `numpy.vstack` / `numpy.append` accumulation.

## What it does
Checks loops that grow a DataFrame or array by re-concatenating it on every iteration:
`df = pd.concat([df, chunk])`, `arr = np.vstack([arr, row])`, `arr = np.append(arr, x)`, and
the other quadratic reallocations of the ecosystem knowledge base. Only loop-carried
accumulation is reported: the result feeds the next iteration and is computed from the previous
value, also when it grows on some iterations only. An update through a project function counts
when that function returns a reallocation of the argument carrying the previous value, directly
or through further helpers (`acc = grow(acc)` where `grow` returns `np.append(acc, x)`), also
when an `isinstance` test picks the method (`if isinstance(g, Grower): acc = g.grow(acc)`) or an
offloading API runs it (`acc = await asyncio.to_thread(grow, acc)`); a helper that reallocates
something else and returns its argument unchanged does not. One-off
concatenations inside a loop are not reported, also on a branch that leaves the variable
unchanged otherwise (`if step: x = np.append(edges, last)`), nor is writing into a buffer passed
as `out=` (`out = np.concatenate(([a], [b]), out=out)` reuses the same buffer): the previous
value must be among the data that is combined. A list holding it counts (`pd.concat([df] +
parts)`), arithmetic on it does not (`x = np.concatenate((x - np.outer(u, v), [a]))`,
`q = np.concatenate([[w * q[0]], w * q[1:]])`): every entry of the new value changed, so each
iteration already works in proportion to the value's size, and there are no unchanged parts to
collect and combine once. A loop whose trip count the code fixes is not reported either
(`for is_p_wave in [False, True]`, `for _ in range(steps)` with `steps = 8`): it copies a fixed
number of times, whatever the input.

## Why is this bad?
Every concatenation copies everything accumulated so far, so the loop is quadratic in the total
size.

## Example
```python
import pandas as pd


def load(chunks: list[pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = pd.DataFrame()
    for chunk in chunks:
        df = pd.concat([df, chunk])  # DATA101
    return df
```

Use instead:
```python
def load(chunks: list[pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return pd.concat(chunks) if chunks else pd.DataFrame()  # `pd.concat([])` raises
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-db-query/

# loop-db-query (EFF103)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Explicit DB query / external RPC executed inside a loop (N+1).

## What it does
Checks loops that run a database query on every iteration (the "N+1 queries" problem):
`cursor.execute(...)`, `session.execute(...)` (awaited ones on async sessions and connections
too), the SQLAlchemy `Query` methods that run the query (`all`, `first`, `one`, `count`, ...)
and iterating a `Query` (`for row in session.query(User):` in an outer loop, a comprehension,
`list(query)`),
the Django `QuerySet` methods that run the query (`get`, `first`, `count`, ... and their `a*`
variants), `pymongo`, `redis`, and DynamoDB commands, `pandas.read_sql`, and project functions
that reach them, also when an offloading API runs them on a worker thread per item (`await
asyncio.to_thread(load, i)`, a function decorated with `@sync_to_async`), including the getter of a property read in the loop and a generator iterated in
the loop (its body runs where it is iterated, as for `EFF101`). A function a builtin calls once
per item runs in a loop as long as the items (`sorted(users, key=lambda u: score(conn, u))`,
`list(map(load, ids))`; see `EFF102` for the builtins and the items whose number the code fixes).

It does not report reading the rows of a statement already executed (`cursor.fetchone()`),
calls that only build a query (`session.query(User).filter(...)`, `QuerySet.filter(...)`,
`Redis.pipeline()`), the bulk APIs, which send many rows in one statement and are called per
batch by design (`QuerySet.bulk_create`, `in_bulk`, pymongo's `insert_many`, `bulk_write`), DDL
statements (SQL starting with `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, or `PRAGMA` run by a DB-API
`execute` / `executemany` / `executescript` or SQLAlchemy's `exec_driver_sql`, also inside a
helper the loop calls: a literal, an f-string, `%`, or `.format()` whose literal start is one,
SQLAlchemy's `text()` of one, and the statements of a module's string constants: the items of a
tuple, the pieces `.split(";")` / `.splitlines()` cut a schema into), migration code
(`upgrade` / `downgrade` functions, files under `migrations/` or `alembic/`), the ORM packages'
own implementation, or loops whose size the code fixes when no data-sized loop is around them
(`for ident in enumerate((1, 2), 1)`, `zip(order, ["m1", "m2"])`, a name bound to a small
display; see `EFF102`).

As for `EFF102`, a query that only runs while an attribute is unset, which the code then sets
(`if self._columns is None: self._columns = cursor.execute(...)`), runs once per object and is
not reported when the loop does not construct the object; so does one in a
`functools.cached_property` getter, and one behind a module global runs once per process. A
query that only runs while a local variable the loop carries is unset or a first-iteration flag
holds (`if first: cursor.execute(...); first = False`), or that every way on from leaves the
loop (`cursor.execute(...)` followed by `return`, `break`, or `raise`), runs once per run of the
loop. A call whose arguments switch off the branch with the query (a constant, a literal
default, a test the caller has made) is not followed into it.

## Why is this bad?
One round trip per item makes the run time grow with the number of rows and with the network
latency to the database. A single batched query is usually orders of magnitude faster.

## Example
```python
import sqlite3


def names(cursor: sqlite3.Cursor, ids: list[int]) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    for i in ids:
        cursor.execute("SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = ?", (i,))  # EFF103
        out.append(cursor.fetchone()[0])
    return out
```

Use instead:
```python
import sqlite3


def names(cursor: sqlite3.Cursor, ids: list[int]) -> list[str]:
    if not ids:
        return []
    marks = ",".join("?" * len(ids))
    cursor.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id IN ({marks})", ids)
    name_of = dict(cursor.fetchall())
    return [name_of[i] for i in ids]  # `KeyError` for an unknown ID (the loop: `TypeError`)
```

The query returns each matching row once and in no particular order, so the result is rebuilt
from the IDs: in their order, with repeated IDs repeated. A database caps the number of
parameters in one statement; split a long list of IDs into chunks.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-invariant-container-rebuild/

# loop-invariant-container-rebuild (OPT130)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Size-dependent loop-invariant container reconstruction (`e in set(keys)`).

## What it does
Checks loops that rebuild the same container on every iteration just to test membership,
`e in set(keys)` (also `list(...)`, `tuple(...)`, `dict(...)`), and suggests building it once
before the loop.

Size-dependent: applied only with `--fix --include-size-dependent` or in profiled hot
functions.

## Why is this bad?
The container is rebuilt from scratch on every iteration, which costs as much as the scan it
was meant to avoid.

## Example
```python
def matches(items: list[int], keys: list[int]) -> int:
    hits = 0
    for i in items:
        if i in set(keys):
            hits += 1
    return hits
```

Use instead:
```python
def matches(items: list[int], keys: list[int]) -> int:
    keys_set = set(keys)
    hits = 0
    for i in items:
        if i in keys_set:
            hits += 1
    return hits
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when the rebuilt expression is a builtin constructor without side effects,
every value it reads is bound outside the loop and not changed inside it, and building it before
the loop cannot raise even when the loop runs zero times (hashable builtin elements). The
container must be used by the membership test only: `(tmp := list(keys))` followed by
`tmp.clear()` would clear the one shared container. Calls with `*` arguments (`list(*args)`
passes the elements of `args`) and method calls with arguments are not hoisted.

Not reported when the loop runs a fixed small number of times, when the rebuilt container is
small whatever the input (`set(paths[:2])`, `tuple(".;:")`), or when nothing is rebuilt:
`tuple(t)` of a tuple returns `t` itself.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-dedup/

# loop-linear-dedup (OPT111)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Size-dependent `if v not in seen: seen.append(v)` -> auxiliary `set`.

## What it does
Checks the de-duplication idiom `if v not in seen: seen.append(v)` inside a loop and suggests
keeping an auxiliary `set` next to the list.

Size-dependent: applied only with `--fix --include-size-dependent` or in profiled hot
functions.

## Why is this bad?
The membership test scans the list, so de-duplicating `n` items costs `n²` comparisons.

## Example
```python
def unique(values: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    seen = []
    for v in values:
        if v not in seen:
            seen.append(v)
    return seen
```

Use instead:
```python
def unique(values: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    seen = []
    seen_set = set()
    for v in values:
        if v not in seen_set:
            seen.append(v)
            seen_set.add(v)
    return seen
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when the list is an exact builtin list owned by the function, the paired
`append` is its only change inside the loop (a removal would make the set stale), no other live
reference could change it, and every element and probe is a hashable builtin scalar.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-list-lookup/

# loop-linear-list-lookup (OPT112)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` · No automatic fix

Size-dependent `list.index` / `list.remove` / `list.count` inside a loop (repeated linear scans).

## What it does
Checks `list.index()`, `list.remove()`, and `list.count()` calls that run on every iteration
of a loop, on a list that outlives the iteration.

The receiver must certainly be a builtin `list`: a list display or comprehension, `list(...)`,
or a `list[...]` / `List[...]` annotation on a parameter, a local, or a class attribute
(`self.items`). Calls on a `set`, a `str`, a project class, or a receiver of unknown type are
not reported. Neither are:

- loops whose size does not depend on the data: small constant ranges and displays
  (`for i in range(3)`, `for s in SUFFIXES` with `SUFFIXES = (".py", ".pyi")`, also through
  `enumerate` / `zip` / `reversed` / `sorted` / `.items()` and `range(ATTEMPTS - 1)` with a
  constant `ATTEMPTS`), retry loops, and daemon polling loops; the iterable of a `for` loop,
  which runs once;
- lists built in the iteration (`parts = [...]` inside the loop) and lists of the loop element
  (`row.cells.index(x)`);
- small lists: a display of at most 16 items that nothing grows (the loop may shrink it with
  `remove()` / `pop()` or replace its items), in the function, as a module global (also of
  another module: `LEVELS = ["low", "mid", "high"]`), or as an attribute its class and
  subclasses only ever assign such a display (`self.preferred = [",", ";"]`, a class
  attribute); also a list the code builds from a fixed iterable (`list(range(7))`, `[c for c
  in LABELS if overflow.get(c)]`) or fills a fixed number of times (`ids.append(card["id"])`
  for each of at most 6 cards a test allowed). A display handed to code that may grow it (any
  call but read-only builtins; a `*items` argument passes the items only) is not small;
- calls after which the loop always ends (`return items.index(x)`, a `break` on every path);
- `index(x, start)`, which scans from a position that usually moves forward.

## Why is this bad?
Each call scans the list from the start (and `remove()` also shifts the elements after the
removed one), so the loop costs the product of the loop size and the list size: O(n²) when both
grow with the input. A `dict` or `set` built once before the loop answers each lookup in
constant time, and `collections.Counter` counts every value in one pass.

## Example
```python
def ranks(names: list[str], winners: list[str]) -> list[int]:
    return [names.index(w) for w in winners]


def drop(items: list[int], unwanted: list[int]) -> None:
    for x in unwanted:
        items.remove(x)
```

Use instead:
```python
def ranks(names: list[str], winners: list[str]) -> list[int]:
    position = {}
    for i, name in enumerate(names):
        position.setdefault(name, i)  # the first index, as `list.index`
    return [position[w] for w in winners]  # `KeyError` where `index` raised `ValueError`


def drop(items: list[int], unwanted: list[int]) -> None:
    gone = set(unwanted)
    items[:] = [x for x in items if x not in gone]
```

The rewrites are not drop-in replacements: `remove()` drops only the first occurrence of each
value and raises `ValueError` for a missing one, and the values must be hashable.

The advice follows what the loop does with the list. Removals can wait for one rebuild after
the loop only when the loop reads the list nowhere else (a membership test guarding the removal,
`if x in items: items.remove(x)`, aside); when it iterates, tests, indexes, or passes on the list
after a removal (a greedy match over the remaining values), the help advises a `set` or a
`dict` with constant-time deletion instead. An index or a count built once before the loop stays
right only while the loop does not change the list, in place or through a project function it
hands the list to (`change(names)` where `change` calls `names.reverse()`); otherwise the
help advises keeping it up to date with each change.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-membership/

# loop-linear-membership (OPT110)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Size-dependent `e in lst` inside a loop -> hoist `set` outside loop.

## What it does
Checks membership tests against a list or tuple inside a loop, `e in lst`, where the list does
not change during the loop, and suggests building a `set` once before the loop.

This is a size-dependent rewrite: it is reported as a suggestion and applied only with
`heki check --fix --include-size-dependent`, or for functions that a `--profile` dump shows
hot. Not reported:

- small containers: at most 16 items that nothing grows, whatever the items are
  (`x in ("a", "b")`, `x in [b"1", b"2"]`, also through a name bound to one, a comprehension
  over one, or `list(range(5))`);
- lists whose elements are dicts, lists, or sets: no `set` can hold them.

## Why is this bad?
`e in lst` scans the list, so the loop costs the product of both sizes. A set lookup is
constant time once the set exists.

## Example
```python
def allowed(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    ok = list(range(0, 1000, 3))
    return [i for i in items if i in ok]
```

Use instead:
```python
def allowed(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    ok = set(range(0, 1000, 3))
    return [i for i in items if i in ok]
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when:

- the container is an exact `list` / `tuple` bound outside the loop and not changed inside it
  (a list mutated in the loop would make the hoisted set stale);
- every element is an `int`, `str`, `bytes`, `bool`, or `float`: building the set cannot raise
  even when the loop runs zero times, and hashing agrees with `==`;
- the probe value is of those types too (an object with a custom `__eq__` could match list
  elements a set lookup never compares with).

A `list[int]` annotation is never trusted: a list subclass can override `__contains__`.

Not reported when the container is small whatever the input, or when the loop runs a fixed
small number of times (`for i in range(3):`): building the set costs about as much as the scans
it saves.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-unpooled-client/

# loop-unpooled-client (EFF102)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Allocating an unpooled HTTP/DB/RPC client or sessionless request inside a loop.

## What it does
Checks loops that allocate a network or database client on every iteration: module-level
request helpers that open a new connection per call (`requests.get`, `httpx.get`), client
constructors, sync and async (`requests.Session()`, `httpx.AsyncClient()`,
`aiohttp.ClientSession()`, `boto3.client(...)`), connection factories (`sqlite3.connect`,
`redis.Redis`, `create_async_engine`, ...), and connection pools (`psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool`),
directly or through project functions,
including the getter of a property read in the loop (`self.client.get(url)` where the `client`
getter builds a new client).

A function a builtin calls once per item runs in a loop too: the function handed to `map`,
`filter`, `itertools.starmap`, `itertools.filterfalse`, and `functools.reduce`, and the `key` of
`sorted`, `list.sort`, `min`, `max`, and `itertools.groupby` (`list(map(fetch, urls))`), whether
it is a lambda, a project function, a bound method, or a `functools.partial` of one. The loop is
as long as the items, which are sized as a `for` loop's iterable: `map(fetch, ("a", "b"))` is
not reported, nor is `max(a, b, key=fetch)`, which compares two values. A lambda written in the
same function as another lambda is not followed: every lambda of a function has the same name
(`f.<locals>.<lambda>`), and heki keeps one summary per name.

The iterable of a `for` loop is evaluated once and is not reported; neither are calls in
loops whose size the code fixes, when no data-sized loop is around them: displays of at most 16
items (also through a name or a module constant bound to one that nothing in the project
grows, a tuple whatever other code does with it short of rebinding it, and through
`enumerate` / `zip` / `reversed` / `sorted` / `.items()`), `range` of integer constants with at
most 16 steps (`range(ATTEMPTS - 1)`), what a builtin constructor, a comprehension, or a fixed
loop of `append`s makes of those (`list(range(7))`, `[n.upper() for n in ("a", "b")]`), slices
with a constant bound (`for case in cases[:3]`), iterables a length test on every path to the
loop caps (`if len(cases) > 3: raise ...`), a `while` loop over a counter the code starts,
steps, and limits with constants (`i = 1` ... `while i < 6:` ... `i += 1`, at most 16 times),
retry loops, and daemon polling loops.

A retry loop repeats one attempt: its body leaves the loop on success or sleeps in an exception
handler, and it runs over a small constant range or a target named like `attempt` / `retry`
(also one name of a tuple target: `for attempt, proxy in enumerate(proxies)`). A loop that
waits on every path back to its test is paced by time, as polls and retries are: a `while` loop,
or a `for` loop whose body never reads its target (`for _ in range(30):`), in which every
iteration sleeps or waits with a timeout (`time.sleep(5)`, `stop.wait(1)`, in a coroutine
`await asyncio.sleep(5)`; `sleep(0)` only yields, and a sleep an exception can skip or a
coroutine does not await does not count). A daemon polling loop runs until a
flag or an event says to stop (`while self._running:`, `while not self._stopped:`, `while not
stop_event.is_set():`), or is a `while True:` loop that waits on every iteration. A `for` loop
reading its target steps through items, also when it sleeps per item.

A client that is only created while an attribute is unset, which the code then sets (lazy
initialization: `if not self._sock: self._sock = connect()`, or `if self._sock: return`
before connecting), is created once per object, not on every iteration: the call is not
reported unless a data-sized loop around it constructs the object in each iteration
(`Connection().send(cmd)`); `conn.send(cmd)` on a connection made before the loop, taken from
a pool, or held by the receiver is not reported. The receiver of a bound method, the arguments a
`functools.partial` holds, and the items a builtin passes are no new objects either:
`map(self.fetch, urls)`, where `fetch` sets `self._session` once, is not reported. A
`functools.cached_property` getter (also imported through a module that re-exports it, such as
`kombu.utils.cached_property`) runs once per instance in the same way, and a lazy
initialization of a module global (`global _session`) once per process.

A client created only while a local variable the loop carries is unset (`if conn is None: conn
= connect()`, `conn = conn or connect()`), or only while a first-iteration flag holds (`if
first: ...; first = False`), is created once per run of the loop, and so is one created where
every way on leaves the loop (`return s.get(url)`, `connect(); break`, `raise` after it). Still
reported: a variable or flag set back in the loop (also by an `except` handler), or set there to
a value the branch does not compute (`prev = row`, which may be `None`), a global the function
also sets back to `None` (before the test, or after the initialization), a branch that does not always set it, a loop around that starts it unset again in each iteration, and a `break` out of
an inner loop, which runs again in each iteration of the outer one.

A call whose arguments switch off the branch that creates the client is not followed into
it: `load(name, cache=False)` does not reach the `urlopen` under `if cache:` in `load`. This
covers constant arguments and the literal defaults of omitted ones (`False`, `None`, `0`, `""`,
empty displays), tests the caller has already made on the same value (`isinstance`, `is None`,
truthiness), and wrappers that pass the value on.

## Why is this bad?
Each new client pays for DNS, TCP, and TLS setup again and throws its connection pool away.
In a loop this dominates the run time and exhausts sockets.

## Example
```python
import requests


def fetch_all(urls: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    for url in urls:
        out.append(requests.get(url).text)  # EFF102: a new connection per iteration
    return out
```

Use instead:
```python
def fetch_all(urls: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    with requests.Session() as session:
        return [session.get(url).text for url in urls]
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/nested-loop-equijoin/

# nested-loop-equijoin (OPT113)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` · No automatic fix

Size-dependent nested-loop equi-join (`for a in A: for b in B: if a.k == b.k`) -> `dict` index.

## What it does
Checks nested loops that join two collections by comparing a key of each with `==`:
`for a in A: for b in B: if a.k == b.k:`, including a comprehension as the inner loop
(`[b for b in B if b.k == a.k]`).

The keys are the loop elements themselves, their unpacked components (`for k, v in pairs`),
attributes (`a.k`, `a.x.y`), and constant subscripts (`a["k"]`, `a[0]`). Both loops must be
`for` loops whose size depends on the data. The rule reports one diagnostic per inner loop, at
its first matching comparison. It does not report:

- traversals, where the inner iterable is computed from the outer element
  (`for b in a.children`, `for b in index[a.k]`, `for b in f(a)`, `for b in xs[i + 1:]`);
- comparisons that do not select pairs: `!=`, a negated `==`, one alternative of an `or`
  (`a.k == b.k or match(a, b)`), a result that is stored instead of tested, a value picked for
  every pair (`1 if a.k == b.k else 0`), a match that only skips to the next iteration
  (`if a == b: continue` in an all-pairs loop), or a comparison whose false side does work:
  an `else` / `elif` body, the failure of an `assert a == b`, a `break` / `return` on a
  mismatch, or statements that only the mismatches run because a match `break`s. They run for
  the pairs an index would skip, so every pair is needed; statements after the `if` that every
  pair runs do not count;
- joins where the code fixes the size of either loop, so that the cost grows with one side
  only: a display of at most 16 items (`for b in ("x", "y")`, also through a name or a module
  constant of this or another module (`NAME`, `module.NAME`, also read in a module body) when
  nothing grows it, a comprehension over one (`[r for r in ("a", "b") if r in seen]`), and
  through `enumerate` / `zip` / `sorted` / `.items()` ...), `range` of integer constants with
  at most 16 steps (`range(10)`, `range(LIMIT)`), and an iterable a length test on every path
  caps (`if len(groups) > 8: raise ...`).

## Why is this bad?
The inner loop runs completely for every outer element, so the join costs O(n·m) comparisons.
Indexing the inner collection by its key once (a `dict` from key to elements, or a `set` of the
keys) makes it O(n + m). A `break` after the first match does not help much: a missing key
still scans the whole inner collection.

## Example
```python
def attach(orders, customers):
    for order in orders:
        for customer in customers:
            if order.customer_id == customer.id:
                order.customer = customer
                break
```

Use instead:
```python
def attach(orders, customers):
    by_id = {}
    for customer in customers:
        by_id.setdefault(customer.id, customer)  # the first match, as the `break`
    for order in orders:
        customer = by_id.get(order.customer_id)
        if customer is not None:
            order.customer = customer
```

The advice follows how the matches are used. When a match leaves the inner loop (`break`,
`return`, `raise`), one element per key is enough: a `set` of the elements, or a `dict` from the
key to its first element, as above. When every match is used (`out.append((a, b))` for each
equal pair), a `set` or a one-element `dict` would drop the repeated matches, so the help
advises a `dict` from each key (or value) to the list of its elements. Each outer key then reads
its list with `.get(key, [])`: a loop over the index instead would drop the outer keys that
match no element, which the nested loops give an empty list.

The keys must be hashable, and `==` must agree with their hash. When a key is known to be a
`list`, `dict`, `set`, or `bytearray` (from its annotation, or as an element of a display of
such displays), the help advises indexing a hashable form of it instead (a `tuple` or
`frozenset` of its items).

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/read-owner-violation/

# read-owner-violation (MUT203)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Reading a guarded attribute (directly, via alias, `getattr`, or `__dict__`) outside declared `read-owners`.

## What it does
Checks reads of attributes that a `[[tool.heki.read-owners]]` contract reserves for a set of
allowed reader functions: the read side of `MUT201`. A read is reported when it happens outside
the allowed readers:

- directly (`ref.children`), also on `self` and through local aliases;
- through `getattr(ref, "children"[, default])` or `object.__getattribute__(ref, "children")`
  with a constant name: a string literal or a string constant, as for `MUT201`;
- through `ref.__dict__["children"]` or `ref.__dict__.get("children")`, also with a string
  constant for the key.

A target names a class and an attribute; it covers the class's subclasses too. A container
entry (`Class.attr["key"]`) is a write target only: reading an entry reads the attribute, so a
read target names `Class.attr` (an entry is a configuration error).

The read object's class is the one heki infers for it, with annotations as hints: a
parameter, local, attribute, or return annotation, including the items of `list[...]`,
`Sequence[...]`, `Iterable[...]`, `Iterator[...]`, `Generator[...]`, `dict[...]`,
`Mapping[...]`, `tuple[...]`, and `set[...]`; a constructor call; and what the object comes
from: a loop over such a container (`for model in models`), a subscript (`models[0]`,
`by_name["a"]`), unpacking (`model, _ = pair`), `dict` views and `get` / `pop`, `enumerate`,
`zip`, `reversed`, `sorted`, `iter`, `next`, `list` / `tuple` / `set`, `itertools.chain`, a
display, the items appended to a local list, or a comprehension or generator expression. A
method call or a `@property` / `cached_property` read has the return annotation of the
definition the receiver's class finds first along its MRO, as for a type checker (`typing.Self`
is the receiver's class); a copy (`copy.copy`, `copy.deepcopy`, `dataclasses.replace`,
`model_copy`) has its original's class, calling a `functools.partial` object returns what the
wrapped function returns, and `typing.cast` names the class. A variable rebound in a loop
(`node = node.parent`) or assigned on some paths only (a walrus inside `and` / `or`) has the
classes of the values reaching it; a value of two or three classes (`Model | Node`, from an
annotation or from different assignments) is each of them, and an `isinstance` check narrows it
in the code it guards (`if isinstance(x, Model): ...`, `if not isinstance(x, Model): return`,
also inside `and` / `or`). A value typed with a project `Protocol` is an instance of the project
classes that implement it structurally (having every member it defines; at most eight, counting
a class and not its subclasses). An object whose class heki cannot see (an unannotated parameter
or return, `Any`, a value of more than three classes) is not tied to the target.

A private helper (`_name`, or a comprehension, generator expression, or lambda scope) with
project callers hands the responsibility to its callers: the read is reported at every call
site of the first non-private callers above it, with the chain of calls as related
information. Reading a `@property` or `functools.cached_property` attribute calls its getter,
so a private getter (`ref._kids` returning `self.children`) hands its read to the functions
reading it. Reads in a class's own initializer on its own `self` are allowed, and so are reads
in a function that only runs inside allowed contexts (every path of callers above it starts in
an allowed reader or an exempt method), as for `MUT201`. One report stands for every read behind
its call (`sites` in JSON), as for `MUT201`. A read runs where the body holding it runs, as for
`MUT201`: a generator's reads where it is iterated, a coroutine's where it is awaited.

## Why is this bad?
Some state is only meaningful through the component that maintains it: an index that keeps a
derived view consistent, a store that resolves references lazily. Reading the raw attribute
elsewhere sees stale or partial data, and the bug only shows up for some inputs. The contract
states which functions may read it once in configuration, with no runtime cost.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.read-owners]]
name = "reference-children"
targets = ["Reference.children"]
allowed-readers = ["*GenerationIndex*"]
message = "read children through GenerationIndex instead"
```

```python
class Reference:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.children: list["Reference"] = []


class GenerationIndex:
    def children_of(self, ref: Reference) -> list[Reference]:
        return list(ref.children)  # allowed reader


def _kids(ref: Reference) -> list[Reference]:
    return ref.children


def render(ref: Reference) -> str:
    return ", ".join(map(str, _kids(ref)))  # MUT203: reads `Reference.children` via `_kids`
```

Use instead:
```python
def render(ref: Reference, index: GenerationIndex) -> str:
    return ", ".join(map(str, index.children_of(ref)))
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.read-owners]]`:
  - `name`: the contract name, shown in messages.
  - `targets`: `Class.attr` entries; globs and dotted suffixes match.
  - `allowed-readers`: functions allowed to read the targets, as dotted names or globs matched
    against the function's qualified name and its `Class.method` qualname.
  - `forbidden-readers`: when set, only reads by these functions are reported (matched like
    `allowed-readers`; `forbidden-readers = ["pkg.parser.*"]`: the parser layer must not read the
    targets); `allowed-readers` and `exempt-methods` stay exceptions inside them. A read is in
    scope when the reporting function or a private helper it hands the read through is
    forbidden.
  - `exempt-methods`: methods allowed to read the targets (`__repr__`, `__deepcopy__`); a plain
    name matches any function or method of that name, an entry with a dot or a glob is matched
    like `allowed-readers`.
  - `message`: the help of every report of the contract.
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`: also report the reads the contract cannot
    tie to a class, under `MUT206`.

Known limitation: a read through a parameter without a project-class annotation
(`def helper(ref): return ref.children`) is not seen, since the read object's class is unknown
there; unlike a write, a read is not handed to the caller that knows it. With
`unresolved = "report"`, `MUT206` reports it.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-param-mutation/

# readonly-param-mutation (MUT110)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Handing a `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `ReadOnly` parameter to a function that changes it in place (directly, through an alias, or through helpers).

## What it does
Checks functions that hand a parameter annotated as a read-only container to code that changes
it in place: a parameter annotated `Sequence[...]`, `Mapping[...]`, or `ReadOnly[...]` (also
inside `Optional`, `| None`, `Annotated`, and quotes), passed as itself or through a local alias
(`alias = items`) to a function that changes its argument in place (`items.sort()`,
`items.append(...)`, `table[key] = ...`), itself or through further helpers, any number of calls
deep.

The rule reports the call that hands the parameter over, with the calls down to the change as
related locations. A generator function changes what it is handed where its generator is
iterated (`for`, `list(...)`, a function iterating it), and is reported there; one that is
created and never iterated changes nothing.

It does not report:

- a change in the function itself (`items.append(1)`, `alias = items; alias.append(1)`): type
  checkers report it on the read-only type;
- a container inside the argument (`values["a"].append(1)` with
  `values: Mapping[str, list[int]]`): only the argument itself counts;
- a call that hands over a copy (`helper(list(items))`, `helper(dict(table))`);
- a helper parameter annotated with a mutable type (`list[int]`, `dict[str, int]`,
  `MutableSequence[int]`, `deque[int]`, ...): the type checker reports the argument;
- a helper parameter annotated read-only: that helper is checked in turn (its own handing over is
  reported, a change in its own body is a type error);
- variadic parameters (`*items: Sequence[int]`).

## Why is this bad?
A `Sequence` or `Mapping` annotation promises the caller that the function only reads its
argument, so callers pass their own lists and dictionaries, shared values, or tuples. A helper
that changes the argument in place breaks the promise: the caller's object changes behind its
back, or the call fails on a tuple. Type checkers trust the helper's signature, so an
unannotated or `Any` helper accepts the `Sequence` and hides the change.

## Example
```python
from collections.abc import Sequence


def sort_values(values):
    values.sort()


def median(values: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    sort_values(values)  # MUT110: reorders the caller's list
    return values[len(values) // 2]
```

Use instead:
```python
from collections.abc import Sequence


def median(values: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    ordered = sorted(values)
    return ordered[len(ordered) // 2]
```

If the helper is meant to change its argument, annotate its parameter with a mutable type
(`def sort_values(values: list[float]) -> None`): the type checker then shows the mismatch at
the call.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
No configuration: the rule reads standard `typing` declarations only.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-return-mutation/

# readonly-return-mutation (MUT202)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Mutating a shared object returned by a declared `readonly-returns` producer or `@lru_cache`, directly or through the functions that return it.

## What it does
Checks mutations of objects returned by a shared producer:

- functions decorated with `@functools.lru_cache` / `@functools.cache` (every caller receives
  the same object), also through an import alias (`lru_cache as _lru_cache`); a `cache`
  decorator the module defines itself is not one;
- producers declared in `[[tool.heki.readonly-returns]]`;
- functions that return a producer's value, or a part of it, on some path: a wrapper is a
  producer itself, without configuration, through any number of wrappers, property getters,
  and recursion.

Mutations through attributes, subscripts, container methods, in-place operators, and helpers
that mutate their argument (also run on a worker thread: `asyncio.to_thread(clear, shared)`) are
followed, also on the call result itself
(`schema_of(raw).items.append(x)`); a generator function mutates its argument only when its
generator is iterated. Copies end the protection: `copy.deepcopy(...)`,
`model.model_copy(deep=True)` (without `update=`, whose values Pydantic assigns to the copy by
reference), and the deep copy sanitizers of the ecosystem knowledge base clear it, shallow copies
(`copy.copy`, `.copy()`, `dataclasses.replace(...)`, `dict(...)`, `list(...)`, `tuple(...)`,
`set(...)`, `frozenset(...)`, displays that only unpack the value (`{**shared}`, `[*rows]`), a
sanitizer declared `copy-sanitizer = "shallow"`, and slices of builtin lists, other builtin
sequences, and values whose class heki cannot infer, `rows()[:]`) free the top level only: the
values below stay shared, so a helper rebinding an attribute of the copy (`b.name = "new"`)
changes nothing shared, and one changing the object an attribute holds (`b.tags.append(x)`, also
on its own shallow copy of the argument) does. A slice of an object of another known class may
be a view of it (`numpy`) and stays shared. A `copy()` method of a project class copies as
deeply as its body does: its result is shared only when the method returns a shared value. A
wrapper that returns a copy on one path and the shared value on another still returns a shared
value.

Filling a memo of the shared object, directly or in a method or helper it is handed to, is no
mutation: an in-place change of an attribute named as a cache or memo (`self._style_cache[k] =
v`, also through the methods of a cache object held there), a store under
`if k not in self._decoders:` or through `setdefault`, and a lazy
initialization (`if self._runtime is None: self._runtime = load()`) leave what the object
computes as it was.

## Why is this bad?
A cached return value is shared by every caller. Mutating it corrupts the cache for everyone
else, usually long after the mutation happened.

## Example
```python
from functools import lru_cache


@lru_cache(maxsize=32)
def schema(name: str) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    return {"fields": [name]}


def schema_of(name: str) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    return schema(name)


def extend(name: str) -> None:
    s = schema_of(name)
    s["fields"].append("extra")  # MUT202: mutates the cached object
```

Use instead:
```python
import copy


def extend(name: str) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    s = copy.deepcopy(schema_of(name))
    s["fields"].append("extra")
    return s
```

## Known limitations
- A shared value stored in an attribute (`self.kept = schema(...)`) and changed in another
  method is not followed.
- A generator's values and a coroutine's result (`await`) are not followed.
- A method call on a shared value whose class heki cannot resolve (a producer returning a type
  variable) is not followed; a wrapper with a concrete return annotation resolves it.
- A dict that also holds values of its own (`{**shared, "extra": []}`,
  `dict(shared, extra=[])`) or unpacks another mapping (`{**shared, **overrides}`) is not
  followed.
- A project method returning a part of a shared receiver (`return self._items[key]`) is not
  followed, nor is a `copy()` method of a project class that shares the receiver's values
  (`return Post(self.tags)`).

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.readonly-returns]]`: `name`, `producers` (function names or globs), `deep`
  (protect nested values too).


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-type-mutation/

# readonly-type-mutation (MUT108)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Opt-in · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Opt-in: changing in place a field that a standard type declares read-only (frozen dataclass / `NamedTuple` / `dataclass_transform` fields, `Final` / `ReadOnly` attributes, `ReadOnly` `TypedDict` keys), directly, through an alias, or in a helper.

## What it does
Checks in-place changes of containers held in fields that a standard type declares read-only,
which type checkers let through because they only stop rebinding:

- a field that holds a container in a `@dataclass(frozen=True)`, a `NamedTuple`, or a class that a
  PEP 681 `dataclass_transform(frozen_default=True)` builds (a decorator function, base class, or
  metaclass carrying it, unless the class passes `frozen=False`), also on an instance of a
  subclass: `config.tags.append(...)`;
- an attribute declared `Final[...]` (`self.items: Final[list[int]] = []` in `__init__`, or a
  `Final` field of a dataclass or `NamedTuple`) or `ReadOnly[...]`, and a `ReadOnly` key of a
  `TypedDict` (`movie["names"].append(...)`).

A `Sequence` / `Mapping` parameter handed to a helper that changes it is `MUT110`
(`readonly-param-mutation`), which shares this analysis.

Changes are followed through local aliases (`tags = config.tags; tags.append(...)`) and through
helpers, annotated or not and any number of calls deep, that change what they are handed: the
attribute itself (`add_default(config.tags)`) or the object holding it (`reset(config)`). Such a
change is reported at the call that hands the attribute or the object over, with the calls down
to the change as related locations. A helper that sees the object's type reports its own change
instead. A generator function changes what it is handed where its generator is iterated, and is
reported there; one that is created and never iterated changes nothing.

The rule does not report:

- rebinding or deleting the attribute (`config.tags = []`, `del config.tags`): type checkers
  report it;
- `object.__setattr__(...)`, `setattr(...)`, and `__dict__` writes: the deliberate way to set up a
  frozen instance, caches included;
- the class's own initialization: `__init__`, `__post_init__`, `__new__`, `model_post_init`,
  `__setstate__` changing their own instance, also through helpers that only run inside them;
- an instance the function constructs itself and fills before anyone else holds it
  (`index = Index({}, {}); index.names["a"] = 1`), directly or through a helper;
- fields declared `field(compare=False)` (state outside the instance's value, such as a cache);
  fields and attributes whose annotation is no container type (an object of a project class
  changes through its own methods); class variables (`ClassVar`); class-level constants of other
  classes; and module-level constants;
- a container inside the read-only one (`config.tables["a"].append(1)` with a frozen
  `tables: dict[str, list[int]]`): only the container in the read-only field counts.

Out of scope: `dataclass_transform`s defined outside the checked files, such as the frozen models
of `attrs` and Pydantic (heki does not analyze installed packages, so it cannot see the
transform); properties with a setter; `TypedDict` values read through `.get()`
(`movie.get("names")`); and objects whose class heki cannot see (an `Any` or unannotated
receiver).

## Why is this bad?
A frozen dataclass or a `NamedTuple` promises immutable instances, so code shares them freely: as
module-level defaults, in caches, or by handing the same value to several owners. An in-place
change of a container inside one is seen by every holder and changes the results of `==`. A
`Final` or `ReadOnly` declaration makes the same promise to the readers of the value. Type
checkers stop the rebinding, but not a change of the container inside, directly, through an
alias, or in a helper that receives a plain `list` or an unannotated value.

## Example
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


def add_default(tags):
    tags.append("default")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Config:
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)


def configure(config: Config) -> None:
    add_default(config.tags)  # MUT108: changes the frozen `Config.tags` in place
```

Use instead:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Config:
    tags: tuple[str, ...] = ()


def configure(config: Config) -> Config:
    return replace(config, tags=(*config.tags, "default"))
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["MUT108"]` (or `--extend-select MUT108`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `MUT` prefix does not enable it.
- No other configuration: the rule reads standard `typing` and `dataclasses` declarations only.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/set-dict-quadratic-merge/

# set-dict-quadratic-merge (OPT102)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` · Safe fix (`--fix`)

Unconditionally profitable `set`/`dict` quadratic merge (`{**d, ...}` with `d` first).

## What it does
Checks loops that rebuild a dict or set every iteration and rewrites them in place:

- `d = {**d, k: v}` → `d[k] = v`, or `d.update({...})` when the remaining entries have side
  effects;
- `d = {**d, **other}` → `d.update(other)`;
- `s = s | {e}` → `s |= {e}` (also `d = d | other` for dicts).

## Why is this bad?
Each rebuild copies the whole container, so the loop is quadratic. The in-place update is never
slower.

## Example
```python
def index(items: list[tuple[str, int]]) -> dict[str, int]:
    d = {}
    for k, v in items:
        d = {**d, k: v}
    return d
```

Use instead:
```python
def index(items: list[tuple[str, int]]) -> dict[str, int]:
    d = {}
    for k, v in items:
        d[k] = v
    return d
```

## Fix safety
Applied by `heki check --fix` only when proven safe, with the same obligations as `OPT101`
(exact builtin, unique, no live alias / iterator / view, evaluation order preserved), plus:

- the accumulator must be the leading `**` entry. `found = {**site, **found}` keeps the keys
  already in `found`, while `found.update(site)` would overwrite them, so it is never rewritten;
- for `|`, the right operand must be an exact `set` / `dict` (a subclass could make
  `__ror__` and `__ior__` disagree);
- the display inserts each entry before it evaluates the next one, and an insertion can run a
  key's `__eq__` (on a hash collision) or a mapping's `keys()` / `__getitem__`. Gathering
  several entries into one `d.update({...})` is applied only when the keys are `int` / `str` /
  `bytes` / `bool` / `float` values and the later entries are constants or local names;
  `d = {**d, **other}` with an unknown mapping `other` is not rewritten;
- an update that inserts several keys stops halfway when an insertion raises, where the display
  left `d` unchanged: it is not applied when an exception handler reads `d`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/summary-effect-regression/

# summary-effect-regression (MUT103)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Opt-in · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Interprocedural mutation/escape/effect regression against saved summary snapshot.

## What it does
Compares the interprocedural side effects of every public function with the summary snapshot
saved by `heki snapshot --write` (`.heki-summary-snapshot.json` at the project root), and reports
functions that gained one of:

- a mutated parameter (the function now changes an argument it receives);
- an escaping parameter (an argument is now stored in an attribute, a container, a global, or a
  variable of an enclosing function);
- a mutated `self` attribute;
- an execution effect (blocking network / database / subprocess / filesystem I/O, sleeping,
  client allocation, database queries), including effects reached through callees.

This rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select MUT103` or `extend-select = ["MUT103"]`.

## Why is this bad?
A pull request that makes a widely used helper start mutating its argument, or start doing
network I/O, often looks harmless in the diff of the helper and breaks callers far away. The
snapshot makes such effect regressions visible in review, the way a lock file makes dependency
changes visible.

## Example
```python
# snapshot taken while `add` was pure
def add(items: list[int], x: int) -> list[int]:
    return items + [x]
```

After an edit:
```python
def add(items: list[int], x: int) -> list[int]:  # MUT103: `add` now mutates parameter `items`
    items.append(x)
    return items
```

The report is on the function's `def` line, which is also where a suppression comment goes.

If the new effect is intended, refresh the snapshot with `heki snapshot --write` and commit it.
The refresh writes nothing while a file of the project cannot be read or parsed (it exits with
2): the snapshot would lose that module's entries. A module with a `.pyi` stub is recorded and
compared with the parameter names of its `.py` file.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["MUT103"]` enables the rule.
- The snapshot lives at `.heki-summary-snapshot.json`; `heki snapshot` prints it without writing.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-call/

# unresolved-guarded-call (MUT207)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Strict mode of a `call-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): calling a method named like a target on an object of unknown class.

## What it does
The strict mode of a `[[tool.heki.call-owners]]` contract that sets `unresolved = "report"`:
reports the calls outside the call owners that `MUT204` cannot tie to a target, so a clean
`MUT204` run says how much it did not check. A call of a method named like a target (the last
name of the target: `replace_reference` for `DataType.replace_reference`, also for a function or
class target) is reported once, at the call, when its receiver is of unknown class: an
unannotated parameter, a loop variable, the result of a call heki does not resolve, a value
annotated `Any` or `object` (unless an `isinstance` test around the call narrows it to a class),
or a protocol whose implementations heki cannot list (one without members, or implemented by
more than eight classes). `obj.replace_reference(...)`, a bound-method alias of it
(`replace = obj.replace_reference`), and `getattr(obj, "replace_reference")(...)` with a
constant name count. A call of a value of unknown origin (`callback()`) names nothing and is not
reported.

The rules of `MUT204` for what is allowed apply: allowed callers, exempt methods, the targets
themselves (they may call each other), functions that only run inside allowed callers, and
`forbidden-callers` (the calling function must be one). `MUT204` does not follow a call into a
parameter that its function does not type, so the callers decide for such a receiver: the call is
reported unless every caller path binds to it an instance of a project class whose method of that
name is no target: a class outside the target's family (`DataType` and its subclasses for
`DataType.replace_reference`) whose MRO finds no method the target names either (for the target
`reset`, any project class's `reset`; a `reset` inherited from a library base is none).

## Why is this bad?
`MUT204` reports a call only when every function it may call is a target, which needs the
receiver's class: a call on an object it cannot type is not seen, so a contract that passes says
nothing about those calls. Name-based checkers report them all; heki reports them separately,
under their own code, so they can be counted, ratcheted with a baseline, and reduced by
annotating the receivers, without mixing them with the violations `MUT204` proves.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.call-owners]]
name = "reference-mutators"
targets = ["DataType.replace_reference"]
allowed-callers = ["pkg.store.GenerationStore.*"]
unresolved = "report"
```

```python
def swap(data_type, ref) -> None:  # no annotation: heki cannot tell what `data_type` is
    data_type.replace_reference(ref)  # MUT207


def rename(text: str) -> str:
    return text.replace("a", "b")  # not reported: a `str`
```

Use instead:
```python
def swap(store: GenerationStore, data_type: DataType, ref: Reference) -> None:
    store.replace_data_type_ref(data_type, ref)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.call-owners]]`:
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`.
