  - `targets`, `allowed-callers`, `forbidden-callers`, `exempt-methods`, `message`: as for
    `MUT204`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-read/

# unresolved-guarded-read (MUT206)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Strict mode of a `read-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): reading an attribute named like a target on an object of unknown class.

## What it does
The strict mode of a `[[tool.heki.read-owners]]` contract that sets `unresolved = "report"`:
reports the reads outside the read owners that `MUT203` cannot tie to a target class, so a clean
`MUT203` run says how much it did not check. A read of an attribute named like a target attribute
(`children` for `Reference.children`, any name for `Reference.*`) is reported once, at the read,
when its object is of unknown class: an unannotated parameter, a loop variable, the result of a
call heki does not resolve, a value annotated `Any` or `object` (unless an `isinstance` test
around the read narrows it to a class), or a protocol whose implementations heki cannot list (one
without members, or implemented by more than eight classes). `obj.children`, a local alias of it,
`getattr(obj, "children")` with a constant name, and `obj.__dict__["children"]` count, as for
`MUT203`.

The rules of `MUT203` for what is allowed apply: allowed readers, exempt methods, functions that
only run inside allowed readers, and `forbidden-readers` (the reading function must be one).
`MUT203` does not follow a read into a parameter that its function does not type, so the callers
decide for such a parameter: the read is reported unless every caller path binds an instance of
a project class outside the targets' classes to it. A parameter some caller binds to an instance
of a target class is reported here: that read is a read of the target that no other rule sees.

## Why is this bad?
`MUT203` reports what it can back with a class: a read through an object it cannot type is not
followed, so a contract that passes says nothing about those reads. Name-based checkers report
them all; heki reports them separately, under their own code, so they can be counted, ratcheted
with a baseline, and reduced by annotating the objects, without mixing them with the violations
`MUT203` proves.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.read-owners]]
name = "reference-children"
targets = ["Reference.children"]
allowed-readers = ["*GenerationIndex*"]
unresolved = "report"
```

```python
def render(ref) -> str:  # no annotation: heki cannot tell what `ref` is
    return ", ".join(map(str, ref.children))  # MUT206


def size(ref: Reference) -> int:
    return len(ref.children)  # MUT203: a typed read
```

Use instead:
```python
def render(ref: Reference, index: GenerationIndex) -> str:
    return ", ".join(map(str, index.children_of(ref)))
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.read-owners]]`:
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`.
  - `targets`, `allowed-readers`, `forbidden-readers`, `exempt-methods`, `message`: as for
    `MUT203`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/

# unresolved-guarded-write (MUT205)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Strict mode of a `write-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): writing an attribute named like a target on an object of unknown class, or a computed attribute name on a guarded class.

## What it does
The strict mode of a `[[tool.heki.write-owners]]` contract that sets `unresolved = "report"`:
reports the writes outside the write owners that `MUT201` cannot tie to a target class, so a clean
`MUT201` run says how much it did not check. Two kinds of writes are reported, each once, at the
write:

- an attribute named like a target attribute (`fields` for `Model.fields`, any name for
  `Model.*`) written on an object of unknown class: an unannotated parameter that no project
  caller binds to an instance of a known class, a loop variable, the result of a call heki does
  not resolve, a value annotated `Any` or `object` (unless an `isinstance` test around the write
  narrows it to a class: `if isinstance(obj, Field): ...`), or a protocol whose implementations
  heki cannot list (one without members, or implemented by more than eight classes). Rebinding
  (`obj.fields = []`), deleting, `setattr` with a constant name, and changing the container the
  attribute holds (`obj.fields.append(x)`, `obj.meta["k"][name] = v`) count;
- an attribute name computed at run time written on an instance of a target class:
  `setattr(model, name, v)`, `model.__dict__[name] = v`, `model.__dict__.update(...)`, and a
  `__dict__` key in a name that is no constant: a module-level name bound twice, in a loop, or
  before a star import, or rebound by another module, a class attribute without `ClassVar` or
  `Final` (an instance may hold its own), one a subclass defines again or inherits first from
  another base, a `Final` field of a dataclass read on an instance (or on a class object with
  `slots=True` along the way), and one stored on its class, a subclass, or an instance outside
  the class body (`Model.KEY = "x"`).

The rules of `MUT201` for what is allowed apply: allowed writers, exempt methods, a class's own
initialization (`setattr(self, name, v)` in `__init__`), functions that only run inside allowed
writers, `forbidden-writers`, and, with `fresh-objects = "allow"`, writes that construct the object
they write. A parameter that every caller path binds to an object of a project class is not
reported: `MUT201` reports the write at those callers. A computed name written on an object of
unknown class is not reported (neither the class nor the attribute is known).

## Why is this bad?
`MUT201` reports what it can back with a class: a write through an object it cannot type is not
followed, so a contract that passes says nothing about those writes. Name-based checkers report
them all; heki reports them separately, under their own code, so they can be counted, ratcheted
with a baseline, and reduced by annotating the objects or naming the attributes with constants,
without mixing them with the violations `MUT201` proves.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.write-owners]]
name = "model-store"
targets = ["Model.fields"]
allowed-writers = ["Store.*"]
unresolved = "report"
```

```python
def touch(model) -> None:  # no annotation: heki cannot tell what `model` is
    model.fields = []  # MUT205


def fill(model: Model, name: str) -> None:
    setattr(model, name, [])  # MUT205: the attribute is computed at run time


def read_only(model: Model) -> int:
    return len(model.fields)  # not reported: a read
```

Use instead:
```python
def touch(model: Model) -> None:
    model.fields = []  # now `MUT201`, outside `Store.*`
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.write-owners]]`:
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`.
  - `targets`, `allowed-writers`, `forbidden-writers`, `exempt-methods`, `fresh-objects`,
    `message`: as for `MUT201`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unretained-async-task/

# unretained-async-task (EFF107)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Opt-in · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Opt-in: an `asyncio.create_task` result bound to a local variable but never awaited, returned, or stored.

## What it does
Checks for the result of `asyncio.create_task(...)`, `asyncio.ensure_future(...)`, or
`loop.create_task(...)` that is bound to a local variable but never kept: never awaited,
returned, yielded, stored (in an attribute, a container, a global, or an enclosing scope),
passed to a call (`tasks.add(task)`, `asyncio.gather(task)`), captured by a closure, cancelled,
or asked for its result.

The factories are known by what their names are bound to: an import alias
(`from asyncio import create_task as spawn`) counts, a project function named `create_task` does
not. `loop.create_task` needs a receiver known to be an event loop (`asyncio.get_running_loop()`,
`get_event_loop()`, `new_event_loop()`, or an annotated `asyncio.AbstractEventLoop`).

It does not report:

- a call whose result is discarded (`asyncio.create_task(work())` as a statement): that is
  Ruff's `RUF006`;
- `asyncio.TaskGroup.create_task`, which keeps its tasks;
- receivers of unknown type;
- an argument known not to be a coroutine, from which no new task is made: the result of a
  project function that is a plain `def` or a generator function without decorators other than
  `staticmethod`, `classmethod`, `abstractmethod`, or `override` (`create_task` raises
  `TypeError` on what it returns, and `ensure_future` returns a future it is handed unchanged),
  or a value typed as a future or a task (`loop.run_in_executor(...)`, `loop.create_future()`,
  `asyncio.gather(...)`, `asyncio.wrap_future(...)`, `executor.submit(...)`, or an annotated
  `asyncio.Future`). An argument of unknown kind (a parameter, an awaitable, a constructed
  object, the result of a decorated function) may be a coroutine and is reported. The argument
  is the first positional one or the one passed as `coro=` / `coro_or_future=`.

A method of the task that is passed to a call, stored, or returned keeps the task too, because
the bound method holds it: `self.addCleanup(task.cancel)`, `loop.call_later(1, task.cancel)`,
`self.stop = task.cancel`.
Being only the receiver of `add_done_callback(...)` or `set_name(...)` does not keep the task:
the callback does not hold it strongly.

## Why is this bad?
The event loop keeps only a weak reference to a task. Once the function that created it returns,
nothing references the task any more, and it can be garbage-collected before it finishes: the
work silently stops halfway.

## Example
```python
import asyncio


async def handle(event: dict[str, str]) -> None:
    task = asyncio.create_task(notify(event))  # EFF107
    task.add_done_callback(log_failure)
```

Use instead:
```python
import asyncio

background_tasks: set[asyncio.Task[None]] = set()


async def handle(event: dict[str, str]) -> None:
    task = asyncio.create_task(notify(event))
    background_tasks.add(task)
    task.add_done_callback(background_tasks.discard)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["EFF107"]` (or `--extend-select EFF107`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `EFF` prefix does not enable it.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/write-owner-violation/

# write-owner-violation (MUT201)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Writing a guarded attribute/container (directly, via alias, or via helper) outside declared `write-owners`.

## What it does
Checks writes to attributes and containers that a `[[tool.heki.write-owners]]` contract
reserves for a set of allowed writer functions. A write is reported when it happens outside the
allowed writers:

- directly (`model.fields = [...]`, `model.fields.append(...)`, `del model.fields`);
- through a local alias (`fields = model.fields; fields.append(...)`);
- through `setattr(model, "fields", ...)` / `object.__setattr__` or `model.__dict__["fields"]`,
  also with a string constant for the name (`model.__dict__[FIELDS_KEY]`, imported or not):
  a module-level name declared `Final` or bound once in its module and rebound by no other, or
  a class-body name declared `ClassVar` or `Final` and bound once (`self.KEY`, `cls.KEY`,
  `Model.KEY`), which every subclass of the object's class finds along its MRO in the same
  class (none defines it again or lists another base defining it first,
  `class Child(Other, Model)`) and no code stores on the class, a subclass, or an instance
  (`Model.KEY = "x"`; another module may store it on the defining class only for a `Final`
  one); on an instance of a protocol, every class implementing it must hold the same constant.
  A `Final` name of a dataclass (or of a class a `dataclass_transform` builds) is a field, which
  each instance holds itself (`Keys("x").KEY`): it names an attribute only when read on the
  class object of a dataclass whose default no class along the way replaces (one with
  `slots=True` or built by a transform);
- into the entries of the container the attribute holds (`model.meta["kw"][name] = v`,
  `model.meta["kw"].append(v)`, through a local alias of the entry): an `item_mut` write;
- through a helper that mutates the container or object it receives (`helper(model.fields)`),
  reported once at the outermost call site. A helper that sees the object's class (an annotated
  parameter, `self` of a method) reports its own write instead, so a write it routes through
  the allowed writers stays allowed for its callers; a helper handed the value of an attribute
  (`helper(field.data_type)`) writes that attribute only when it changes the value in place,
  and otherwise writes the value's own attributes. A helper that does not see the class and
  only hands the value on to an allowed writer or an exempt method writes inside the owner.

A target names a class and an attribute; it covers the class's subclasses too (the target's
class family). A target can also name one entry of the container an attribute holds,
`Class.attr["key"]`: it matches the writes of that key (`field.extras["init"] = v`,
`field.extras[INIT]` with a string constant, `field.extras.pop("init")`,
`del field.extras["init"]`, `field.extras["init"].append(v)`), not a write of the whole
container (`field.extras = {}`, `field.extras.update(...)`) or with a computed key, which are
writes of `Class.attr`. When a contract names both a container and one of its entries, a write of
the entry is reported once, under the entry.

The written object's class is the one heki infers for it, with annotations as hints: a
parameter, local, attribute, or return annotation, including the items of `list[...]`,
`Sequence[...]`, `Iterable[...]`, `Iterator[...]`, `Generator[...]`, `dict[...]`,
`Mapping[...]`, `tuple[...]`, and `set[...]`; a constructor call; and what the object comes
from: a loop over such a container (`for model in models`), a subscript (`models[0]`,
`by_name["a"]`), unpacking (`model, _ = pair`), `dict` views and `get` / `pop`, `enumerate`,
`zip`, `reversed`, `sorted`, `iter`, `next`, `list` / `tuple` / `set`, `itertools.chain`, a
display, the items appended to a local list, or a comprehension or generator expression. A
method call or a `@property` / `cached_property` read has the return annotation of the
definition the receiver's class finds first along its MRO, as for a type checker (`typing.Self`
is the receiver's class); a copy (`copy.copy`, `copy.deepcopy`, `dataclasses.replace`,
`model_copy`) has its original's class, calling a `functools.partial` object returns what the
wrapped function returns, and `typing.cast` names the class. A variable rebound in a loop
(`node = node.parent`) or assigned on some paths only (a walrus inside `and` / `or`) has the
classes of the values reaching it; a value of two or three classes (`Model | Node`, from an
annotation or from different assignments) is each of them, and an `isinstance` check narrows it
in the code it guards (`if isinstance(x, Model): ...`, `if not isinstance(x, Model): return`,
also inside `and` / `or`). A value typed with a project `Protocol` is an instance of the protocol
and of the project classes that implement it structurally (having every member it defines; at
most eight, counting a class and not its subclasses), also when it is handed to a helper that
does not type it: a target on the protocol and one on an implementation both cover its writes. An
object whose class heki cannot see (an unannotated parameter or return, `Any`, a value of more
than three classes, a protocol without members or with more implementations) is not tied to the
target.

A private helper (`_name`, or a comprehension, generator expression, or lambda scope) with
project callers hands the responsibility to its callers: the write is reported at the call
sites of the first non-private callers, with the chain of calls as related information. A
private function that only its own recursion calls (`_walk` calling itself, handed out as a
callback) has no such caller and reports its writes itself. One
report stands for every write behind that call (`sites` in JSON), so a Ratchet baseline counts a
second write inside a recorded helper. A write reached through an allowed writer on one path and
around it on another (or through a forbidden writer on one path only) is reported for the path
the contract does not allow.
Reading a `@property` or `functools.cached_property` attribute calls its getter, so a private
getter hands its writes to the functions reading it; a read never calls a property's setter.

A write runs where the body holding it runs. Calling a generator function only creates the
generator: its writes run where it is iterated (as for `EFF101`), so a generator created by an
allowed writer and iterated elsewhere writes elsewhere, and one handed to an allowed writer that
iterates it writes inside the owner. A generator that is created and never iterated writes
nothing. A coroutine that is never awaited or driven at a project call (handed to
`asyncio.create_task`, `ensure_future`, `gather`, ...) runs on the event loop: a private one
reports its own writes instead of handing them to the function that created it. Functions run on
another thread by an offloading decorator (`@sync_to_async`, ...) are not followed either.

A function that only runs inside the owner's operations is not reported either: it has project
callers, and every path of callers above it starts in an allowed writer, an exempt method, or
the class's own initialization (a mutator method that only the store and `__init__` call). A
function without project callers, one that is also called from anywhere else, or one reached
only through a cycle of other functions stays reported.

A class's own initialization is allowed: a write inside an initializer (`__init__`,
`__post_init__`, `__new__`, `model_post_init`, `__setstate__`) of a class of the target's
family is not reported when the written object is the initializer's own `self`, whether it
writes it directly, through a local alias, through `super().__init__()`, or through helpers it
passes `self` to (`self._init_fields()`, `_setup(self)`). An object that may be `self`
(`self if flag else other`) gets the benefit of the doubt. Writes to objects that are provably
not `self` stay reported: another parameter, an attribute of `self`.

A write that constructs the object it writes is allowed too (`fresh-objects = "allow"`, the
default): the object was allocated in the same call chain, by calling its class, by copying
(`copy.copy`, `copy.deepcopy`, `dataclasses.replace`, `.copy()`, `.model_copy()`), or by a
project function that returns such an object, and nothing else can hold it yet: no store into
another object, a container, a global, or a closure, no `yield`, and no call that may keep it
ran before the write. A project function keeps an object it stores, yields, or hands to code
heki does not follow or to a function that keeps it; reading or writing it keeps nothing. Writes
that a helper makes to a new object its caller hands it count as well. A shallow copy shares its
containers with the original, so only rebinding its attributes constructs it
(`copied.data_types = [...]`); `copied.data_types.append(x)` changes the original's list and is
reported. `fresh-objects = "report"` reports these writes like any other.

## Why is this bad?
Large code bases often have one component that owns a piece of shared state (a store, a
registry, a cache). Writes from anywhere else bypass its invariants and make bugs that depend
on call order. The contract states the ownership once in configuration, with no runtime cost
and no decorators.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.write-owners]]
name = "model-store"
targets = ["Model.fields"]
allowed-writers = ["Store.*"]
exempt-methods = ["__deepcopy__"]
message = "use Store.add_field() instead"
```

```python
class Model:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.fields: list[str] = []  # allowed: the class's own initialization

    def __deepcopy__(self, memo: dict) -> "Model":
        new = Model()
        new.fields = list(self.fields)  # allowed: exempt method
        return new


class Store:
    def add_field(self, model: Model, name: str) -> None:
        model.fields.append(name)  # allowed writer


def parse(model: Model) -> None:
    model.fields.append("id")  # MUT201: outside `Store.*`
```

Use instead:
```python
def parse(model: Model, store: Store) -> None:
    store.add_field(model, "id")
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.write-owners]]`:
  - `name`: the contract name, shown in messages.
  - `targets`: `Class.attr` entries; globs and dotted suffixes match (`Model.fields`,
    `pkg.model.Model.*`).
  - `allowed-writers`: functions allowed to write the targets, as dotted names or globs matched
    against the function's qualified name and its `Class.method` qualname (`Store.*`,
    `pkg.parser.generation.*`).
  - `forbidden-writers`: when set, only writes by these functions are reported (matched like
    `allowed-writers`, `pkg.render.*`); `allowed-writers` and `exempt-methods` stay exceptions
    inside them. A write is in scope when a function on its chain (the reporting function, the
    private helpers it hands the write through, or the writer) is forbidden.
  - `exempt-methods`: construction and copy methods allowed to write the targets. A plain name
    (`__deepcopy__`, `copy_deep`) matches any function or method of that name; an entry with a
    dot or a glob (`Model.copy_deep`, `create_*`) is matched like `allowed-writers`. A write is
    allowed when any function on its chain (the writer and the private helpers between) is an
    allowed writer or an exempt method.
  - `message`: the help of every report of the contract (`use Store.add_field() instead`).
  - `forbid-cached-property-on`: classes on which a `@cached_property` is itself reported.
  - `fresh-objects`: `"allow"` (default) or `"report"`: whether writes that construct the object
    they write are reported.
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`: also report the writes the contract
    cannot tie to a class, under `MUT205`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/write-without-invalidation/

# write-without-invalidation (MUT109)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · Severity `error` · No automatic fix

Writing a declared `invalidation` target (directly, via alias, or via helper) without reaching one of its invalidators on every path to the function's return.

## What it does
Checks writes to attributes declared in an `[[tool.heki.invalidation]]` contract: after the
write, every path to the function's normal return must call one of the contract's
`invalidators` (the call that announces the change to whatever derives facts from the
attribute: an index, a cache, a revision counter).

A write is followed through local aliases, container methods (`.append()`, `[k] = v`),
`setattr` / `__dict__`, and helpers: a private helper that writes without announcing the change
passes the obligation to its callers, and the call of such a helper must be announced like a
direct write (one report at the call stands for every write behind it, and a Ratchet baseline
counts each of them: `sites` in JSON output). A private generator's writes run where it is
iterated, or inside the function it is handed to that iterates it, and are reported there. A
helper changing an argument it does not type (`_add(xs): xs.append(1)` called as
`_add(model.items)`, `_set(o): o.x = 1` called as `_set(model)`) writes the field or instance
the caller binds to it: the caller's call is the write, once for each class the instance may be
(a protocol-typed one is the protocol and each implementation), against that class's targets.
An invalidator counts when it is called directly, in each branch, or through
calls (a helper that calls an invalidator on every path to its own return), also behind a
boolean flag set after the write (`changed = True ... if changed: notify()`); one called before
the write does not count, nor an `async` invalidator that is not awaited. A call of a method
announces the change when every implementation it may run does (the definition the receiver's
class finds and the overrides of its subclasses; an `@abstractmethod` never runs): calling
`hook.done()` on a `Hook` whose own `done` does nothing announces nothing, whatever a subclass
does.

It does not report:

- a function named in `exempt-writers` (the owner's operations announce or batch the change
  themselves), nor calls from one;
- writes to objects that did not exist before the call: the class's own initialization (an
  initializer writing its own `self`, directly or through a helper it hands `self` to; an
  object reached through `self`'s attributes, such as a model it was given, existed before)
  and objects the function constructs or copies, which
  nothing has derived facts from yet; objects it gets from a call are left alone too, since
  heki cannot tell whether they are new;
- a function whose every caller announces the change after calling it (invalidation in bulk by
  a caller, at any distance);
- paths that leave the function by raising: exception edges are not followed and only normal
  returns count.

## Why is this bad?
Code that keeps derived facts (an index of a model graph, a memo, a cached rendering) relies on
every writer announcing its change. A writer that forgets it on one path leaves the derived
facts stale: nothing fails at the write, and the wrong value shows up later, on an input that
takes that path.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.invalidation]]
name = "graph-index"
targets = ["DataType.data_types", "DataModel.fields"]
invalidators = ["GenerationStore.note_changed_models", "GenerationStore.refresh_now"]
exempt-writers = ["pkg.parser.generation.*"]
message = "tell the store which models changed"
```

```python
def narrow(store: GenerationStore, owner: DataModel, node: DataType, item: DataType) -> None:
    node.data_types = [item]  # MUT109: the path where `owner.fields` is empty tells nobody
    if owner.fields:
        store.note_changed_models(owner)
```

Use instead:
```python
def narrow(store: GenerationStore, owner: DataModel, node: DataType, item: DataType) -> None:
    node.data_types = [item]
    store.note_changed_models(owner)
```

## Known limitations
- Deferred modes: a context manager whose exit announces the change
  (`with store.defer_refresh(): ...`) is not followed. List such deferred writers in
  `exempt-writers`, or call the invalidator.
- A generator a function returns is iterated by its callers: its writes are not followed there.
  A helper that announces the change counts when its body runs at its call; a generator may be
  iterated only in part, so an invalidator inside one does not count.
- Two different helpers that each announce the change on one branch are not combined (two
  direct invalidator calls are); a helper counts when it announces the change on all of its own
  paths.
- A branch is read as two feasible paths unless its condition is a constant or a boolean flag
  the path sets (`changed = True` after the write, then `if changed: notify()`): a helper whose
  result says whether it wrote (`if model.unbind(names): notify()`) is not followed.
- Callers heki cannot resolve (a function passed as a callable, a method of a class held in a
  variable) are not seen: a public function without visible callers announces its own changes
  or is listed in `exempt-writers`, like a construction method; a private helper without
  visible callers is not checked.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix: where to announce the change is a design decision.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.invalidation]]`: `name`, `targets` (`Class.attr`, subclasses included),
  `invalidators` (functions or methods), `exempt-writers`, `message`. The diagnostic target is
  `<name>:<target>` (`graph-index:DataModel.fields`): two contracts naming one write are two
  reports.
